punctuated:
胡宗憲〔貫直隸徽州府績溪縣民籍，縣學附學生，治書經，字汝欽，行一，十二十七，九月二十六日生〕。曾祖若川〔壽官〕，祖崑〔義官〕，父尚仁，母方氏。具慶下，兄宗虞，弟宗廷，娶章氏。應天府鄉試第一百名，會試第八十四名。

蕭軾〔貫江西吉安府吉水縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字仲敬，行五，年三十一，五月十六日生〕。曾祖世禎，祖延通〔贈刑部主事〕，父晚〔按察司副使〕，母楊氏〔封安人〕。具慶下，兄幹，弟轍〔貢士〕，娶胡氏。江西鄉試第八十一名，會試第二百七十七名。

諸敬之〔貫浙江紹興府餘姚縣民籍，縣學附學生，治易經，字守禮，行三，年三十二，正月二十七日生〕。曾祖琳，祖永言，父巽，母徐氏。重慶下，兄桂，弟學之，娶王氏。浙江鄉試第三十四名，會試第二百九十九名。

譚大初〔貫廣東南雄府始興縣民籍，府學生，治詩經，字宗元，行二，年三十五，九月三十日生〕。曾祖遜〔縣丞〕，祖昇，父驥〔訓科〕，嫡母劉氏，生母劉氏。慈侍下，兄大中〔訓科〕，娶陳氏。廣東鄉試第七十五名，會試第二百四十六名。
translation_en:
Hu Zongxian, registered in a civilian household in Jixi County, Huizhou Prefecture, Zhili, was an attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Ruqin; he ranked first in his family and was aged twenty-seven [?; the age wording is garbled], born on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Ruochuan, an honorary official for longevity; his grandfather was Kun, an honorary official for meritorious contributions; his father was Shangren, and his mother was née Fang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Zongyu and his younger brother Zongting. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed one hundredth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xiao Shi, registered in a civilian household in Jishui County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zhongjing; he ranked fifth in his family and was aged thirty-one, born on the sixteenth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Shizhen; his grandfather was Yantong, posthumously appointed a secretary in the Ministry of Justice; his father was Wan, a surveillance vice commissioner; and his mother was née Yang, granted the title Lady of Peace. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Gan and his younger brother Che, a tribute scholar. He married a woman née Hu. He placed eighty-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and two hundred seventy-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Jingzhi, registered in a civilian household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was an attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Shouli; he ranked third in his family and was aged thirty-two, born on the twenty-seventh day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Lin, his grandfather Yongyan, his father Xun, and his mother née Xu. Parents and grandparents were living. His elder brother was Gui and his younger brother Xuezhi. He married a woman née Wang. He placed thirty-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and two hundred ninety-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tan Dachu, registered in a civilian household in Shixing County, Nanxiong Prefecture, Guangdong, was a prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Zongyuan; he ranked second in his family and was aged thirty-five, born on the thirtieth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Xun, a county vice magistrate; his grandfather was Sheng; and his father was Ji, a medical instructor. His legal mother and birth mother were both née Liu. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Dazhong, a medical instructor. He married a woman née Chen. He placed seventy-fifth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and two hundred forty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

punctuated:
徐鶴齡〔貫浙江杭州府海寧縣軍籍，府學增廣生，治易經，字仁甫，行一，年三十一，正月二十六日生〕。曾祖慶，祖蘭，父文卿〔冠帶生員〕，母王氏。重慶下，弟鶴翔、鶴鳴、鶴生、鶴年，娶沈氏，繼娶孫氏。浙江鄉試第五十九名，會試第二百四十七名。

萬文彩〔貫雲南臨安衛官籍，江西南昌縣人，國子生，治詩經，字國華，行二，年三十二，三月十一日生〕。曾祖俊，祖昂，父祚〔八品散官〕，母賈氏。慈侍下，兄言策〔貢士〕、文奎，弟文光，娶何氏。雲貴鄉試第三十一名，會試第二百八十二名。

邵梗〔貫浙江杭州府仁和縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字良用，行三，年三十六，二月三十日生〕。曾祖惟政〔贈文林郎、大理寺評事〕，祖琮〔按察司副使，進階三品〕，父𨺢，母陳氏。嚴侍下，弟楷、椿、槐、桂、桐、檟、榴、梓，娶趙氏。浙江鄉試第五十一名，會試第二百九十二名。

李僅可〔貫直隸廣平府清河縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字子與，行一，年三十五，正月初三日生〕。曾祖祥，祖璽，父隆，母閻氏。具慶下，弟學可、許可，娶張氏。順天府鄉試第三十一名，會試第一百二十七名。
translation_en:
Xu Heling, courtesy name Renfu, was registered in a military household in Haining County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. An additional student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-one, and born on the twenty-sixth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qing; his grandfather, Lan; his father, Wenqing, a government student granted the cap and girdle of official status; and his mother, née Wang. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Hexiang, Heming, Hesheng, and Henian. He married a woman née Shen and subsequently a woman née Sun. He placed fifty-ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 247th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Wencai, courtesy name Guohua, was registered in an official household of Lin'an Guard, Yunnan, and was originally from Nanchang County, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the eleventh day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jun; his grandfather, Ang; his father, Zuo, an eighth-rank titular official; and his mother, née Jia. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Yance, a tribute scholar, and Wenkui; his younger brother was Wenguang. He married a woman née He. He placed thirty-first in the Yunnan–Guizhou Provincial Examination and 282nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shao Geng, courtesy name Liangyong, was registered in a civilian household in Renhe County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was third in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the thirtieth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather, Weizheng, was posthumously granted the title Gentleman for Service and the office of Case Reviewer in the Court of Judicial Review. His grandfather, Cong, was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner, advanced to the third rank. His father was 𨺢 [reading uncertain], and his mother was née Chen. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Kai, Chun, Huai, Gui, Tong, Jia, Liu, and Zi. He married a woman née Zhao. He placed fifty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 292nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Jinke, courtesy name Ziyu, was registered in a civilian household in Qinghe County, Guangping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-five, and born on the third day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xiang; his grandfather, Xi; his father, Long; and his mother, née Yan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Xueke and Xuke. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed thirty-first in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 127th in the Metropolitan Examination.

羅崇奎〔貫江西南昌府南昌縣，民籍，國子生，治易經，字子文，行八，年三十一，五月十三日生〕。曾祖九錫〔義官〕，祖貢任，父大輔，母賈氏。慈侍下，兄崇貞、崇進，弟崇信、崇睿、崇簡、崇明、崇震，娶徐氏。江西鄉試第二十一名，會試第二十七名。

陳珂〔貫直隸涿鹿左衛，官籍，順天府薊州遵化縣人，州學附學生，治書經，字仲聲，行六，年二十八，七月二十四日生〕。曾祖玉〔昭勇將軍指揮使〕，祖廣〔昭勇將軍指揮使〕，父淵〔戶部員外郎〕，母郭氏〔封安人〕。永感下，兄珮〔昭勇將軍指揮使〕、瑞〔七品散官〕、珍〔七品散官〕，弟琨、璜、瑤、珙，娶王氏。順天府鄉試第一百五名，會試第一百八十三名。

孟養性〔貫山東濟南府齊河縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字存甫，行一，年三十，十一月十九日生〕。曾祖昉，祖璉，父宗儒〔監生〕，母楊氏。嚴侍下，娶趙氏。山東鄉試第四十四名，會試第一百九十八名。

阮朝策〔貫湖廣黃州府麻城縣，民籍，國子生，治春秋，字子定，行七，年三十八，八月十八日生〕。曾祖剛〔縣丞〕，祖大用〔壽官〕，父圭〔贈承德郎〕，前母賀氏，母蔡氏〔贈安人〕。永感下，兄朝陽〔貢士〕、朝東〔按察司提學副使〕、朝南、朝端、朝隨〔貢士〕、朝士、朝儀〔同知〕、朝倚、朝任，娶梅氏。湖廣鄉試第八名，會試第一百十名。
translation_en:
Luo Chongkui, registered in Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Ziwen. He was eighth in birth order, aged thirty-one, and born on the thirteenth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Jiuxi, an honorary official recognized for public benefactions; his grandfather was Gongren; his father was Dafu; and his mother was née Jia. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Chongzhen and Chongjin; his younger brothers were Chongxin, Chongrui, Chongjian, Chongming, and Chongzhen. His wife was née Xu. He placed twenty-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and twenty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Ke was registered in an official household in Zhuolu Left Guard, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Zunhua County, Jizhou, Shuntian Prefecture. He was an attached student of the subprefectural school and specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zhongsheng. He was sixth in birth order, aged twenty-eight, and born on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather Yu and grandfather Guang both held the prestige title General of Manifest Courage and served as Guard Commanders. His father, Yuan, was a Vice Director in the Ministry of Revenue; his mother, née Guo, was invested with the title Lady of Tranquility. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Pei, a Guard Commander with the prestige title General of Manifest Courage, and Rui and Zhen, both holders of seventh-rank prestige titles. His younger brothers were Kun, Huang, Yao, and Gong. His wife was née Wang. He placed 105th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 183rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Meng Yangxing, registered in Qihe County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was a county-school student. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Cunfu. He was first in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the nineteenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Fang; his grandfather was Lian; his father was Zongru, a student of the Directorate of Education; and his mother was née Yang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His wife was née Zhao. He placed forty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 198th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ruan Chaoce, registered in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Ziding. He was seventh in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the eighteenth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather Gang was a County Vice Magistrate; his grandfather Dayong held an honorary title granted for longevity; and his father Gui was posthumously awarded the title Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. His father's former wife was née He; his mother, née Cai, was posthumously awarded the title Lady of Tranquility. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Chaoyang, a tribute scholar; Chaodong, an Education Intendant serving as Vice Commissioner of a Provincial Surveillance Commission; Chaonan; Chaoduan; Chaosui, a tribute scholar; Chaoshi; Chaoyi, a Vice Prefect; Chaoyi; and Chaoren. His wife was née Mei. He placed eighth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 110th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhou Shan, registered in Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Ziren. He ranked first among his brothers, was aged forty-eight, and was born on the twelfth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhongjie; his grandfather, Yu; his father, Rong; and his mother, née Wu. His mother was living and his father deceased. He married a woman née Xu. He placed 128th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 260th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Yu, registered in Wan’an County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Weishi. He ranked first among his brothers, was aged twenty-seven, and was born on the seventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shouyue; his grandfather, Ziyun, held an honorary official title for philanthropy; his father was Shiyou; and his mother was née Liao. His parents and members of the grandparental generation were living. His younger brothers were Ting, Xiao, Zhan, and Ji. He married a woman née Liu. He placed twenty-fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and twenty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ou Sixian, registered in Jizhou, Shuntian Prefecture, belonged to a civilian household and was originally from Lianjiang County, Fujian. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Xifu. He ranked fifth among his brothers, was aged thirty-five, and was born on the seventh day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bao, posthumously granted the title of Director in the Ministry of Revenue; his grandfather was Jun; his father was Hongde, an Assistant Prefect promoted to the prestige title Gentleman for Receiving Virtue; and his mother, née Meng, was granted the title Lady of Peace. Both his parents were living. His elder brothers were Silian, who held an honorary official title for philanthropy; Sicheng, Right Assistant Judge in the Court of Judicial Review; and Sixiao. His younger brothers were Siqi, who held an honorary official title for philanthropy; Sichun; Siwan; and Siqian. He married a woman née Jia. He placed sixtieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 262nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Jie, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was a prefectural government school student. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Tongqing. He ranked nineteenth among his brothers, was aged thirty-two, and was born on the thirteenth day of the intercalary first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cha, posthumously granted the prestige title Grand Master for Upright Service and the title Vice Director in the Ministry of Personnel; his grandfather was Zan, Left Administration Vice Commissioner in a Provincial Administration Commission; his father was Bao; and his mother was née Weng. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Lu, Xi, and Cao. He married a woman née Lin. He placed sixty-fifth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 305th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:

His courtesy name was Ziyuan; he ranked second in birth order, was aged thirty-four, and was born on the twenty-second day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Qin, an honorary official for public service; his grandfather was Luan, an honorary official for longevity; his father was Hua, and his mother was née Zhao. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yingjie, and his younger brothers were Yingxia, Yingqiu, and Yingdong. His wife was née Wang. He placed fifty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and sixty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Chong, registered in a civilian household in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Yuanxun; he ranked second in birth order, was aged thirty, and was born on the fifth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Pufang, an Instructor in Daoist Arts; his grandfather was Tang; his father was Wenyu, a government student granted the cap and girdle of official status; and his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Cai, a Judge, and his younger brothers were Zai, Nan, Mei, and Le. His wife was née Zou. He placed thirty-eighth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 202nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Yaori, registered in a civilian household in Luyi County, Guide Subprefecture, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Mingshi; he ranked third in birth order, was aged thirty-seven, and was born on the twenty-first day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Zhi, a Guard Registrar; his grandfather was Ji; his father was Cong, a Keeper of the Seal; his mother was née Pu, and his stepmother was née Luo. His father alone was living. His elder brothers were Yaochun and Yaonian, and his younger brothers were Yaoshi, Yaochen, and Yaojie. His wife was née Wan. He placed ninth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 173rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wei Mengxian, registered in a civilian household in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Liangfu; he ranked tenth in birth order, was aged twenty-nine, and was born on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Da, his grandfather was Ying, and his father was Chun. His father's former wife was née Wang, and his mother was née Zhu. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Mengbu, and his wife was née Zhu. He placed seventy-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and seventy-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

張玶〔貫直隸河間府景州東光縣民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字子珍，行一，年三十四，六月十九日生〕。曾祖薦，祖安，父慶，母息氏。永感下，娶王氏，繼娶莊氏。順天府鄉試第一百十四名，會試第八十二名。

朱鵠〔貫廣西桂林府陽朔縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字秉直，行九，年三十二，正月初一日生〕。曾祖龍光，祖聲〔府經歷，贈刑部員外郎〕，父璧〔監生〕，母容氏。永感下，兄鸞〔知縣〕、鵬〔知縣〕、鷺、鶚〔監生〕、鵾、鴻、鷙、鶉，娶王氏。廣西鄉試第二十名，會試第一百十七名。
translation_en:
Gu Qiao 谷嶠, courtesy name Weisheng, was registered in an officer household of the Xingzhou Front Garrison Guard in Zhili and came from Xi County, Henan. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the twenty-third day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather Liang was an Assistant Commander; his grandfather was Yong, his father Xuan, and his mother née Dong. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Luan, and his wife was née Yang. He placed twenty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 303rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wen Xin 温新, courtesy name Boming, was registered in an officer household of the Luoyang Central Escort Guard in Henan and came from Yidu County, Shandong. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged forty-eight, and born on the twelfth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather Quan, grandfather Hou, and father Sheng were all Vice Commanders. His mother, née Wang, was granted the title of Lady (shuren); his stepmother was née Zhang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His younger brothers were Xiu, a Battalion Commander, and Xi. His wife was née Wang. He placed second in the Henan Provincial Examination and 316th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Ping 張玶, courtesy name Zizhen, was registered in a civilian household in Dongguang County, Jingzhou, Hejian Prefecture, Zhili. A county school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the nineteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jian, his grandfather An, his father Qing, and his mother née Xi. Both parents were deceased. His wife was née Wang; he subsequently married a woman née Zhuang. He placed 114th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Hu 朱鵠, courtesy name Bingzhi, was registered in a civilian household in Yangshuo County, Guilin Prefecture, Guangxi. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes, he was ninth in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the first day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Longguang. His grandfather Sheng was a Prefectural Registrar, posthumously granted the title of Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice. His father Bi was an Imperial University student, and his mother was née Rong. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Luan and Peng, both County Magistrates; Lu; E, an Imperial University student; Kun; Hong; Zhi; and Chun. His wife was née Wang. He placed twentieth in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and 117th in the Metropolitan Examination.

林大有〔貫廣東潮州府潮陽縣民籍，國子生，治書經，字端時，行一，年二十四，正月二十日生〕。曾祖永恩，祖繒綬，父惠前，母趙氏，母范氏。具慶下，弟大壯、大畜，娶蕭氏。廣東鄉試第六十名，會試第二百三十五名。

王崇義〔貫山東濟南府淄川縣軍籍，國子生，治詩經，字子由，行四，年三十，閏九月十六日生〕。曾祖俊，祖振，父達，母魯氏，繼母曹氏。具慶下，兄崇德、崇儒〔省祭官〕、崇仁，弟崇文、崇學、崇化，娶許氏，繼娶劉氏。山東鄉試第十六名，會試第一百二十九名。

汪柏〔貫江西饒州府浮梁縣民籍，府學生，治易經，字廷節，行二十九，年二十六，二月十二日生〕。曾祖文琦，祖鈞，父泗，母張氏。具慶下，兄槓、札、松、林，弟梧、栗、枰，娶鄭氏。江西鄉試第十六名，會試第一百二十六名。
translation_en:
Yin Lun, registered in a civilian household in Qihe County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, and a native of Dezhou, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Ruyu, he ranked fourth in the family, and he was thirty-nine years old, born on the eighteenth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Jin, his grandfather Qin, and his father Tianzhang, a Police Chief; his mother was née Wang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Tang, Chao, and Jing, and his wife was née Li. He placed twenty-first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 255th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Dayou, registered in a civilian household in Chaoyang County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents; his courtesy name was Duanshi, he ranked first in the family, and he was twenty-four years old, born on the twentieth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Yong’en, his grandfather Zengshou, and his father Huiqian; his mothers were recorded as née Zhao and née Fan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Dazhuang and Dachu, and his wife was née Xiao. He placed sixtieth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 235th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Chongyi, registered in a military household in Zichuan County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Ziyou, he ranked fourth in the family, and he was thirty years old, born on the sixteenth day of the intercalary ninth month. His great-grandfather was Jun, his grandfather Zhen, and his father Da; his mother was née Lu and his stepmother née Cao. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Chongde, Chongru, a sacrificial official (shengjiguan), and Chongren; his younger brothers were Chongwen, Chongxue, and Chonghua. His wife was née Xu, and his subsequent wife née Liu. He placed sixteenth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 129th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Bai, registered in a civilian household in Fuliang County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a prefectural school student specializing in the Classic of Changes; his courtesy name was Tingjie, he ranked twenty-ninth in the family, and he was twenty-six years old, born on the twelfth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Wenqi, his grandfather Jun, and his father Si; his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Gang, Zha, Song, and Lin; his younger brothers were Wu, Li, and Ping. His wife was née Zheng. He placed sixteenth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 126th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄

王心〔貫直隸龍江右衛，軍籍，浙江定海縣人，國子生，治易經，字惟一，行二，年三十八，七月十四日生〕。曾祖敬祥，祖雷，父浩，母楊氏。慈侍下，兄言，娶張氏。應天府鄉試第三十一名，會試第二百六十七名。
translation_en:
Wang Daping, registered in Anqiu County, Qingzhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was a county school student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Xiangxing; he ranked fourth in family seniority and was twenty-eight years old, born on the seventeenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhen, his grandfather Bocheng, his father Yu, and his mother née Li; both parents were living. His elder brothers were Dahua, Daren, and Dajun, and his younger brothers Daye, Dayong, Daxi, Dagao, and Daming. He married a woman née Cao. He placed sixteenth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 206th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Yingkui, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was an supplementary student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Fuyuan; he ranked fifth in family seniority and was twenty-nine years old, born on the second day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yu, an Imperial University student; his grandfather Zhong, a vice prefect; and his father Huai, a government student granted the cap and belt of official status. His mother was née Yong and his birth mother née Yang; grandparents and parents were living. His elder brothers were Zaibang, Zaike, an official awaiting selection for appointment, Zaixian, and Zaitian. He was betrothed to a woman née Zheng. He placed twenty-ninth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 284th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Zheng, registered in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a military household and was a supplementary student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Zimin; he ranked 204th in family seniority and was twenty years old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shuzhi, his grandfather Yuhuan, his father Shixi, and his mother née You; grandparents and parents were living. His younger brothers were Bian, Zhuo, Zhuan, Zhuo, Yang, and Jie. He was betrothed to a woman née Zou. He placed twenty-third in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and seventy-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Xin, registered in Longjiang Right Guard in Zhili, belonged to a military household and was originally from Dinghai County, Zhejiang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Weiyi, ranked second in family seniority, and was thirty-eight years old, born on the fourteenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jingxiang, his grandfather Lei, his father Hao, and his mother née Yang; his father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Yan. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed thirty-first in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 267th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xu Wenheng 徐文亨 was registered in an official household of the Dingliao Rear Guard in Liaodong and was originally from Yugan County, Jiangxi. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Daoxing and ranked second in his family. He was thirty-four years old, born on the twelfth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bodi, a Company Commander; his grandfather was Ang, posthumously granted the title of Battalion Commander; his father was Yuan, and his mother was née Wan. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Wenxian and Wenfang; his younger brothers were Wenzhen, Wenzhong, Wenhe, and Wenzheng. He married a woman née Wang. He placed 113th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 304th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Niu Shendu 牛沈度 was registered in a civilian household in Ye County, Nanyang Prefecture, Henan. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Xuanfan and ranked first in his family. He was forty-four years old, born on the twenty-sixth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lin; his grandfather was Duo, posthumously granted the title of Director in the Ministry of Personnel; his father was Feng, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices at Nanjing; and his mother was née Ren, granted the title of Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His younger brother Shenyu was a tribute scholar (gongshi). He married a woman née Li and subsequently another woman née Li. He placed thirty-ninth in the Henan Provincial Examination and twenty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Song Weiyuan 宋惟元 was registered in a salt-producing household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he had the courtesy name Yizhen and ranked fourth in his family. He was forty-two years old, born on the seventh day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tingfang, posthumously granted the title of Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate; his grandfather was Lian, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his father was Xuan, a County Clerk; and his mother was née Wang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Weixing, Weikui, Weixin, and Weiji. He married a woman née Chen and subsequently women née Hu and née Xu. He placed ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 213th in the Metropolitan Examination.

text:

謂嚴刻乃作言曰
上任刑以為治非
三代之治也却一
不之反於己三代
===
===

義臨而自持惟恐
放侈今之人果三
代之同歟將欲利
之是貪慾之是縱

translation_en: …as soon as the ruler acts according to righteousness, they call him harsh and severe, saying: “The sovereign relies on punishments to govern; this is not the governance of the Three Dynasties.” Yet they never once turn their scrutiny upon themselves. The people of the Three Dynasties were all human beings too: without waiting for righteousness to be imposed upon them, they restrained themselves, fearing only that they might become unbridled and extravagant. Are people today really the same as those of the Three Dynasties? Or would they greedily pursue gain and give free rein to their desires…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄

恤以至於上下禮
度悉不之慎為之
君人者可不一教

虐民之圖奚為用
哉尔多士師孔子

punctuated: 國而罔思，民而罔恤，以至於上下禮度悉不之慎。為之君人者，可不一教一治之是非當否，抑果當乎？朕祗承天位，惟民是保。何官人者比比皆負國虐民之圖，奚為用哉？尔多士師孔子
translation_en: …giving no thought to the state and showing no concern for the people, to the point that those above and below alike disregard ritual propriety and established norms. Can one who rules over them fail to consider whether each act of instruction and government is right or wrong, fitting or unfitting—or is this indeed fitting[?]? I have reverently received Heaven’s throne and seek only to protect the people. Why do those serving as officials so often scheme to betray the state and oppress the people? What use are they? You, assembled scholars, take Confucius as your teacher …

translation_en:
…learning, you must surely take Confucius’s heart as your own. Set forth in your essays the impartiality and rectitude of this heart, and elaborate the way of eliminating abuses and eradicating selfish interests into methods of nurturing with benevolence and deciding with righteousness, to inform me. The fifteenth day of the third month of the seventeenth year of Jiajing (1538).

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣茅瓚
臣對臣聞帝王之御臨天下也內必有敬天
之心而外必有憲天之政夫天者理之原也
人君代天理物故其所行必求端於天天之
道雖廣博而難終窮神妙而不可測而其端
不過有二曰陰與陽而已矣陽居大夏以長
育為事有剛道焉王者繼天而為之子則用
仁而凡為慈愛為謙屈無非仁之統體矣陰
居秋冬以肅殺為事有柔道焉王者繼天而
為之子則用義而凡為果斷為裁制無非義
===
之散殊矣故天道運而無所積帝德運而無
所私以此存之於中是謂敬天純王之心也
以此發之於事是謂憲天純王之政也合心
與政皆純乎天夫是之謂格天之治而堯舜
禹湯文武由此其選也奚獨三代之治為然
乎欽惟
皇帝陛下稟剛健中正之資備文武聖神之德自
即位以來信賞必罰威行如雷霆發姦擿伏明
照如日月對時茂育容保如
天地蓋粹乎斯道之中而建維皇之極者也臣也

punctuated:
臣茅瓚

臣對：臣聞帝王之御臨天下也，內必有敬天之心，而外必有憲天之政。夫天者，理之原也。人君代天理物，故其所行必求端於天。天之道雖廣博而難終，窮神妙而不可測，而其端不過有二，曰陰與陽而已矣。陽居大夏，以長育為事，有剛道焉。王者繼天而為之子，則用仁，而凡為慈愛、為謙屈，無非仁之統體矣。陰居秋冬，以肅殺為事，有柔道焉。王者繼天而為之子，則用義，而凡為果斷、為裁制，無非義之散殊矣。故天道運而無所積，帝德運而無所私。以此存之於中，是謂敬天，純王之心也；以此發之於事，是謂憲天，純王之政也。合心與政，皆純乎天，夫是之謂格天之治，而堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武由此其選也。奚獨三代之治為然乎？

欽惟皇帝陛下，稟剛健中正之資，備文武聖神之德。自即位以來，信賞必罰，威行如雷霆；發姦擿伏，明照如日月；對時茂育，容保如天地。蓋粹乎斯道之中，而建維皇之極者也。臣也
translation_en:
Your servant, Mao Zan.

Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings govern All Under Heaven, inwardly they must possess a heart that reveres Heaven, and outwardly they must establish government that takes Heaven as its model. Heaven is the source of principle. The ruler governs things on Heaven’s behalf; therefore, in all his actions he must seek his starting point in Heaven. Though Heaven’s Way is vast and difficult to encompass, fathoming the spiritually wondrous and remaining beyond measure, its fundamental aspects are only two: yin and yang. Yang occupies high summer [?] and makes growth and nurture its work; therein lies the way of firmness. The king succeeds Heaven and becomes its son, and accordingly employs benevolence. All his acts of loving kindness and humble deference belong to the unified whole of benevolence. Yin occupies autumn and winter and makes stern destruction its work; therein lies the way of yielding. The king succeeds Heaven and becomes its son, and accordingly employs righteousness. All his acts of decisive judgment and regulation belong to the differentiated applications of righteousness. Thus Heaven’s Way moves without accumulation, and imperial virtue operates without partiality. To preserve this inwardly is called revering Heaven: it is the heart of pure kingship. To express it in affairs is called modeling oneself on Heaven: it is the government of pure kingship. When heart and government alike accord wholly with Heaven, this is called government that reaches Heaven. Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu were its outstanding exemplars through following this course. How could this have been true only of government under the Three Dynasties?

I reverently consider that Your Imperial Majesty is endowed with firmness, vigor, centrality, and correctness, and possesses the virtues of civil refinement, martial prowess, sageliness, and spiritual insight. Since ascending the throne, you have faithfully bestowed rewards and unfailingly imposed punishments, your authority moving like thunder; you have exposed wickedness and uncovered hidden wrongdoing, your discernment shining like the sun and moon; you have fostered flourishing growth in accord with the seasons, embracing and protecting like Heaven and Earth. You have indeed attained purity within this Way and established the imperial supreme standard. As for your servant, …

punctuated:
竊伏草茅，遥被治化久矣。乃者叨有司之薦，得以與於大廷之對，而清問及焉。永惟聖經之言，而有取於仁義並行之道；既而有慨於庶官之龐，而欲以兼夫治教之法；且冀臣等以除弊革私之道，為仁育義斷之方，而戒之以勿諱勿欺也。顧臣之愚陋，何足以仰裨休德之萬一乎？雖然，有所言而不實，是之謂欺，則上負陛下矣；有所言而不盡，是之謂諱，則下負所學矣。上負天子，下負所學，疇昔之所自許者謂何？朝廷之作養者謂何？而可如此也？臣敢披瀝衷悃，就陛下之所問及者而條陳之。陛下試垂聽焉。
臣惟天下之道，有經有權。經也者，一定而不可易者也；權也者，或相兼以適其宜，或相濟以補其所不及者也。人君撫輿圖之廣，臨兆民之衆，天下之所恃以立命者也。
translation_en:
…living humbly in obscurity, I have long received, even from afar, the transforming influence of Your Majesty’s government. Recently, through the unmerited recommendation of the responsible officials, I have been able to participate in answering questions at the great court, and Your Majesty’s august inquiry has reached me. Reflecting deeply upon the words of the sagely classics, Your Majesty has embraced the Way of exercising benevolence and righteousness together. Concerned, moreover, about the multitude of officials, you wish to combine the methods of government and moral instruction. You further hope that we, your servants, will propose ways to eliminate abuses and eradicate selfish practices, thereby enabling benevolent nurture and righteous decision, and you admonish us to conceal nothing and offer no deception. Yet how could someone as ignorant and uncultivated as I contribute even the smallest fraction to your splendid virtue? Nevertheless, to speak without truth is deception, and would be to fail Your Majesty above; to speak without saying all is concealment, and would be to betray my learning below. If I failed the Son of Heaven above and betrayed my learning below, what would become of the aspirations I have long cherished? What would become of the court’s efforts to foster and educate me? How could I act thus? I venture to lay bare my innermost sincerity and set out, point by point, my responses to Your Majesty’s questions. May Your Majesty graciously hear me.
Your servant considers that the Way governing all under Heaven comprises both constant principles and discretionary judgment. Constant principles are fixed and cannot be altered. Discretionary judgment sometimes combines approaches to suit the circumstances, and sometimes makes them supplement one another to remedy their respective deficiencies. The ruler presides over an immense territory and governs a vast multitude of people; he is the one upon whom all under Heaven depend for their livelihood.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
苟一於義則威之太震民畏之而不敢親一
於仁則惠之太褻民狎之而不知敬是仁之
與義猶天之有陰陽而不容以或偏也臣故
曰道之一定而不可易者也然德教以象天
之生育仁矣而義者未嘗不防之於中刑戮
以象天之震撼義矣而仁者未始不貫乎其
内是仁義之交相為用猶陰陽之互為其根
臣故曰道之相兼以適其宜也然天下之勢
有強弱而人君之政有德與刑乘弱之後者
利用威而乘強之後者利用惠此其斟酌操
===

動而風以散既成萬物而人莫窺其神臣故

之為道也一定而不可易者以立天下之經
或相兼以適其宜相濟以補其所不及者以
達天下之變稽之於聖經驗之於往古何莫

縱之間猶之天道之兩以潤而日以晅雷以
動而風以散旣成萬物而人莫窺其神　臣故
曰道之相濟以補其所不及者也是故仁義
之爲道也一定而不可易者以立天下之經
或相兼以適其宜相濟以補其所不及者以
達天下之變稽之於聖經驗之於往古何莫
不然彼某夫義以爲論專任德而不用刑者
何其失之偏乎　臣伏讀
聖制之篇而有以辨人言之爲妄矣人之言曰人
君纔一用義卽謂之嚴刻任刑非三代之治
punctuated:
苟一於義，則威之太震，民畏之而不敢親；一於仁，則惠之太褻，民狎之而不知敬。是仁之與義，猶天之有陰陽，而不容以或偏也。臣故曰，道之一定而不可易者也。然德教以象天之生育，仁矣，而義者未嘗不防之於中；刑戮以象天之震撼，義矣，而仁者未始不貫乎其内。是仁義之交相為用，猶陰陽之互為其根。臣故曰，道之相兼以適其宜也。然天下之勢有強弱，而人君之政有德與刑。乘弱之後者，利用威；而乘強之後者，利用惠。此其斟酌操縱之間，猶之天道之雨以潤，而日以晅，雷以動，而風以散，既成萬物，而人莫窺其神。臣故曰，道之相濟以補其所不及者也。
是故仁義之為道也，一定而不可易者，以立天下之經；或相兼以適其宜，相濟以補其所不及者，以達天下之變。稽之於聖經，驗之於往古，何莫不然？彼其去義以為論，專任德而不用刑者，何其失之偏乎！臣伏讀聖制之篇，而有以辨人言之為妄矣。人之言曰：「人君纔一用義，即謂之嚴刻任刑，非三代之治。」
translation_en:
If a ruler relies exclusively on righteousness, his authority becomes too fearsome: the people fear him and dare not draw close. If he relies exclusively on benevolence, his favors become too familiar: the people grow presumptuous and cease to show respect. Benevolence and righteousness are thus like Heaven’s yin and yang: neither may be favored to the exclusion of the other. This is why your servant calls them principles of the Way that are fixed and cannot be altered. Yet moral instruction, which emulates Heaven’s nurturing of life, is benevolent, while righteousness invariably supplies restraints within it. Punishment and execution, which emulate Heaven’s shaking and startling, are righteous, while benevolence invariably runs through them. Benevolence and righteousness thus operate together, just as yin and yang each serve as the root of the other. This is why your servant speaks of principles of the Way being combined to suit what is appropriate. Yet the condition of the realm may be strong or weak, and a ruler’s government employs both virtue and punishment. A ruler who succeeds a period of weakness should employ authority; one who succeeds a period of strength should employ kindness. His weighing of circumstances and his tightening or loosening of control resemble the workings of Heaven: rain moistens, sunlight warms, thunder stirs, and wind disperses. These bring all things to fulfillment, yet no one can fathom their wondrous workings. This is why your servant speaks of principles of the Way assisting one another to make up for what each cannot accomplish alone.
Thus, in the Way of benevolence and righteousness, what is fixed and unalterable establishes the constant principles of the realm; combining them as circumstances require and using each to make up for the other’s shortcomings allows one to respond to changes in the realm. If we consult the sages’ classics and test this against antiquity, where do we find it otherwise? How one-sided and mistaken are those whose arguments discard righteousness, relying exclusively on virtue and dispensing with punishment! Your servant has reverently read Your Majesty’s composition and thereby gained the means to discern the falsity of such claims. People say: “As soon as a ruler employs righteousness, this is called harshness and severity, a reliance on punishment, and not the government of the Three Dynasties.”

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣愚以為用義之與嚴刻任刑不同也既曰
用義則不可謂之嚴刻任刑曰嚴刻任刑則
不得謂之用義人君之於天下何容心哉視
其理之所宜而已矣苟於義所當用則雖殺
人而不可謂之嚴雖致人於死而不得謂之
刻盖以義之為道當如是也至謂用義非三
代之治此尤非所謂知理者臣不暇遠引泛
取即以三代之事明之禹之承舜也先罰後
賞以示威湯之革夏也申伐誓眾以張武而
文武之繼殷也驅除元惡殲滅暴國以救民
===
故夏有禹刑商有湯刑周有甫刑三代之得
天下雖曰以仁而未嘗專倚於仁有義以濟
其仁之所不及也後世事不師古遂以為三
代之治純用德而不用刑何失之遠歟是故
不朝者賜之几杖受賂者媿之金錢言寬仁
者莫如漢之文帝矣然姑息成風乾綱罔斷
故不再傳而有指大如股脛大如腰之患刑
以不殺為威財以不蓄為富言仁厚者亦莫
如宋之仁宗矣然聲容盛而武備衰議論多
而成功少故不再傳而有流言道路變令推

用義則不可謂之嚴刻任刑曰嚴刻任刑則

===

以不殺爲威財以不蓄爲富言仁厚者亦莫
如宋之仁宗矣然聲容盛而武備衰議論多
而成功少故不再傳而有流言道路變令推
punctuated:
臣愚以為，用義之與嚴刻任刑不同也。既曰用義，則不可謂之嚴刻任刑；曰嚴刻任刑，則不得謂之用義。人君之於天下，何容心哉？視其理之所宜而已矣。苟於義所當用，則雖殺人而不可謂之嚴，雖致人於死而不得謂之刻，盖以義之為道當如是也。至謂用義非三代之治，此尤非所謂知理者。臣不暇遠引泛取，即以三代之事明之：禹之承舜也，先罰後賞以示威；湯之革夏也，申伐誓眾以張武；而文武之繼殷也，驅除元惡，殲滅暴國以救民。故夏有禹刑，商有湯刑，周有甫刑。三代之得天下，雖曰以仁，而未嘗專倚於仁，有義以濟其仁之所不及也。後世事不師古，遂以為三代之治純用德而不用刑，何失之遠歟！
是故，不朝者賜之几杖，受賂者媿之金錢，言寬仁者莫如漢之文帝矣。然姑息成風，乾綱罔斷，故不再傳而有指大如股、脛大如腰之患。刑以不殺為威，財以不蓄為富，言仁厚者亦莫如宋之仁宗矣。然聲容盛而武備衰，議論多而成功少，故不再傳而有流言道路、變令推
translation_en:
Your servant humbly considers that applying righteousness differs from being harsh and cruel and relying on punishments. If it is called applying righteousness, it cannot be described as harshness, cruelty, and reliance on punishments; if it is called harshness, cruelty, and reliance on punishments, it cannot be described as applying righteousness. How could the ruler allow personal motives to intrude in his dealings with all under Heaven? He considers only what principle makes appropriate. Wherever righteousness requires its application, even killing someone cannot be called harsh, and even putting someone to death cannot be called cruel, for the Way of righteousness requires precisely this. As for saying that applying righteousness was not the government of the Three Dynasties, this shows still less understanding of principle. Your servant need not seek distant precedents or gather examples widely; the affairs of the Three Dynasties themselves make this clear. When Yu succeeded Shun, he imposed punishments before bestowing rewards to display his authority. When Tang overthrew Xia, he undertook punitive campaigns and addressed his assembled followers with an oath to manifest his martial power. When Kings Wen and Wu succeeded Yin, they expelled the chief evildoers and destroyed violent states to save the people. Thus Xia had the Punishments of Yu, Shang had the Punishments of Tang, and Zhou had the Punishments of Fu. Although the Three Dynasties are said to have gained all under Heaven through benevolence, they never relied exclusively upon it: righteousness supplemented what their benevolence could not accomplish. Later generations failed to model their conduct on antiquity and consequently supposed that the Three Dynasties governed solely through virtue, without using punishments. How far astray they went!
Thus, to those who did not attend court, he bestowed armrests and staffs; those who accepted bribes, he shamed with gifts of money. In generosity and benevolence, none could equal Emperor Wen of Han. Yet indulgence became customary, and sovereign authority failed to act decisively. Consequently, before the throne had passed twice, there arose the affliction of fingers as large as thighs and shins as large as waists. In punishment, he made refraining from killing his source of awe; in finances, he made refraining from accumulation his wealth. In benevolence and generosity, likewise none could equal Emperor Renzong of Song. Yet ceremonial splendor flourished while military preparedness declined; discussions were plentiful, but accomplishments few. Consequently, before the throne had passed twice, there arose talk circulating along the roads, changing decrees and extending…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
恩之譏夫二君則漢宋之良也一於仁而不
義而其流弊猶不免有如此者若是而謂三
代之專於任德後世之專於任刑可乎不可
乎由是觀之三代之所以治隆俗美者以其
仁義之並用內有敬天之心而外有憲天之
政也後世之所以不古若者以其仁義之或
偏而不能審時以度勢其於天也或褻焉而
不知敬或悖焉而不知法也我
太祖高皇帝承元人積弊之後故其所以
創制立法者大率以嚴為本及天下已定又戒
===
聖子神孫不得復用國初之典是其仁義之並行
剛柔之相濟其所以察乎天人之際審乎消
息之宜而為萬世慮者深矣但
國家承平日久重熙累洽民志日趨於玩愒事
體日廢於因循蓋自正德以来茲弊極矣肆
陛下入繼
大統始振起而一新之故自
臨馭十有七年以来革者故鼎者新蟄者奮困
者蘇天下欣欣咸覩太平於有象矣而
陛下猶有歎於官人者負國虐民若追羡於三代

息之宜而爲萬世慮者深矣但

體日廢於因循蓋自正德以來茲弊極矣肆

者蘇天下欣欣咸覩太平於有象矣而
陛下猶有歎於官人者負國虐民若追羨於三代
punctuated:
恩之譏。夫二君則漢宋之良也，一於仁而不義，而其流弊猶不免有如此者。若是而謂三代之專於任德，後世之專於任刑，可乎？不可乎？由是觀之，三代之所以治隆俗美者，以其仁義之並用，內有敬天之心，而外有憲天之政也。後世之所以不古若者，以其仁義之或偏，而不能審時以度勢；其於天也，或褻焉而不知敬，或悖焉而不知法也。
我太祖高皇帝承元人積弊之後，故其所以創制立法者，大率以嚴為本。及天下已定，又戒聖子神孫不得復用國初之典。是其仁義之並行，剛柔之相濟，其所以察乎天人之際，審乎消息之宜，而為萬世慮者深矣。但國家承平日久，重熙累洽，民志日趨於玩愒，事體日廢於因循。蓋自正德以来，茲弊極矣。肆陛下入繼大統，始振起而一新之。故自臨馭十有七年以来，革者故，鼎者新，蟄者奮，困者蘇，天下欣欣，咸覩太平於有象矣。而陛下猶有歎於官人者負國虐民，若追羡於三代
translation_en:
…criticism concerning the extension of favors. These two rulers were among the worthy sovereigns of the Han and Song, yet they devoted themselves exclusively to benevolence without righteousness, and could not avoid such harmful consequences. Given this, can one say that the Three Dynasties relied exclusively on virtue and later ages exclusively on punishment? Can such a claim stand? Viewed in this light, the Three Dynasties attained excellent government and fine customs because they employed benevolence and righteousness together: inwardly they revered Heaven, and outwardly their government took Heaven as its model. Later ages failed to equal antiquity because they sometimes favored one over the other and could not assess the times and weigh the circumstances. In their dealings with Heaven, they either treated it irreverently, without knowing to respect it, or acted contrary to it, without knowing to follow its example.
Our Emperor Taizu Gao inherited the accumulated abuses of Yuan rule. Thus, in establishing institutions and laws, he generally took severity as his foundation. Once the realm was settled, however, he also admonished his sagely sons and divine grandsons that they must not again apply the statutes of the dynasty’s founding years. In this, benevolence and righteousness operated together, and firmness and gentleness complemented each other. Profound indeed was his foresight for all future generations, grounded in his scrutiny of the relationship between Heaven and humanity and his discernment of what was appropriate as circumstances waned and waxed. Yet the state has long enjoyed peace, with prosperity and harmony accumulating through successive reigns. The people’s dispositions have increasingly inclined toward idle neglect, and public affairs have increasingly fallen into disrepair through habitual inaction. Since the Zhengde reign, these abuses have reached their extreme. Then Your Majesty succeeded to the imperial throne and began to rouse the realm and renew it completely. Thus, in the seventeen years since Your Majesty assumed rule, the old has been reformed and the new established; the dormant have been stirred to action and the distressed revived. All under Heaven rejoice, witnessing tangible signs of great peace. Yet Your Majesty still laments that officials betray the state and oppress the people, seemingly yearning to emulate the Three Dynasties…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
之英而未之逮者臣愚以為雖堯舜在上不
能無小人此在君人者馭之得其道耳馭之
之道臣前所謂仁義之並用者是也盖嘗聞
之法禁之不行自上犯之也而小民之所以
敢為非義者庶官之貪頑者啓之也今天下
之大其在於
朝廷輦轂豈無有秉義竭忠之臣然而違上所
好朋家作仇者未盡無也其在於百工庶府
豈無有亮采惠疇之臣然而脅權相滅誣上
行私者未盡無也其在於都邑藩省豈無有
===
旬宣和惠之臣然而違道干譽尸禄養望者
未盡無也甚者削民之膏脂以肥其家竊君
之榮寵以張其勢掠眾之美以示其恩恣已
之私以敗其度者未盡無也
陛下尊禮大臣愈久益親體悉羣臣有隆弗替其
於股肱之良而謨明弼諧者固嘗
撫之以恩而動之以禮矣而於此不悛之徒明
罰勅法懲一以警其百是猶春陽之後而震
之以雷雨之威天下方將感
陛下之仁而畏

陛下之仁而畏
punctuated:
之英而未之逮者。臣愚以為，雖堯舜在上，不能無小人，此在君人者馭之得其道耳。馭之之道，臣前所謂仁義之並用者是也。盖嘗聞之：法禁之不行，自上犯之也；而小民之所以敢為非義者，庶官之貪頑者啓之也。今天下之大，其在於朝廷輦轂，豈無有秉義竭忠之臣？然而違上所好、朋家作仇者，未盡無也。其在於百工庶府，豈無有亮采惠疇之臣？然而脅權相滅、誣上行私者，未盡無也。其在於都邑藩省，豈無有旬宣和惠之臣？然而違道干譽、尸禄養望者，未盡無也。甚者，削民之膏脂以肥其家，竊君之榮寵以張其勢，掠眾之美以示其恩，恣已之私以敗其度者，未盡無也。
陛下尊禮大臣，愈久益親；體悉羣臣，有隆弗替。其於股肱之良而謨明弼諧者，固嘗撫之以恩而動之以禮矣。而於此不悛之徒，明罰勅法，懲一以警其百，是猶春陽之後而震之以雷雨之威。天下方將感陛下之仁而畏
translation_en:
…the outstanding men of the Three Dynasties, whom you have yet to equal. In my humble judgment, even when Yao and Shun ruled, they could not entirely avoid having petty men among their subjects. It is simply for the ruler to find the proper way to govern them. That way is what I spoke of earlier: employing benevolence and righteousness together. I have heard it said that laws and prohibitions fail to take effect because those above violate them; and that ordinary people dare to act unrighteously because greedy and recalcitrant officials set them the example. In this vast realm, are there no ministers at court and in the capital who uphold righteousness and serve with utmost loyalty? Yet neither are those wholly absent who oppose their sovereign’s wishes, form partisan factions, and make themselves his adversaries. Among the many offices and government departments, are there no ministers who faithfully discharge their duties and cooperate harmoniously with their colleagues? Yet neither are those wholly absent who wield power to intimidate and destroy one another, deceive their sovereign, and pursue private ends. In the cities and provinces, are there no ministers who proclaim imperial commands throughout their jurisdictions and bring harmony and beneficence? Yet neither are those wholly absent who depart from the Way to court praise, draw salaries without fulfilling their duties, and cultivate their reputations. Worse still, there remain those who strip the people of their wealth to enrich their own households, appropriate the sovereign’s honors and favors to expand their own influence, seize credit for the good done by others to display it as their own beneficence, and indulge their private desires to undermine established rules.
Your Majesty honors and treats the great ministers with ritual courtesy, drawing ever closer to them as time passes; your sympathetic consideration for all your ministers grows without diminishing. Those worthy ministers who serve as your limbs, whose counsel is clear and whose assistance brings harmony, you have indeed cherished with favor and inspired through ritual propriety. As for these unrepentant men, make punishments clear and enforce the laws, punishing one to warn a hundred. This would be like following the warmth of spring sunshine with the awe-inspiring force of thunder and rain. All under Heaven would then be moved by Your Majesty’s benevolence and stand in fear of…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
陛下之法奚爲而不可行乎雖然處今之時勢而
義之所當用者非獨一馭臣爲然也夷狄跳
梁而横於西北則薄伐之師不可以不整也
庶民僭越而擬於王章則奢汰之禁不可以
不嚴也軍旅疲弊而闕於勇敢則簡閱之令
不可以不怒也凡若此者要皆以精明之治
而敦夫渾厚之體以立君道之紀綱以躋
中興之盛業道莫有先於此者矣抑臣又聞之
仁育而義正者王者之政也所以主是政者

天之政謂非有敬天之心不可也臣嘗莊誦
陛下敬一之箴而有以知
陛下之心直可以質諸
天地而無疑也有德弗敦是違天之所喜矣敢不
敬歟有惡弗懲是渝天之所怒矣敢不敬歟
以此常存於心兢兢業業罔敢失墜夫然後
以達於政也仁足以育天下而天下莫不歸
於仁義足以正天下而天下莫不彊於義憲
天之政由是而會其全格天之功至是以要
其極矣雖然敬亦未易言也隱微之間真妄

陛下之法，奚爲而不可行乎？雖然，處今之時勢，而義之所當用者，非獨一馭臣爲然也。夷狄跳梁而横於西北，則薄伐之師不可以不整也；庶民僭越而擬於王章，則奢汰之禁不可以不嚴也；軍旅疲弊而闕於勇敢，則簡閱之令不可以不怒也。凡若此者，要皆以精明之治，而敦夫渾厚之體，以立君道之紀綱，以躋中興之盛業，道莫有先於此者矣。
抑臣又聞之，仁育而義正者，王者之政也。所以主是政者，心也。故必有純王之心，斯有純王之政，而憲天之政，謂非有敬天之心不可也。臣嘗莊誦陛下敬一之箴，而有以知陛下之心，直可以質諸天地而無疑也。有德弗敦，是違天之所喜矣，敢不敬歟？有惡弗懲，是渝天之所怒矣，敢不敬歟？以此常存於心，兢兢業業，罔敢失墜。夫然後以達於政也，仁足以育天下，而天下莫不歸於仁；義足以正天下，而天下莫不彊於義。憲天之政，由是而會其全；格天之功，至是以要其極矣。雖然，敬亦未易言也。隱微之間，真妄
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s laws: what, then, could not be put into effect? Nevertheless, under present circumstances, the application of righteousness is required not merely in controlling ministers. When the barbarians run rampant and act with violence in the northwest, the forces for punitive campaigns must be put in order. When commoners overstep their station and imitate royal ceremonial distinctions, prohibitions against extravagance must be strictly enforced. When the troops are exhausted and debilitated and lack courage, orders for selection and inspection must be made stern [?]. In all such matters, the essential thing is to employ discerning government to strengthen a generous and substantial foundation, establish the guiding principles of rulership, and bring the great undertaking of dynastic restoration to its flourishing height. No course takes precedence over this.
Your servant has further heard that nurturing through benevolence and rectifying through righteousness constitute the government of a true king. What presides over this government is the heart. Thus, only with the heart of a true king, wholly pure, can there be the government of a true king, wholly pure; and government modeled on Heaven cannot exist without a heart that reveres Heaven. Your servant has reverently recited Your Majesty’s Admonition on Reverent Oneness (Jingyi zhen), and thereby knows that Your Majesty’s heart can indeed be submitted to Heaven and Earth for judgment without any doubt. To fail to foster virtue is to oppose what Heaven delights in: dare one be irreverent? To fail to punish evil is to contravene what Heaven condemns: dare one be irreverent? Keep this constantly in the heart, vigilant and cautious, never daring to let it slip. Only then can it find expression in government. Benevolence will suffice to nurture all under Heaven, and none under Heaven will fail to turn toward benevolence; righteousness will suffice to rectify all under Heaven, and none under Heaven will fail to exert themselves in righteousness. Government modeled on Heaven will thereby attain its completeness, and the achievement of moving Heaven will thus reach its highest fulfillment. Nevertheless, reverence is not easily discussed. Amid what is hidden and subtle, the true and the false…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
錯雜毫釐之差千里之繆苟辨察之功不悉
於幾微持守之力不繼於厭服則人得以勝
天欲得以奪理又惡知其爲仁而在所當體
惡知其爲義而在所當用也哉故曰勿參以
三勿貳以二行顧其言終如其始靜虚無欲
日新不已然則
陛下之言固可謂能自得師者矣除弊革私之道
仁育義斷之方豈外此而他求乎哉臣始以
仁義並行之道爲
陛下告終以主敬協一之功爲
===
陛下勉初非有驚世可喜之論然直意
陛下以言求士而臣之所以獻言於
陛下者惟以明諸其心上不敢負
明問下不敢負所學而已惟
陛下矜其愚不録其罪而
留神採納焉臣不勝惓惓隕越之至臣謹對

punctuated: 錯雜，毫釐之差，千里之繆。苟辨察之功不悉於幾微，持守之力不繼於厭服，則人得以勝天，欲得以奪理，又惡知其爲仁而在所當體，惡知其爲義而在所當用也哉？故曰：「勿參以三，勿貳以二，行顧其言，終如其始。」靜虚無欲，日新不已。然則陛下之言，固可謂能自得師者矣。除弊革私之道，仁育義斷之方，豈外此而他求乎哉？臣始以仁義並行之道爲陛下告，終以主敬協一之功爲陛下勉。初非有驚世可喜之論，然直意陛下以言求士，而臣之所以獻言於陛下者，惟以明諸其心，上不敢負明問，下不敢負所學而已。惟陛下矜其愚，不録其罪，而留神採納焉。臣不勝惓惓隕越之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…are intermingled; an error of a hair’s breadth leads to a discrepancy of a thousand li. If the work of discernment does not fully encompass the subtlest beginnings, and the strength of steadfast observance does not persist in satisfied conviction [?], then the human can overcome Heaven, and desire can displace principle. How, then, could one recognize benevolence as what one ought to embody, or righteousness as what one ought to put into practice? Thus it is said: “Do not divide it into three; do not split it into two. Let your conduct accord with your words, and let the end be like the beginning.” Be still and empty of desire, renewing yourself daily without cease. Your Majesty’s words may therefore indeed be said to show that you can find a teacher within yourself. How could the way to eliminate abuses and eradicate selfish interests, or the means of nurturing through benevolence and deciding through righteousness, be sought anywhere beyond this?

Your servant began by explaining to Your Majesty the way of practicing benevolence and righteousness together, and concludes by urging Your Majesty to undertake the work of making reverent attentiveness the guiding principle and maintaining unity. From the outset, I have offered no startling discourse to delight the world. I have simply thought that Your Majesty seeks worthy men through their words, and that the words your servant presents to Your Majesty serve only to make clear what is in his heart. Toward my sovereign, I dare not fail your enlightened inquiry; on my own part, I dare not betray what I have learned. That is all. May Your Majesty pity my foolishness, refrain from recording my offense, and give these words your attention and acceptance. Your servant is overwhelmed by earnest devotion and the utmost trepidation. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣羅珵
臣對臣聞人君法天以爲治有仁以育天下
必有義以裁天下夫天之於物也有春生必
有秋殺有長養必有斂蔵非有心於物也公
而已矣不如是不足以爲天之道也人君宰
制天下嚮明而治所以成一統之治繫四海
之心者亦惟法天之公而已矣是故慶賞爵
秩懋官懋禄所以奔走天下之豪傑仁以爲
治猶之天之於物春以生之也威嚴以督責
教戒而懲創所以振起一時之怠惰義以爲
===
治猶之天之於物秋以止之也故一於仁則
流於姑息其失也則縱一於義則流於苛刻
其失也則嚴仁義並用恩威兼舉乂安長治
不外是也然仁義之爲施雖殊而君人之爲
心則一是故父母之於子也撫摩而鞠育之
愛也勞苦而鞭策之亦愛也知天之於萬物
之心則知父母於子之心矣知父母於子之
心則知人君於臣之心矣故曰父母愛之喜
而勿忘父母惡之勞而無怨又曰惟天聰明
惟聖時憲唐虞三代所以成雍熈悠久之治

惟聖時憲唐虞三代所以成雍熙悠久之治
punctuated:
臣羅珵。

臣對：臣聞人君法天以爲治，有仁以育天下，必有義以裁天下。夫天之於物也，有春生必有秋殺，有長養必有斂蔵，非有心於物也，公而已矣。不如是，不足以爲天之道也。人君宰制天下，嚮明而治，所以成一統之治、繫四海之心者，亦惟法天之公而已矣。是故慶賞爵秩，懋官懋禄，所以奔走天下之豪傑，仁以爲治，猶之天之於物，春以生之也；威嚴以督責，教戒而懲創，所以振起一時之怠惰，義以爲治，猶之天之於物，秋以止之也。故一於仁，則流於姑息，其失也則縱；一於義，則流於苛刻，其失也則嚴。仁義並用，恩威兼舉，乂安長治，不外是也。然仁義之爲施雖殊，而君人之爲心則一。是故父母之於子也，撫摩而鞠育之，愛也；勞苦而鞭策之，亦愛也。知天之於萬物之心，則知父母於子之心矣；知父母於子之心，則知人君於臣之心矣。故曰：「父母愛之，喜而勿忘；父母惡之，勞而無怨。」又曰：「惟天聰明，惟聖時憲。」唐虞三代所以成雍熈悠久之治
translation_en:
Your servant, Luo Cheng 羅珵.

Your servant replies: I have heard that the ruler of men models his government on Heaven. If he possesses benevolence with which to nurture all under Heaven, he must also possess righteousness with which to regulate all under Heaven. In Heaven’s dealings with living things, spring’s generation necessarily entails autumn’s destruction, and growth and nurture necessarily entail gathering and storing. Heaven has no deliberate designs upon things; it is simply impartial. Without this, it would not suffice to constitute the Way of Heaven. The ruler governs all under Heaven, facing the light to conduct government. What enables him to establish unified rule and bind the hearts of all within the Four Seas is likewise nothing more than modeling himself on Heaven’s impartiality. Thus, rewards and honors, noble ranks and official grades, and the bestowal of offices and emoluments for merit serve to bring the outstanding men of the realm eagerly into service. Governing through benevolence resembles Heaven’s bringing things to life in spring. Using stern authority to supervise and hold men accountable, instructing and admonishing them, and punishing them to deter further wrongdoing serve to rouse the indolent of the age. Governing through righteousness resembles Heaven’s bringing the growth of things to a halt in autumn. Hence, exclusive reliance on benevolence lapses into indulgence, with laxity as its failing; exclusive reliance on righteousness lapses into harshness, with excessive severity as its failing. Employing benevolence and righteousness together, and exercising favor and authority in tandem: peaceful order and lasting good government require nothing beyond this.

Yet although benevolence and righteousness differ in their application, the intention of the ruler who employs them is one. Thus, when parents caress and rear their children, this is love; when they make them toil and discipline them with the rod, this too is love. Understanding Heaven’s intentions toward the myriad things, one understands parents’ intentions toward their children; understanding parents’ intentions toward their children, one understands the ruler’s intentions toward his ministers. Thus it is said: “When your parents love you, rejoice and do not forget them; when your parents dislike you, toil without resentment.” It is also said: “Heaven alone is keen of hearing and clear of sight; the sage alone takes it as his model.” The reason the rulers of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties achieved harmonious, flourishing, and enduring government …

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
者仁義無偏舉之弊也漢唐宋所以治不古
若者或一於仁或一於義均之各有所失也
欽惟
皇帝陛下剛健純粹之資高明光大之學仁以育
萬民而天下皆覆冒於陽春嫗煦之內義以
正萬民而天下皆震悚於風行電刷之餘道
洽政治大法小廉一十七年于茲矣乃謂承
平既久玩愒或生慨然欲興起而振刷之
萬幾之暇進臣等于
廷而
===
賜之清問臣有以知
陛下之心即天地之於物父母之於子也臣雖至
愚陋敢不摭拾所聞以對乎夫世之稱極治
者曰唐虞曰三代然稽諸往牒考之前聞則
其治道班班可見故稱堯曰其仁如天稱舜
曰其德好生固也然而四凶之誅三苗之伐
其於義未嘗偏廢也稱禹曰文命四敷稱湯
曰德及禽獸稱文武曰仁厚立國固也然五
刑之用五罰之訓八刑之糾其於義亦未嘗
偏廢也雖曰不賞而民勸不怒而民威未施

punctuated:
者，仁義無偏舉之弊也。漢唐宋所以治不古若者，或一於仁，或一於義，均之各有所失也。
欽惟皇帝陛下，剛健純粹之資，高明光大之學，仁以育萬民，而天下皆覆冒於陽春嫗煦之內；義以正萬民，而天下皆震悚於風行電刷之餘。道洽政治，大法小廉，一十七年于茲矣。乃謂承平既久，玩愒或生，慨然欲興起而振刷之。萬幾之暇，進臣等于廷，而賜之清問。臣有以知陛下之心，即天地之於物、父母之於子也。臣雖至愚陋，敢不摭拾所聞以對乎？
夫世之稱極治者，曰唐虞，曰三代。然稽諸往牒，考之前聞，則其治道班班可見。故稱堯曰：「其仁如天。」稱舜曰：「其德好生。」固也。然而四凶之誅、三苗之伐，其於義未嘗偏廢也。稱禹曰：「文命四敷。」稱湯曰：「德及禽獸。」稱文武曰：「仁厚立國。」固也。然五刑之用、五罰之訓、八刑之糾，其於義亦未嘗偏廢也。雖曰：「不賞而民勸，不怒而民威。」未施
translation_en:
…was that benevolence and righteousness were practiced without the defect of favoring either alone. The reason government under the Han, Tang, and Song did not equal that of antiquity was that they sometimes relied exclusively on benevolence and sometimes exclusively on righteousness; each approach had its shortcomings.
Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor: you possess a firm, vigorous, and pure disposition, and lofty, enlightened, and comprehensive learning. Through benevolence you nurture the myriad people, so that all under Heaven are sheltered within the kindly warmth of spring; through righteousness you set the myriad people right, so that all under Heaven tremble in awe after the sweep of your wind and the cleansing flash of your lightning. The Way pervades the realm and government is well ordered; great officials observe the law and lesser officials remain incorrupt. It has now been seventeen years. Yet you judge that prolonged peace may have bred complacency and idleness, and earnestly wish to rouse and reinvigorate the realm. Amid your myriad affairs, you have summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed your illuminating questions upon us. Thus I know that Your Majesty's heart is like that of Heaven and Earth toward all things, or of parents toward their children. Though your servant is exceedingly ignorant and uncultivated, dare I fail to gather what I have heard and offer a reply?
When people speak of the highest achievements in government, they name the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. If we examine past records and investigate the accounts handed down to us, their principles of government are plainly visible. Thus Yao is praised with the words, “His benevolence was like Heaven,” and Shun with “His virtue cherished life.” This is certainly true. Yet in the punishment of the Four Malefactors and the campaign against the Sanmiao, righteousness was never neglected. Yu is praised with “His civilizing influence spread to the four quarters,” Tang with “His virtue extended even to birds and beasts,” and Wen and Wu with “They founded their state upon benevolence and generosity.” This, too, is certainly true. Yet in the application of the Five Punishments, the injunctions concerning the five penalties, and correction through the eight punishments, righteousness likewise was never neglected. Although it is said, “Without rewards, the people were encouraged; without anger, the people stood in awe,” before putting into practice …

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
信而民信未施敬而民敬而威克愛克剛克

…trustworthiness, yet the people were trustworthy; before reverence was displayed, the people were reverent. Yet whether authority or love prevailed, whether firmness or gentleness prevailed, those who governed the age and responded to affairs through punishments and blessings, giving and taking away, restraining and promoting, advancing and withdrawing, now tightening and now relaxing, never secured one at the expense of the other, or employed one while abandoning the other. Thus, if Heaven had yin but no yang, its power to shelter the myriad things would almost cease; if Earth had softness but no firmness, its power to sustain the myriad things would almost cease. If a ruler possesses benevolence but is deficient in righteousness, how can he assist the transforming and nurturing work of Heaven and Earth, standing alongside them as the third? A transmitted teaching says: “Punishments must not be relaxed within the state; punitive expeditions must not be relaxed throughout the realm; whipping and beating must not be relaxed within the household.” Do those who advocate dispensing with righteousness understand what the essentials of government require? There are also arguments that a true king prizes virtue and relaxes punishments, and that sages establish institutions according to the times they encounter. These are the partial views of narrow-minded scholars who do not understand the perfectly balanced and supremely upright Way by which sages govern.

Human feelings generally incline toward license and dislike restraint, delight in ease and comfort, and resent rules and standards. People do not understand that benevolence and righteousness are precisely the means by which a ruler governs his subjects. Benevolence does not mean indulgence: it is the means of winning their hearts. Righteousness does not mean cruelty: it is the means of restraining their wrongdoing. “The three sovereigns accomplished their work, bringing abundance to the people. The judicial officer regulated the common people, teaching them to revere virtue. text:
惠並舉仁以主之義以輔之惠以維之威以
懾之無偏而不全之敝固不一於仁而忘乎
義也有兼而並用之美固不專乎威而弛乎
惠也唐虞尚矣夏之四百商之六百周之八
百且過其歷何莫而不本於此哉是雖三代
之人心忠信誠愨而三代之英君誼辟所以
維持天下之具防範人心之道者則一言以
蔽之曰仁與義而已矣臣嘗觀之天下之日
趨於變也猶江河之日趨於下也然挽而回
之其機端有在也我
===
皇上勵精圖治風勵天下大小臣工奉承
休德百工既已惟時庶績既已惟凝軼唐虞三

祖宗矣而恬嬉之念猶不忘焉

而民或罔恤矣上下紀綱愆而不修
國之禮度其何賴焉

translation_en:
…beneficence is exercised together with authority. Benevolence guides them, righteousness assists them, beneficence holds them together, and authority awes them. There is no defect of partiality or incompleteness: one certainly does not adhere solely to benevolence and forget righteousness. There is the excellence of combining and employing both: one certainly does not rely exclusively on authority and relax beneficence. Tang and Yu belong to remote antiquity; but the four hundred years of Xia, the six hundred of Shang, and the more than eight hundred of Zhou—how could any of these dynasties’ longevity have failed to rest upon this? Although the people of the Three Dynasties were loyal, trustworthy, sincere, and honest at heart, the means by which their illustrious rulers and righteous sovereigns sustained the realm, and the ways by which they guarded against wayward inclinations in people’s hearts, can be summed up in a single phrase: benevolence and righteousness, nothing more.
Your servant has observed that the realm’s daily movement toward change resembles the daily downward flow of rivers. Yet there is indeed a means of drawing it back and reversing its course. Our Emperor devotes his energies to good government and inspires the realm. Officials great and small uphold your excellent virtue; the hundred offices already function in due order, and all undertakings have already been firmly established. You have surpassed Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, and matched the virtue of your imperial ancestors. Yet you remain mindful of complacency and idleness. Your servant dares not assert that the matters of concern in your sagely policy question are necessarily absent. Thus, some lose their sense of integrity and shame and pursue profit alone; some abandon their steadfast principles and give free rein to desire. Some are bound by concern for their households and give no thought to the state; some are consumed by the desire to fill their purses and give no care to the people. When discipline and order among superiors and subordinates are impaired and left unrepaired, on what can the state’s rites and institutions depend? You labor from before dawn until late at night, regarding the people as your children, yet those charged with shepherding the people remain complacent and pay them no heed. This …

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
聖慮所以惓惓而不能已也臣惟斯民也三代之
所以直道而行也臣願
陛下憲天聰明明示意嚮務令天下改絃易轍奬
恬退以勵士風抑奔競以端習尚則素絲羔
羊之節著而惟利是貪者無足慮矣清介自
持者必錄貪墨自污者必擯則琴鶴自隨之
士見而惟慾是縱者無足慮矣公爾而忘私
國爾而忘家何有於國之罔念乎恫瘝之在
乃身饑寒之切其體何有於民之罔恤乎至
於上下禮度則我
===
祖宗之成憲異代如見我
皇上之制作萬世不刊申戒所司各遵彜則上下
有章而民志定矣貴賤有等而
朝廷尊矣否則天冠地屨之分森不敢犯者彼

字不以繭絲先保障而凡負國虐民者擯而
棄之終身不齒則龔遂卓茂之輩寇恂黃覇
之徒民受其福
國承其休矣否則以私滅公之法凛不容逭者
彼將何所贖哉凡臣所願于

translation_en:
…this is why Your Majesty’s concern is so earnest and cannot cease. Your servant considers that these people are the very people among whom the Three Dynasties followed the straight Way. I wish that Your Majesty would model your perceptiveness upon Heaven and clearly declare your intentions, ensuring that all under Heaven change their course. Reward quiet restraint and withdrawal to encourage proper conduct among scholars; curb competitive self-advancement to rectify prevailing habits. Then the integrity symbolized by plain silk and lambskin will become manifest, and those who covet only profit will give no cause for concern. Invariably employ those who maintain purity and uprightness, and invariably dismiss those who sully themselves through greed and corruption. Then men who travel accompanied only by a zither and a crane will emerge, and those who merely indulge their desires will give no cause for concern. If they devote themselves to public affairs and forget private interests, and to the state and forget their households, how could they neglect the state? If they feel the people’s suffering as though it were in their own bodies, and hunger and cold as though these afflicted their own flesh, how could they fail to care for the people?

As for the ritual standards governing superior and inferior, the established statutes of our imperial ancestors remain as vividly present as ever across the ages; the institutions of our emperor will stand unaltered for ten thousand generations. Renew the admonitions to the responsible officials, requiring each to observe the enduring rules. When superior and inferior have their prescribed order, the people’s minds will be settled; when noble and humble have their respective ranks, the court will be honored. Otherwise, the distinctions between high and low—as between Heaven and Earth, cap and shoes—are so stern that none dare violate them: how could offenders escape?

In governing the people, require officials not to put tax collection before nurturing them, nor the extraction of revenue, like reeling silk from cocoons, before protecting them. As for all who betray the state and oppress the people, dismiss and cast them out, excluding them from office for life. Then men like Gong Sui and Zhuo Mao, Kou Xun and Huang Ba will arise, and the people will receive their blessings while the state enjoys their beneficent achievements. Otherwise, the laws against sacrificing public interests to private ends are stern and permit no evasion: how could offenders redeem themselves? All that your servant wishes of…

惟辟作威

法守臣惟欽若而民惟從乂唐虞三代之休

punctuated: 陛下者，固非欲一於義而棄乎仁也，亦非欲一乎治而忘乎教也。臯陶曰：「天命有德，五服五章哉！天討有罪，五刑五用哉！」箕子曰：「惟辟作福，惟辟作威。」陛下之深仁厚澤、至恩美意，固已浹民肌膚，淪民骨髓矣。然所以行乎義者，正所以濟乎仁也；所以正之者，正所以教之也。仁與義並行而不悖，治與教兼舉而無遺，上有道揆而下有法守，臣惟欽若而民惟從乂，唐虞三代之休復見於今日，功光祖宗，德流後裔矣。而何有於用義嚴刻、任刑為治之虞乎？惟陛下一轉移之間，而天下皆已改觀易聽，洗心滌慮矣。俄頃功化，神速如此！抑臣學於孔子而有聞焉。孔子曰：「政寬則民慢，慢則糾之以猛，民猛則民殘，殘則施之以寬。寬猛相濟，政是以和。」又曰：「張而不弛，文武不為也；弛而不張，文武不為也。」

…of Your Majesty is certainly not that you should devote yourself exclusively to righteousness and abandon benevolence, nor that you should devote yourself exclusively to governing and forget moral instruction. Gao Yao said: “Heaven appoints the virtuous: let the five kinds of ceremonial robes distinguish their five ranks! Heaven punishes the guilty: let the five punishments be applied in their five respective uses!” Jizi said: “Only the sovereign may confer blessings; only the sovereign may exercise awe.” Your Majesty’s profound benevolence, abundant bounty, utmost kindness, and fine intentions have already permeated the people’s skin and sunk into their very marrow. Yet the means of practicing righteousness are precisely the means of assisting benevolence; the means of correcting the people are precisely the means of instructing them. Benevolence and righteousness will proceed together without conflict; government and moral instruction will both be carried out, with neither neglected. Above, conduct will be measured by the Way; below, established laws will be upheld. Ministers will reverently comply, and the people will submit to good order. The glories of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties will appear again today; your achievements will bring glory to your ancestors, and your virtue will flow down to your descendants. What grounds would there then be to fear that practicing righteousness entails harsh severity, or that government rests on punishment?

With but a single change of direction by Your Majesty, all under Heaven will already look and listen anew, cleansing their hearts and purifying their thoughts. In a moment, transforming achievements will come with such wondrous speed! Moreover, your servant has learned from Confucius and has heard the following. Confucius said: “When government is lenient, the people grow lax; when they grow lax, correct them with severity. When the people are severe [?], the people are injured; when they are injured, apply leniency. Leniency and severity complement each other, and government thereby achieves harmony.” He also said: “To draw the bow taut without relaxing it was something Kings Wen and Wu would not do; to relax it without drawing it taut was something Kings Wen and Wu would not do. …”

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
一張一弛文武之道也此在
今日除弊革私之道仁育義斷之方無有出於
是焉臣不敢漫為臆說干瀆
聰聽伏惟
陛下採而行之抑臣於篇終尚有
獻焉臣愚又聞之曰為治之道仁可過也義不
可過也夫天以春夏成萬物而長用於生育
長養之地以秋冬止萬物而常積於空虛無
用之地孔子曰導之以政齊之以刑民免而
無耻道之以德齊之以禮有耻且格孟子曰
===
善政不如善教之得民也善教民愛之善教
得民心故稱舜德之罔愆者必曰宥過無大
罪疑惟輕又曰欽哉欽哉惟刑之恤夫聖人
制刑特以為輔治之具而期于無刑則又聖
人之初意也伏願
陛下必如舜之眚災肆赦德洽民心必如湯之開
釋無辜亦克用勸必如文之懷保小民敬明
乃罰寬而有制從容以和立精明之治功存
渾厚之治體於整齊嚴肅之中寓曲成造就
之意則天下幸甚

translation_en:
…“To alternate tension and relaxation is the Way of Kings Wen and Wu.” For eliminating abuses and eradicating private interests today, for nurturing through benevolence and deciding through righteousness, no method surpasses this. Your servant dares not recklessly advance conjectures and intrude upon Your Majesty’s august hearing. I humbly hope that Your Majesty will adopt and implement this counsel. Yet at the end of this essay, your servant still has something to offer.

Your ignorant servant has also heard it said: “In the way of governing, benevolence may go too far, but righteousness must not.” Heaven brings all things to fruition through spring and summer, continually exercising its powers in the realm of generation and nurture; through autumn and winter it brings all things to rest, continually accumulating them in a realm of emptiness and disuse [?]. Confucius said: “Guide them through governmental measures and regulate them through punishments, and the people will evade punishment but have no shame. Guide them through virtue and regulate them through ritual, and they will have shame and set themselves right.” Mencius said: “Good government does not win the people as good teaching does. With good teaching, the people love it [?]; good teaching wins the people’s hearts.” Thus, those who praise the faultlessness of Shun’s virtue invariably say: “Pardon inadvertent offenses, however great; where guilt is doubtful, impose the lighter penalty.” They also say: “Be reverent! Be reverent! Be solicitous in the use of punishments.” The sages established punishments solely as an instrument to assist government, while aspiring to make punishment unnecessary: this, too, was their original intention.

I humbly wish that Your Majesty would follow Shun in freely pardoning inadvertent offenses and those arising from misfortune, so that your virtue may suffuse the people’s hearts; follow Tang in releasing the innocent, thereby also encouraging goodness; and follow King Wen in cherishing and protecting the common people and applying punishments reverently and discerningly. Be lenient, yet maintain regulation; proceed calmly and harmoniously. Establish the achievements of clear-sighted government while preserving its generous and substantial character. Amid order and strict discipline, embody the intention to nurture and perfect each according to their circumstances. Then all under Heaven would be most fortunate…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣袁煒
臣對臣聞聖王之弘化於天下也有孚天之
德而仁義之具也無所偏有憲天之政而治
教之行也無所悖夫不偏而後德之本諸身
者見中正之軌不悖而後政之達諸民者見
皇極之敷德焉中正而孚天之妙盡之矣政
焉皇極而憲天之道盡之矣夫是以育諸仁
而天下莫不循其教以為勸斷諸義而天下
莫不順其治以為懲紀綱理而庶官以貞人
心正而風俗以美精純和粹之化不亦四達
===
而大同乎治古之君有見於此其蘊之而為
德也仁義未始不相須其發之而為政也治
教未始不相濟是故當時之人咸知夫君之
有所愛者固所以仁天下而其有所不愛者
亦所以仁天下罔不洗心滌慮防貪窒慾而
在位者皆廉吏在野者皆良民敏德以從乂
時雍而迓衡治古之化迥乎弗可及也已矣
三代以還是說不明孚天之德既荒憲天之
政亦敝偏於仁以敷教者不免於因循怠弛
之病偏於義以飭治者或罹夫嚴刻苛切之

之病偏於義以飭治者或罹夫嚴刻苛切之
punctuated:
臣袁煒。

臣對：臣聞聖王之弘化於天下也，有孚天之德，而仁義之具也無所偏；有憲天之政，而治教之行也無所悖。夫不偏而後德之本諸身者見中正之軌，不悖而後政之達諸民者見皇極之敷。德焉中正，而孚天之妙盡之矣；政焉皇極，而憲天之道盡之矣。夫是以育諸仁，而天下莫不循其教以為勸；斷諸義，而天下莫不順其治以為懲。紀綱理而庶官以貞，人心正而風俗以美，精純和粹之化，不亦四達而大同乎？治古之君有見於此，其蘊之而為德也，仁義未始不相須；其發之而為政也，治教未始不相濟。是故當時之人咸知夫君之有所愛者，固所以仁天下，而其有所不愛者，亦所以仁天下。罔不洗心滌慮，防貪窒慾，而在位者皆廉吏，在野者皆良民，敏德以從乂，時雍而迓衡。治古之化，迥乎弗可及也已矣！三代以還，是說不明，孚天之德既荒，憲天之政亦敝。偏於仁以敷教者，不免於因循怠弛之病；偏於義以飭治者，或罹夫嚴刻苛切之
translation_en:
Your servant, Yuan Wei.

Your servant replies: I have heard that when sage kings extend their transforming influence throughout the realm, they possess virtue that accords with Heaven, and their endowment of benevolence and righteousness is free of partiality; they possess government that takes Heaven as its model, and their exercise of governance and instruction is free of discord. Only through freedom from partiality does virtue rooted in the ruler’s own person manifest the standard of centrality and uprightness; only through freedom from discord does government reaching the people manifest the extension of the August Ultimate, the sovereign standard. When virtue achieves centrality and uprightness, the subtle perfection of accord with Heaven is fully realized; when government embodies the August Ultimate, the Way of taking Heaven as its model is fully realized. Thus, when the ruler nurtures through benevolence, everyone under Heaven follows his instruction and finds encouragement in it; when he adjudicates through righteousness, everyone under Heaven submits to his governance and finds admonition in it. The governing order is well regulated, and all officials are upright; people’s hearts are rectified, and customs become fine. Does not such a transformation, refined and pure, harmonious and unalloyed, reach in every direction and bring about great concord?

The rulers of well-governed antiquity understood this. In what they nurtured inwardly as virtue, benevolence and righteousness invariably depended upon one another; in what they expressed outwardly as government, governance and instruction invariably reinforced one another. Thus, the people of that time all understood that what their ruler cherished was indeed a means of extending benevolence throughout the realm, and that what he did not cherish was also a means of extending benevolence throughout the realm. All cleansed their hearts and purified their thoughts, guarded against greed, and checked their desires. Those holding office were all incorrupt officials, and those outside office were all good subjects. They diligently cultivated virtue and followed good order, attaining harmony and welcoming peace. The transforming influence of well-governed antiquity was indeed far beyond anything later ages could attain!

Since the Three Dynasties, this principle has ceased to be understood. Virtue that accords with Heaven has been neglected, and government that models itself on Heaven has likewise deteriorated. Those who incline exclusively toward benevolence in extending instruction cannot escape the fault of complacency and laxity; those who incline exclusively toward righteousness in enforcing order sometimes fall into severity and oppressive harshness …

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
愆此所以惠褻而教衰刑肅而俗弊寵賂章
於有位禮義潰於匪彝而化理之所成者終
不能登之於古也欽惟
皇帝陛下天縱之資既有以涵乎仁義之懿而日
躋之敬又有以慎乎刑賞之權惠行而天下
欣戴威發而海內震慄廉恥達於君子信義
行於小人中興之治固有咸五登三而陋漢
唐宋於不居矣然猶慮仁恩之過或足以長
淫縱破義之風而德教之專不能無刓敝不
振之患乃進臣等於
===
廷降
賜清問而咨以除弊革私之道仁育義斷之方
是將以明作之功濟惇大之裕使天下回心
而嚮道也臣濡沃
陛下仁義之澤範圍治教之中蓋有年矣敢不掇
拾所聞以對揚
休命於萬一乎臣竊惟天道運於上而萬物資
始者陰陽之相禪也地道運於下而萬物資
生者剛柔之相濟也使天地有陽而無陰有
柔而無剛則化生形色何自而各正性命也
