punctuated:
愆。此所以惠褻而教衰，刑肅而俗弊，寵賂章於有位，禮義潰於匪彝，而化理之所成者，終不能登之於古也。
欽惟皇帝陛下，天縱之資，既有以涵乎仁義之懿，而日躋之敬，又有以慎乎刑賞之權。惠行而天下欣戴，威發而海內震慄，廉恥達於君子，信義行於小人。中興之治，固有咸五登三，而陋漢唐宋於不居矣。然猶慮仁恩之過，或足以長淫縱破義之風，而德教之專，不能無刓敝不振之患，乃進臣等於廷，降賜清問，而咨以除弊革私之道、仁育義斷之方。是將以明作之功，濟惇大之裕，使天下回心而嚮道也。臣濡沃陛下仁義之澤，範圍治教之中，蓋有年矣。敢不掇拾所聞，以對揚休命於萬一乎？
臣竊惟天道運於上，而萬物資始者，陰陽之相禪也；地道運於下，而萬物資生者，剛柔之相濟也。使天地有陽而無陰，有柔而無剛，則化生形色，何自而各正性命也
translation_en:
…the fault. This is why favors become debased and moral instruction declines, punishments become severe and customs deteriorate, favoritism and bribery flourish among those in office, and ritual propriety and righteousness collapse amid lawlessness. The achievements of moral transformation and good government thus ultimately fail to reach the standard of antiquity.
With reverence I consider that Your Majesty the Emperor, through your Heaven-endowed qualities, already embraces the excellence of benevolence and righteousness; through your daily increasing reverence, you also exercise care in wielding the authority to punish and reward. When your beneficence is extended, all under Heaven joyfully acclaim you; when your might is displayed, all within the seas tremble. Integrity and a sense of shame prevail among gentlemen, while trustworthiness and righteousness are practiced among the common people. Your rule of restoration assuredly equals that of the Five Emperors and surpasses that of the Three Kings, relegating the Han, Tang, and Song to an inferior standing with which you will not rest content. Yet you still fear that excessive benevolent favor might foster a tendency toward indulgence and license that violates righteousness, and that exclusive reliance on moral instruction cannot avoid the danger of deterioration and loss of vigor. You therefore brought us, your servants, into court and graciously bestowed your searching questions, asking about the way to eliminate abuses and reform selfish practices, and the means of nurturing through benevolence and deciding through righteousness. Your purpose is to supplement ample generosity with the efficacy of clear-sighted action, so that all under Heaven may turn their hearts toward the Way. Your servant has been steeped in the blessings of Your Majesty’s benevolence and righteousness, and shaped within your government and moral instruction, for many years. How could I dare not gather what I have heard, to respond to and extol even one ten-thousandth part of your gracious command?
Your servant humbly considers that the Way of Heaven operates above, and the myriad things draw upon it for their beginnings, through the alternation of yin and yang; the Way of Earth operates below, and the myriad things draw upon it for their life, through the mutual assistance of firmness and yielding. If Heaven and Earth possessed yang but no yin, yielding but no firmness, then through what means could things be transformed and generated, acquire form and color, and each attain its proper nature and allotted destiny …

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
哉夫天地者人君之父母也人君者天地之
子也人君繼天地而為之子則任德以行吾
之仁而類其生殖長育任刑以行吾之義而
類其震曜殺戮者信乎可相有而不可相無
矣古今帝王未之有改故如天之仁好生之
洽堯舜之所以仁天下也而四凶之誅有苗
之北未嘗不裁之以義焉文命之敷兆民之
殖咸和之施三王之所以仁天下也而升陑
之師密黎之戡亦未嘗不治之以義焉司馬
遷曰教笞不可廢於家刑罰不可弛於國甲
===
兵不可偃於天下蓋言義之所以成乎仁也
刑之所以弼乎教也彼去義之論宋儒容或
有見而折諸聖經三才之旨不亦失於偏乎
是何也人君之為國也有元氣有神氣深仁
厚澤優游而浸灌焉者所以培元氣也明罰
勅法果敢而奮厲焉者所以作神氣也傳曰
昭我王度式如玉式如金其是之謂乎說者
徒以漢文之玄默足以措刑而漢宣之嚴毅
祗以開釁宋仁之恭儉足以延祚而神宗之
厲精適以滋亂遂謂義之可去而刑之不必

徒以漢文之玄默足以措刑而漢宣之嚴毅
祗以開釁宋仁之恭儉足以延祚而神宗之
厲精適以滋亂遂謂義之可去而刑之不必
punctuated:
哉！夫天地者，人君之父母也；人君者，天地之子也。人君繼天地而為之子，則任德以行吾之仁，而類其生殖長育；任刑以行吾之義，而類其震曜殺戮者，信乎可相有而不可相無矣。古今帝王未之有改。故如天之仁、好生之洽，堯舜之所以仁天下也；而四凶之誅、有苗之北，未嘗不裁之以義焉。文命之敷、兆民之殖、咸和之施，三王之所以仁天下也；而升陑之師、密黎之戡，亦未嘗不治之以義焉。司馬遷曰：「教笞不可廢於家，刑罰不可弛於國，甲兵不可偃於天下。」蓋言義之所以成乎仁也，刑之所以弼乎教也。彼去義之論，宋儒容或有見，而折諸聖經三才之旨，不亦失於偏乎？

是何也？人君之為國也，有元氣，有神氣。深仁厚澤，優游而浸灌焉者，所以培元氣也；明罰勅法，果敢而奮厲焉者，所以作神氣也。傳曰：「昭我王度，式如玉，式如金。」其是之謂乎？說者徒以漢文之玄默足以措刑，而漢宣之嚴毅祗以開釁；宋仁之恭儉足以延祚，而神宗之厲精適以滋亂，遂謂義之可去，而刑之不必
translation_en:
…indeed! Heaven and Earth are the ruler’s parents, and the ruler is their son. As their successor and son, the ruler employs virtue to enact his benevolence, emulating their generation, nurture, and growth of living things; he employs punishment to enact his righteousness, emulating their thunderous might and destruction. These truly must coexist: neither can do without the other. The sovereigns of antiquity and later times have never altered this principle. Benevolence resembling Heaven’s and an all-pervading love of life were how Yao and Shun treated all under Heaven with benevolence; yet in punishing the Four Evildoers and defeating the Miao, they invariably exercised judgment through righteousness. The spreading of civil instruction, the flourishing of the myriad people, and the extension of harmony to all were how the Three Kings treated all under Heaven with benevolence; yet the army that ascended E and the subjugation of Mi and Li likewise brought order through righteousness. Sima Qian said: “Instruction and flogging cannot be abolished in the household; punishments cannot be relaxed in the state; arms cannot be laid aside throughout the realm.” This means that righteousness brings benevolence to completion, and punishment supports moral instruction. As for the argument that righteousness should be discarded, the Song Confucians may perhaps have had some insight; but measured against the purport of the sages’ classics concerning the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—does it not err in being one-sided?

Why is this? In governing a state, the ruler must attend to both its primal vitality and its animating spirit. Profound benevolence and abundant beneficence, gently permeating and nourishing it, cultivate its primal vitality. Making punishments clear and putting the laws in order, acting decisively and with vigor, arouse its animating spirit. The commentary says: “Make manifest our royal standards: take jade as the model; take gold as the model.” Is this not what it means? Those who advance this argument merely suppose that Emperor Wen of Han’s quiet reserve sufficed to set punishments aside, whereas Emperor Xuan of Han’s stern resolve served only to provoke discord; that Emperor Renzong of Song’s reverence and frugality sufficed to prolong the dynasty’s mandate, whereas Emperor Shenzong’s strenuous exertions served only to foster disorder. They therefore claim that righteousness may be discarded and that punishment need not…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
任也而豈知所謂獨陽不生獨陰不成者乎
是賢者之言不免於私反而聖人之經信百
王不易之軌矣臣又伏讀
聖策曰今之人大非賢者及人君纔一用義即為
嚴刻乃作言曰上任刑以為治非三代之治
也却一不之反於已三代之人皆人也不待
義臨而自持惟恐放侈今之人果三代之同
歟至哉
皇言真足以破世俗之見而啓復古之機也盖以
三代之君仁漸義染禮陶樂淑而所以化導
===
乎天下者固不專恃乎刑罰之加然淫用匪
彝率怠弗協者未始不繩之以法故夏有官
刑商有湯刑周有祥刑皆所以贊吾德教之
所不及也謂任刑為三代之治固不可謂三
代之治去乎刑豈得為通論哉又况政教章
明人心丕式不臨之以義而莫非畏義之士
不迫之以刑而皆切懷刑之心貴名檢而賤
放侈重節行而惡貪叨三代之人固不可得
而訾也已然臣竊因是而疑焉
陛下臨御以来十有七年于兹仁以育之而被其

任也，而豈知所謂獨陽不生、獨陰不成者乎？是賢者之言不免於私，反而聖人之經，信百王不易之軌矣。
臣又伏讀聖策曰：「今之人大非賢者，及人君纔一用義，即為嚴刻，乃作言曰：『上任刑以為治，非三代之治也。』却一不之反於已。三代之人皆人也，不待義臨而自持，惟恐放侈。今之人果三代之同歟？」至哉，皇言！真足以破世俗之見而啓復古之機也。盖以三代之君，仁漸義染，禮陶樂淑，而所以化導乎天下者，固不專恃乎刑罰之加。然淫用匪彝、率怠弗協者，未始不繩之以法。故夏有官刑，商有湯刑，周有祥刑，皆所以贊吾德教之所不及也。謂任刑為三代之治，固不可；謂三代之治去乎刑，豈得為通論哉？又况政教章明，人心丕式，不臨之以義，而莫非畏義之士；不迫之以刑，而皆切懷刑之心。貴名檢而賤放侈，重節行而惡貪叨，三代之人固不可得而訾也已。

translation_en:
…be employed. Yet how could they understand the saying, “Yang alone cannot bring forth life; yin alone cannot bring things to completion”? Thus the words of worthy men cannot escape partiality; turning instead to the sages’ classics, we find truly an unchanging standard for all kings.
Your servant has also reverently read Your Majesty’s policy question: “People today fall far short of worthiness. Yet whenever a ruler employs righteousness, even once, they immediately regard it as harshness and severity, declaring: ‘The sovereign relies on punishments to govern; this is not the government of the Three Dynasties.’ Yet they never turn back to examine themselves. The people of the Three Dynasties were all human too; without waiting for righteousness to be brought to bear upon them, they restrained themselves, fearing only that they might become unbridled and extravagant. Are people today truly the same as those of the Three Dynasties?” How consummate are these imperial words! They are indeed sufficient to dispel conventional views and open the way to restoring antiquity. For the rulers of the Three Dynasties steeped their people in benevolence, imbued them with righteousness, molded them through ritual, and improved them through music. In transforming and guiding all under Heaven, they certainly did not rely exclusively on the imposition of punishments. Yet those who wantonly practiced what violated established norms, or were persistently negligent and uncooperative, were invariably restrained by law. Thus the Xia had the Punishments for Officials, the Shang had the Punishments of Tang, and the Zhou had auspicious punishments. All served to supplement what moral instruction could not reach. To say that reliance on punishment constituted the government of the Three Dynasties is certainly inadmissible; but to say that their government dispensed with punishment—how could that be a sound general judgment? Moreover, government and instruction were manifest and clear, and people’s hearts greatly conformed to their standards. Though righteousness was not brought to bear upon them, all revered it; though punishment did not press upon them, all kept it earnestly in mind. They valued reputation and self-restraint and disdained license and extravagance; they prized integrity and conduct and loathed greed. The people of the Three Dynasties were indeed beyond reproach.
Yet this very consideration privately gives your servant cause for doubt. Your Majesty has now occupied the throne for seventeen years. You have nurtured the people with benevolence, and those who have received its…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
澤者廣博而深厚義以斷之而服其明者遷
善而敏德是宜洒濯其心明徵其度在位者
勵周官之六計而臨民者畏楊震之四知利
不貪而純心以報
國慾不縱而苦節以厚民羔羊之風上匹乎周
而闔郡不舉之耻下刷乎漢可也而何怙
天子之仁而不知檢之以義裴寬之鹿未見其瘞
也而儲椒如元載者不能無羊續之魚未見
其懸也而耀幛如王愷者不能免清介如趙
抃不多得也而罔不酌貪泉以自爽儉素如
===
楊綰未之有也而莫非欲竭澤以為漁上負
君國而弗之悟下瘵民生而弗之卹吏治如此烏
足以臻三代之化哉夫直道無間於古今而
斯民可追乎三代古以義今以利貪古以理
今以慾縱是豈三代終不可企乎無亦
陛下之所以教之者純乎仁而所以治之者未盡
斷以義歟夫吏以贓敗則終身不齒於縉紳
政以賄成則祿位不甄於清要古之所以訓
廉者如此也
陛下誠能不循姑息不撓權貴清操自厲者擢以

punctuated:
澤者廣博而深厚，義以斷之，而服其明者遷善而敏德。是宜洒濯其心，明徵其度，在位者勵周官之六計，而臨民者畏楊震之四知，利不貪而純心以報國，慾不縱而苦節以厚民。羔羊之風，上匹乎周，而闔郡不舉之耻，下刷乎漢，可也。而何怙天子之仁，而不知檢之以義？裴寬之鹿，未見其瘞也，而儲椒如元載者不能無；羊續之魚，未見其懸也，而耀幛如王愷者不能免。清介如趙抃，不多得也，而罔不酌貪泉以自爽；儉素如楊綰，未之有也，而莫非欲竭澤以為漁。上負君國而弗之悟，下瘵民生而弗之卹。吏治如此，烏足以臻三代之化哉？

夫直道無間於古今，而斯民可追乎三代。古以義，今以利貪；古以理，今以慾縱。是豈三代終不可企乎？無亦陛下之所以教之者純乎仁，而所以治之者未盡斷以義歟？夫吏以贓敗，則終身不齒於縉紳；政以賄成，則祿位不甄於清要。古之所以訓廉者如此也。陛下誠能不循姑息，不撓權貴，清操自厲者擢以
translation_en:
…those who receive Your Majesty’s beneficence enjoy its breadth and depth; through righteous judgment, those who submit to your discernment turn toward goodness and strive in virtue. They ought therefore to cleanse their hearts and make their standards manifest. Those holding office should exert themselves according to the six criteria for assessing officials in the Offices of Zhou, and those governing the people should stand in awe of Yang Zhen’s “four who know”—Heaven, the spirits, oneself, and the other party. They should shun greed for profit and serve the state with undivided hearts, restrain their desires and maintain austere integrity to enrich the people. The spirit celebrated in “The Lamb” might then equal that of the Zhou, while the disgrace of an entire commandery having no worthy candidate to recommend, as occurred under the Han, might be wiped away. Why, then, do they rely upon the Son of Heaven’s benevolence without knowing how to restrain themselves through righteousness? We have yet to see them bury a deer as Pei Kuan did to reject a gift, yet there are still those who hoard pepper like Yuan Zai. We have yet to see them hang up a fish as Yang Xu did to refuse a gift, yet there are still those who flaunt screens like Wang Kai [?]. Men as pure and upright as Zhao Bian are rarely found; instead, all drink from the Spring of Greed and compromise their integrity. Men as frugal and plain as Yang Wan have yet to appear; instead, all wish to drain the marsh to catch its fish. Above, they betray their sovereign and state without recognizing it; below, they afflict the people’s livelihood without pity. With officials governing in this fashion, how could we attain the transforming influence of the Three Dynasties?

The upright Way makes no distinction between antiquity and the present, and the people of today can equal those of the Three Dynasties. In antiquity, righteousness guided them; today, profit makes them greedy. In antiquity, principle guided them; today, desire makes them unrestrained. Does this mean that the Three Dynasties can never be emulated? Might it instead be that Your Majesty’s instruction rests entirely upon benevolence, while your governance has not yet fully exercised judgment through righteousness? When an official was disgraced for illicit gains, he was excluded from the ranks of the official elite for life; when government business was settled through bribes, the culprit was not selected for a salaried post of purity and importance. Such were the means by which the ancients inculcated incorruptibility. text:
不次之位貪墨不法者加以不貸之刑則賞
罰以公功罪以當吏治不有瘳乎
國之與民不亦具有賴乎臣又伏讀
聖策曰朕祗承
天位惟民是保何官人者皆負國虐民之圖奚為
用哉嗚呼
陛下興言及此寔天下生靈之福也
宗社無疆之休也在昔臯陶之謨曰在知人在安
民知人則哲安民則惠此論官理民之所必
稽也臣觀
===
陛下踐祚以来孜孜保民精選舉以公入仕之途
嚴考課以杜冗官之弊而又裁抑僥倖之風
痛懲奔競之習科目必得乎真才銓曹必核
其實行凡所以慎於知人而篤於安民者無
弗詳且密也而吏不廉平一至於此
陛下何賴於斯人而用之哉則夫制為祿位以勸
其從嚴斷刑罰以威其淫如丘明之所載者
可行也辨賢否以别忠邪之分核功罪以公
賞罰之施如荀悅之所論者可行也不然官
之失德寵賂章也國家之敗由官邪也僖伯

臣觀陛下踐祚以来，孜孜保民，精選舉以公入仕之途，嚴考課以杜冗官之弊，而又裁抑僥倖之風，痛懲奔競之習。科目必得乎真才，銓曹必核其實行。凡所以慎於知人而篤於安民者，無弗詳且密也。而吏不廉平，一至於此，陛下何賴於斯人而用之哉？則夫制為祿位以勸其從，嚴斷刑罰以威其淫，如丘明之所載者，可行也；辨賢否以别忠邪之分，核功罪以公賞罰之施，如荀悅之所論者，可行也。不然，官之失德，寵賂章也；國家之敗，由官邪也。僖伯

…to positions beyond the normal order of promotion, and impose punishment without pardon upon those who are corrupt and lawless. Then rewards and punishments would be impartial, and merit and guilt would receive their due. Would official administration not recover? Would not both the state and the people have something to rely upon? Why do those serving as officials all harbor designs to betray the state and oppress the people? What use is there in employing them?” Ah! That Your Majesty should voice such concerns is truly a blessing for all living souls under Heaven and an inexhaustible source of good fortune for the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain. You have also curbed the tendency to seek advancement through undeserved favor and sternly punished the practice of scrambling for office. The examinations must identify genuine talent, and the personnel authorities must scrutinize candidates’ actual conduct. All the measures by which you exercise care in knowing men and show earnest commitment to bringing peace to the people are thorough and meticulous. Yet officials’ lack of integrity and fairness has reached such a point! What reliance can Your Majesty place upon these men that you should employ them? text:
之言可鑒矣夫勑刑以詰姦正義以防慾固
陛下以孚天之德達憲天之政矣然化裁必本於
身而推行當自於近何者後宫有大練之飾
則天下以紈綺為羞大臣有脫粟之節則天
下以膏粱為愧
陛下惟懷永圖慎乃儉德自宫闈而達之
朝廷自朝廷而達之天下則清化行而人皆浴
德大義孚而士皆惇節孰肯自陷於簠簋不
飾之地以上負吾
君下虐吾民也哉然
===
聖策之終策臣等曰爾多士師孔子之學必心孔
子之心將此心之平正陳為篇列以除弊革
私之道衍為仁育義正之方以告我是
陛下聖不自聖詢于芻蕘之心也臣聞孔子之學
在仁育而義斷而帝王之治貴觀變以協中
是故過於仁則政寬民慢而教焉有所不行
過於義則政猛民殘而治焉有所不繼伏望
陛下變通以盡其利鼓舞以盡其神惠有所當加
賞不以無功而得如書所謂爵罔及惡德官
不及私昵者而後可也威有所當立罰不以

之言可鑒矣夫勑刑以懲貪立義以防慾固
陛下以孚天之德達憲天之政矣然化裁必本於
身而推行當自於近何者後宮有大練之飾
則天下以紈綺爲羞大臣有脱粟之節則天
下以膏粱爲愧
陛下惟懷永圖慎乃儉德自宮闈而達之
朝廷自朝廷而達之天下則清化行而人皆浴
德大義孚而士皆惇節孰肯自陷於簠簋不
飾之地以上負吾

punctuated:
之言可鑒矣。夫勑刑以詰姦，正義以防慾，固陛下以孚天之德、達憲天之政矣。然化裁必本於身，而推行當自於近。何者？後宫有大練之飾，則天下以紈綺為羞；大臣有脫粟之節，則天下以膏粱為愧。陛下惟懷永圖，慎乃儉德，自宫闈而達之朝廷，自朝廷而達之天下，則清化行而人皆浴德，大義孚而士皆惇節，孰肯自陷於簠簋不飾之地，以上負吾君，下虐吾民也哉？
然聖策之終，策臣等曰：「爾多士師孔子之學，必心孔子之心，將此心之平正陳為篇列，以除弊革私之道，衍為仁育義正之方，以告我。」是陛下聖不自聖，詢于芻蕘之心也。臣聞孔子之學在仁育而義斷，而帝王之治貴觀變以協中。是故過於仁，則政寬民慢，而教焉有所不行；過於義，則政猛民殘，而治焉有所不繼。伏望陛下變通以盡其利，鼓舞以盡其神。惠有所當加，賞不以無功而得，如《書》所謂「爵罔及惡德，官不及私昵」者，而後可也。威有所當立，罰不以
translation_en:
…his words offer a warning. Regulating punishments to investigate wrongdoing and upholding righteousness to guard against desire are indeed how Your Majesty accords with Heaven’s virtue and carries out government modeled upon Heaven. Yet adapting institutions to circumstances must be rooted in your own person, and their implementation should begin with those close to you. Why? If the rear palace is adorned with coarse silk, all under Heaven will be ashamed to wear fine silks and brocades; if high ministers show their restraint by eating unhusked grain, all under Heaven will be ashamed of rich meats and fine grain. May Your Majesty cherish enduring plans and attend carefully to your virtue of frugality, extending it from the palace quarters to the court, and from the court to all under Heaven. Then purifying influence will spread, and everyone will bathe in your virtue; great righteousness will inspire trust, and scholars will all strengthen their integrity. Who would willingly fall into official corruption—what is called “failing to keep the ritual vessels in order”—thereby betraying our sovereign above and oppressing our people below?
Yet at the end of the imperial policy question, you question us, your servants, saying: “You many scholars take Confucius’s learning as your model; you must also make Confucius’s heart your own. Set forth in writing the fairness and uprightness of this heart, expanding the means of eliminating abuses and abolishing selfish practices into methods of nurturing through benevolence and correcting through righteousness, and tell me of them.” This expresses Your Majesty’s resolve, though a sage, not to presume upon your sagacity, but to consult even gatherers of grass and firewood. Your servant has heard that Confucius’s learning lies in nurturing through benevolence and deciding through righteousness, while the government of emperors and kings prizes observing changes so as to accord with the mean. Thus, an excess of benevolence makes government lax and the people negligent, so that moral instruction cannot be fully carried out; an excess of righteousness makes government harsh and leaves the people afflicted, so that good government cannot be sustained. I humbly hope that Your Majesty will adapt to changing circumstances to realize every benefit, and inspire the people to bring this wondrous efficacy fully into play. Bestow favor where it is fitting; rewards must not be obtained without merit. Only by following what the Book of Documents calls “Do not grant noble rank to those of evil virtue, nor office to personal favorites” will this be proper. Assert authority where it is fitting; punishments must not be…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
無罪而施亦如書所謂欽哉欽哉惟刑之恤
哉者而後可也仁義交相為用治教並行不
悖茲非愚臣之惓惓於
陛下者乎不然漢元非無仁也而優柔不斷終以
基新室之禍漢明非不義也而苛察過當終
不足於弘人之度將以除弊而弊日滋將以
革私而私日固其何以懲庶官之貪而示帝
王之神武哉雖然仁可過而義不可過昔人
嘗有是言矣然
今日之患正坐於仁之過而義之不足也何則
===
紀綱所由以出治也而今或上下無別貴賤
無章不能無陵替之患振而舉之不有望於
馮河之勇乎守令所恃以安民也而今或以
利滅義誣上行私不能無瘝官之誚飭而厲
之不有望於黜陟之嚴乎將帥所以握兵而
衛國也而或付諸乳臭之童甚者晚唐債帥
復見於今矣釐而正之不有望於赳赳之
宸斷乎刑罰所以詰奸而懲慝也而或委諸吏胥
之手甚者刻木不對誠可哀痛矣督而責之
不有望於明明之

punctuated:
無罪而施，亦如《書》所謂「欽哉！欽哉！惟刑之恤哉」者，而後可也。仁義交相為用，治教並行不悖，茲非愚臣之惓惓於陛下者乎？不然，漢元非無仁也，而優柔不斷，終以基新室之禍；漢明非不義也，而苛察過當，終不足於弘人之度。將以除弊而弊日滋，將以革私而私日固，其何以懲庶官之貪而示帝王之神武哉？雖然，仁可過而義不可過，昔人嘗有是言矣。然今日之患，正坐於仁之過而義之不足也。何則？
紀綱所由以出治也，而今或上下無別，貴賤無章，不能無陵替之患。振而舉之，不有望於馮河之勇乎？守令所恃以安民也，而今或以利滅義，誣上行私，不能無瘝官之誚。飭而厲之，不有望於黜陟之嚴乎？將帥所以握兵而衛國也，而或付諸乳臭之童，甚者晚唐債帥復見於今矣。釐而正之，不有望於赳赳之宸斷乎？刑罰所以詰奸而懲慝也，而或委諸吏胥之手，甚者刻木不對，誠可哀痛矣。督而責之，不有望於明明之
translation_en:
…be inflicted upon the innocent. Only when this also accords with what the Book of Documents calls “Be reverent! Be reverent! Be solicitous in imposing punishments!” will it be acceptable. Benevolence and righteousness should serve one another, and government and moral instruction proceed together without conflict. Is this not what your foolish servant so earnestly wishes of Your Majesty? Otherwise, consider Emperor Yuan of Han: he was not without benevolence, yet his irresolution and failure to act ultimately laid the foundations for the calamity of the Xin dynasty. Emperor Ming of Han was not without righteousness, yet his excessively harsh scrutiny ultimately fell short of the magnanimity needed to accommodate others. If, while intending to eliminate abuses, one lets abuses multiply daily, and while intending to eradicate selfish interests, one lets them grow more entrenched daily, how can one punish the greed of the various officials and display an emperor’s divine martial prowess? Nevertheless, people of old did indeed say that benevolence may be excessive, but righteousness must not be. Yet the trouble today arises precisely from excessive benevolence and insufficient righteousness. Why is this?
Discipline and order are the means by which good government is established. Yet today superiors and inferiors sometimes lack distinction, and the noble and lowly lack clearly defined ranks; there is inevitably a danger of the established hierarchy breaking down. To restore and uphold it, must we not look to the courage of one who would ford a river on foot? Prefects and magistrates are those upon whom we rely to bring peace to the people. Yet today some sacrifice righteousness for profit, deceive their superiors, and pursue private interests; they inevitably incur reproach for neglecting their offices. To set them in order and spur them to exertion, must we not look to strictness in demotion and promotion? Generals and commanders are charged with directing troops and defending the state. Yet these responsibilities are sometimes entrusted to mere infants still smelling of milk; worse still, the debt-ridden commanders of the late Tang, who borrowed to purchase their commands, have reappeared today. To rectify this, must we not look to Your Majesty’s vigorous resolve? Punishments are the means of investigating wrongdoing and chastising wickedness. Yet they are sometimes left in the hands of petty clerks; in extreme cases, people would refuse to answer even a wooden effigy of an official. This is truly grievous. To supervise those responsible and hold them accountable, must we not look to the brilliantly enlightened …

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
廟謨乎凡此皆
今日玩弛之弊而
陛下所當武斷而不恤者也雖然捄弊固存乎正
義而精義又在于知幾使幾有不知則理欲
混淆真妄錯雜未有不以義為利而以利為
義者矣伏望
陛下清心講學極深研幾見天下之賾而不亂通
天下之故而不遺由是以仁惠天下則天下
莫不以為恩以義威天下則天下莫不以為
武庶官惟敘百姓用康而王道神矣易曰惟
===
幾也故能成天下之務願
陛下加之意焉臣草茅不識忌諱惟
陛下矜其愚不錄其罪則愚臣幸甚天下幸甚臣
謹對

武庶官惟欽百姓用康而王道神矣易曰惟
===
幾也故能成天下之務願
陛下加之意焉〔臣〕草茅不識忌諱惟
陛下矜其愚不錄其罪則愚〔臣〕幸甚天下幸甚〔臣〕
謹對
punctuated: 廟謨乎？凡此皆今日玩弛之弊，而陛下所當武斷而不恤者也。雖然，捄弊固存乎正義，而精義又在于知幾。使幾有不知，則理欲混淆，真妄錯雜，未有不以義為利而以利為義者矣。伏望陛下清心講學，極深研幾，見天下之賾而不亂，通天下之故而不遺。由是以仁惠天下，則天下莫不以為恩；以義威天下，則天下莫不以為武。庶官惟敘，百姓用康，而王道神矣。《易》曰：「惟幾也，故能成天下之務。」願陛下加之意焉。臣草茅，不識忌諱，惟陛下矜其愚，不錄其罪，則愚臣幸甚，天下幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…the court’s enlightened counsels? All these are abuses arising from today’s negligence and laxity, which Your Majesty ought to remedy with firm resolve, undeterred by misgivings. Yet although correcting abuses depends upon establishing righteousness, discerning righteousness precisely depends in turn upon recognizing the first subtle signs of change. If these signs go unrecognized, principle and desire become confused, and truth and falsehood intermingle; inevitably, righteousness will be mistaken for profit, and profit for righteousness.

I humbly hope that Your Majesty will clear your mind and pursue learning, plumb the depths and investigate these subtle signs, perceive the intricacies of all under Heaven without confusion, and comprehend the causes of its affairs without omission. Thus, if you bestow benefits upon all under Heaven through benevolence, none will fail to regard this as gracious favor; if you inspire awe throughout all under Heaven through righteousness, none will fail to regard this as martial authority. The many officials will be duly ordered, the people will thereby enjoy well-being, and the kingly Way will attain wondrous efficacy. The Book of Changes says: “Only through discerning the subtle beginnings can one bring the affairs of all under Heaven to completion.” May Your Majesty give this your attention.

Your servant is a humble man from the countryside, ignorant of taboos. If Your Majesty will pity his foolishness and refrain from recording his offense, this foolish servant will be most fortunate, and all under Heaven most fortunate. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

translation_en:
Record of Metropolitan Graduates of the Seventeenth Year of Jiajing (1538)

The Imperial Voice

On the ninth day of the third month of the seventeenth year of Jiajing, your servant Yan Song, Minister of Rites concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy, and others memorialized at Fengtian Gate:

“Concerning the civil-service examinations: in the Metropolitan Examination of provincial graduates from throughout the realm, 320 candidates have been selected. For the Palace Examination on the fifteenth day of the third month this year, we duly propose sixty-four officials as readers and other officiants, including Li Shi, Junior Mentor concurrently serving as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Huagai Hall. The classes of jinshi qualification shall respectfully follow the standards imperially established by Emperor Taizu Gao. The first class shall, as customary, comprise three men: the first shall receive lower sixth rank, and the second and third upper seventh rank, with the distinction ‘jinshi with honors.’ Those in the second class shall receive lower seventh rank and the distinction ‘regular jinshi.’ Those in the third class shall receive upper eighth rank and the distinction ‘associate jinshi.’”

The imperial edict was received: “Approved.” Respect this.

Readers

Li Shi, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Mentor concurrently serving as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Huagai Hall. 〔Metropolitan graduate of the renxu year.〕

Xia Yan, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Guardian concurrently serving as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Rites, and Grand Secretary of the Wuying Hall. 〔Metropolitan graduate of the dingchou year.〕

Xu Zan, Grand Master for Glorious Happiness, Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Personnel. 〔Metropolitan graduate of the bingchen year.〕

translation_en:
Sequence of Imperial Favors and Honors
On the morning of the fifteenth day of the third month of the seventeenth year of Jiajing (1538), the tribute scholars (gongshi) proceeded to the inner palace for the Palace Examination. The emperor took his seat in Fengtian Hall and personally bestowed the policy question.
On the morning of the nineteenth day of the third month, all civil and military officials attended in court dress, standing in their assigned ranks. That day, the Embroidered-uniform Guard arranged the imperial ceremonial regalia at the vermilion steps and within the vermilion courtyard. The emperor took his seat in Fengtian Hall, and officials of the Court of State Ceremonial transmitted the imperial decree and called out the names. Officials of the Ministry of Rites carried the yellow proclamation, led by drums and music, out through Chang’an Left Gate and posted it outside. When this was done, officials of Shuntian Prefecture escorted the first-place graduate (zhuangyuan) back to his residence with a ceremonial parasol and retinue.
On the twentieth day of the third month…

translation_en:
…a banquet was bestowed at the Ministry of Rites. After the banquet, the graduates proceeded to the Court of State Ceremonial to rehearse the ceremonies.
On the twenty-second day of the third month, the first-ranked graduate was granted court robes, a cap, and a girdle, and the metropolitan graduates (jinshi) were granted paper currency.
On the twenty-third day of the third month, the first-ranked graduate led the other metropolitan graduates in submitting a memorial of gratitude for imperial favor.
On the twenty-fourth day of the third month, the first-ranked graduate led the other metropolitan graduates to the temple of Confucius, the First Teacher, to perform the rite of offering vegetables.
The Ministry of Rites memorialized the throne, requesting that the Ministry of Works be ordered to erect a stone stele at the Directorate of Education and inscribe the graduates’ names upon it.

羅珵〔貫江西吉安府泰和縣，軍籍，國子生，治書經，字邦珍，行一，年四十六，十一月十五日生〕。曾祖鐸〔舉人，署訓導事，贈通議大夫、吏部右侍郎〕，祖用俊〔國子監助教，累封通議大夫、吏部右侍郎〕，父欽德〔按察司副使〕，母康氏〔封宜人〕。具慶下，弟瑺，娶楊氏。江西鄉試第三十八名，會試第二百三十二名。

袁煒〔貫浙江寧波府慈谿縣，民籍，縣學附學生，治詩經，字懋中，行三，年三十一，十月十八日生〕。曾祖完，祖鑑，父汝舟，母汪氏，繼母張氏。具慶下，兄炤、煥，弟灼，娶管氏。浙江鄉試第二名，會試第一名。
translation_en:
First Class: three men, granted metropolitan graduate (jinshi) status with honors.

Mao Zan 茅瓚 was registered in Qiantang County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, in an artisan household. An added-quota student at the county Confucian school, he specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Bangxian; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty years old, born on the sixth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Shi’an; his grandfather, Mao; and his father, Lin, an official awaiting selection for appointment. His mother was née Zhang, and his stepmother née Ru. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Zhen and Ke, and his wife was née Fang. He placed twenty-second in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 244th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Luo Cheng 羅珵 was registered in Taihe County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Bangzhen; he ranked first among his brothers and was forty-six years old, born on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather, Duo, was a provincial graduate (juren) who served as acting Assistant Instructor and was posthumously granted the titles Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of Personnel. His grandfather, Yongjun, was an Instructor in the Directorate of Education and received successive honorary grants culminating in the titles Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of Personnel. His father, Qinde, was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner; his mother, née Kang, was granted the title Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Chang, and his wife was née Yang. He placed thirty-eighth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 232nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yuan Wei 袁煒 was registered in Cixi County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. An attached student at the county Confucian school, he specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Maozhong; he ranked third among his brothers and was thirty-one years old, born on the eighteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Wan; his grandfather, Jian; and his father, Ruzhou. His mother was née Wang, and his stepmother née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Zhao and Huan, and his younger brother was Zhuo. His wife was née Guan. He placed second in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and first in the Metropolitan Examination.

吳源〔貫浙江杭州府錢塘縣，民籍，國子生，治禮記，字宗乾，行九，年四十六，八月二十三日生〕。曾祖志學〔贈通議大夫、都察院右副都御史〕，祖燾〔八品散官〕，父璿〔府同知，進階朝列大夫〕，嫡母陳氏，生母林氏。永感下，兄濟、沂、海、漢、泰、洵、深，弟澹〔冠帶醫士〕、澯〔冠帶醫士〕、漳〔義官〕、洲〔義官〕、潮、潤、滂、瀕、浩、洽、涵、浹、泳，娶陸氏。浙江鄉試第三十一名，會試第一百五十名。
translation_en:
Second class: ninety-five men, granted metropolitan graduate (jinshi) status.

Zhang Weiyi, registered in Ansu County, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Shouzhong; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-six years old, born on the fifteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Hao, his grandfather Heng, and his father Yu, a School Instructor; his mother was née Li. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Weijing, and his younger brothers were Weishi, Weiji, Weiyun, and Weihan. He married a woman née Hu. He placed first in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and sixty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Yingyun, registered in Haiyan County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a medical household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Conglong; he ranked second among his brothers and was forty-six years old, born on the eighteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jin, his grandfather Yu, who held an honorary official title for longevity, and his father Jin (縉); his mother was née Feng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Lei, and his younger brothers were Dian, Ji, and Zhan. He married a woman née Sun. He placed sixtieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 288th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Yuan, registered in Qiantang County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Record of Rites. His courtesy name was Zongqian; he ranked ninth among his brothers and was forty-six years old, born on the twenty-third day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhixue, posthumously granted the titles Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His grandfather Tao held a prestige title of the eighth rank. His father Xuan was a Vice Prefect, advanced to the prestige title Grand Master for Court Service. His father's principal wife was née Chen, and his birth mother was née Lin. His parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ji, Yi, Hai, Han, Tai, Xun, and Shen. His younger brothers were Dan and Can, both physicians authorized to wear official caps and girdles; Zhang and Zhou, both holders of honorary official titles for public beneficence; and Chao, Run, Pang, Pin, Hao, Qia, Han, Jia, and Yong. He married a woman née Lu. He placed thirty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 150th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Mo Ruzhong, courtesy name Ziliang, was registered in a civilian household in Huating County, Songjiang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. An annual tribute student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty years old, born on the seventh day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ang; his grandfather, Hao, was an assistant prefect; his father, Yu, was a tribute scholar; and his mother was née Zhu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Ruxin, Rude, Rujue, and Ruyi. He married a woman née Tang and subsequently a woman née Yang. He placed second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 238th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Shidao, courtesy name Zizhuan, was registered in a civilian household in Wu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Changzhou County. A prefectural school student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-nine years old, born on the eighth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yong; his grandfather, Wei; his father, Ping; and his mother, née Chen. His mother was living and his father deceased. His younger brother was Andao. He married a woman née Cao and subsequently a woman née Wu. He placed thirty-third in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 193rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lun Yishen, courtesy name Yanqun, was registered in a civilian household in Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong. A Confucian scholar specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked eighth among his brothers and was thirty-seven years old, born on the twenty-second day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jing; his grandfather, Ming, received the honorary title of Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy. His father, Wenxu, was Right Admonisher in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently serving as Expositor in the Hanlin Academy, and was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master for Court Discussion and Chancellor of the Nanjing Directorate of Education. His mother, née Ou, received the title of Grand Respectful Lady. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Yiliang, a bureau director in the Ministry of Personnel, and Yixun, Chancellor of the Nanjing Directorate of Education; his younger brothers were Yirang, Yizou, Yichen, Yidang, Yi'e, Yimo, Yiyu, Yicheng, Yimi, Yizan, and Yifang. He married a woman née Deng. He placed twentieth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and eighty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fang Guozuo, courtesy name Junying, was registered in a civilian household in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian. An attached student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first among his brothers and was forty-one years old, born on the thirteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jingda; his grandfather, Xuewen; his father, Shikong; and his mother, née Zheng. His mother was living and his father deceased. His younger brothers were Guolie, Guozhao, Guoxiu, and Guofu. He married a woman née Huang. He placed twenty-fourth in both the Fujian Provincial Examination and the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Qiao Shining, registered in Yaozhou, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Jingshu; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-six, born on the eighteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gang, his grandfather Zhiyu, and his father Zhongjie. His father’s former wife was née Yao, his mother née Li, and his stepmother née Bai. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brother Shiding held an honorary office for philanthropy. He married a woman née Song. He placed first in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and twentieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Zheng, registered in Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a military household and was an additional student of the prefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Zhuangyu; he ranked third among his brothers and was aged twenty-eight, born on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Chao, his grandfather Wenxiang, who held an honorary office conferred for longevity, and his father Liangyu. His mother was née Huo. His parents and grandparents were living. His elder brothers were Zhao and Jun, and his younger brother was Jie. He was betrothed to a woman née Chen. He placed first in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and fifty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Chun, registered in Guixi County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Yirong; he ranked nineteenth among his brothers and was aged twenty-seven, born on the twenty-fourth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather Jiamou held an honorary office conferred for longevity. His grandfather Shouxu was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master for Administration and Director in the Ministry of War. His father Daonan was a Director in the Ministry of War. His mother, née Shu, was granted the title Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Tai, Feng, and Zou; Feng and Zou were students of the Directorate of Education. His younger brothers were Zhen and Quan [?]; Quan was also a student of the Directorate of Education. He married a woman née Xia. He placed tenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Kun, registered in Wujiang County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to an artisan household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Meizhi; he ranked fourth among his brothers and was aged thirty-seven, born on the eleventh day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather Bo’ang was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master of the Palace and Chief Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud. His grandfather Zhang was granted the title Secretary in the Ministry of Justice and posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master of the Palace and Chief Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud. His father Hong was Minister of Justice at Nanjing, advanced in rank to Grand Master for Fostering Virtue and Senior Minister of Correct Governance, and posthumously granted the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent. His father’s former wives, née Zhou and née Xia, were each posthumously granted the title Lady; his mother, née Wang, was granted the title Lady. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Shan, Left Assistant Censor-in-Chief in the Censorate and formerly Right Vice Censor-in-Chief; Yan 巖, Right Administration Vice Commissioner in the Sichuan Provincial Administration Commission; and Yan 巘, formerly Archivist in the Court of Imperial Entertainments. He married a woman née Chen and subsequently married women née Wang and née Hong. He placed eighty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 266th in the Metropolitan Examination.

董子儀〔貫直隸松江府上海縣，民籍，國子生，治書經，字羽吉，行一，年三十七，正月二十二日生〕。曾祖和，祖經，父龍，母喬氏。嚴侍下，弟子傚、子佩，娶黃氏。應天府鄉試第八十九名，會試第一百二十名。
translation_en:
Yao Zhang, registered in Yuanling County, Chenzhou Prefecture, Huguang, belonged to a civilian household and was a prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Ruyu; he ranked third in his family, was thirty years old, and was born on the twenty-eighth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zongxian, a District Magistrate; his grandfather was Rang; and his father was Shitai, an honorary official (yiguan). His father's former wife was née He, his legal mother née Li, and his birth mother née Dong. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Qiong, Ying, and Rui, and his younger brothers Wei and Xuan. He married a woman née Xiao. He placed first in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 277th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Kui, registered in Haiyan County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Wenming; he ranked first in his family, was thirty-nine years old, and was born on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rong, his grandfather Ben, and his father Xuan. His mother was née Chen; his successive stepmothers were née Wu 吳 and née Wu 伍. His father was living and his mother deceased. He married a woman née Zhu and subsequently a woman née Wu. He placed forty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Lian, registered in Anzhou Subprefecture, Baoding Prefecture, Zhili, belonged to a civilian household and was a subprefectural school student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Boqing; he ranked second in his family, was thirty-five years old, and was born on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gui; his grandfather was Mian, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi); and his father was Hanqing, an Assistant Instructor. His mother was née Zhuang. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother Lan was a tribute student (gongshi). He married a woman née Zhang. He placed 124th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 113th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Dong Ziyi, registered in Shanghai County, Songjiang Prefecture, Zhili, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Yuji; he ranked first in his family, was thirty-seven years old, and was born on the twenty-second day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was He, his grandfather Jing, and his father Long. His mother was née Qiao. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Zixiao and Zipei. He married a woman née Huang. He placed eighty-ninth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 120th in the Metropolitan Examination.

王健〔貫浙江温州府永嘉縣，軍竈籍，國子生，治易經，字偉純，行十，年三十七，二月初三日生〕。曾祖文燠〔贈通議大夫、禮部左侍郎〕，祖祚〔封翰林院編修、文林郎，贈通議大夫、禮部左侍郎〕，父瓚〔南京禮部左侍郎，贈禮部尚書〕，母應氏〔封淑人〕。永感下。兄僎、偁〔監生〕、儒、備、傅〔監生〕、儶、傲、侹〔南京督察院都事〕、倅；弟佐。娶戴氏。順天府鄉試第二名，會試第十一名。

丁以忠〔貫江西南昌府新建縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字崇義，行五，年四十，十月十九日生〕。曾祖用治，祖儀，父大章，母程氏。永感下。兄以誠。娶余氏。江西鄉試第六十八名，會試第二十九名。

王問〔貫直隸常州府無錫縣，民籍，國子生，治書經，字子裕，行二，年四十二，十一月二十四日生〕。曾祖經，祖宗〔壽官〕，父澤〔封戶部主事〕，母錢氏〔封安人〕。具慶下。兄召〔州同知，前戶部員外郎〕；弟咨。娶李氏，繼娶袁氏。應天府鄉試第二十八名，會試第七十六名。

郭乾〔貫直隸河間府任丘縣，民籍，國子生，治書經，字易甫，行四，年二十八，五月二十九日生〕。曾祖欽〔縣主簿〕，祖源，父勝，前母郝氏，母張氏。慈侍下。兄節。娶劉氏。順天府鄉試第九十五名，會試第三百一名。
translation_en:
Wang Jian 王健 was from Yongjia County, Wenzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, registered in a military salt-producing household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Weichun and ranked tenth among his brothers. He was thirty-seven, born on the third day of the second month. His great-grandfather, Wenyu, was posthumously granted the titles Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites. His grandfather, Zuo, was granted the titles Hanlin Academy Compiler and Gentleman of Literary Service, and posthumously granted those of Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites. His father, Zan, was Left Vice Minister of Rites at Nanjing and was posthumously granted the title Minister of Rites. His mother, née Ying, was granted the title Lady of Virtue (shuren). Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Zhuan 僎, Cheng 偁 (an Imperial University student), Ru 儒, Bei 備, Fu 傅 (an Imperial University student), Hui 儶, Ao 傲, Ting 侹 (Office Manager of the Nanjing Censorate [?]), and Cui 倅; his younger brother was Zuo 佐. He married a woman née Dai. He placed second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eleventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ding Yizhong 丁以忠 was from Xinjian County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, registered in a civilian household. A county school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Chongyi and ranked fifth among his brothers. He was forty, born on the nineteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Yongzhi; his grandfather, Yi; his father, Dazhang; and his mother, née Cheng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Yicheng. He married a woman née Yu. He placed sixty-eighth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and twenty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Wen 王問 was from Wuxi County, Changzhou Prefecture, the directly administered metropolitan region, registered in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Ziyu and ranked second among his brothers. He was forty-two, born on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Jing. His grandfather, Zong, held an honorary official title conferred for longevity. His father, Ze, was granted the title Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue; his mother, née Qian, was granted the title Lady of Repose (anren). Both parents were living. His elder brother, Zhao, was a Department Vice Magistrate and formerly a Vice Director in the Ministry of Revenue; his younger brother was Zi. He married a woman née Li and subsequently a woman née Yuan. He placed twenty-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Qian 郭乾 was from Renqiu County, Hejian Prefecture, the directly administered metropolitan region, registered in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Yifu and ranked fourth among his brothers. He was twenty-eight, born on the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather, Qin, was a County Registrar; his grandfather was Yuan; and his father, Sheng. His father's former wife was née Hao, and his mother was née Zhang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brother was Jie. He married a woman née Liu. He placed ninety-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and three hundred and first in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhu Yong, registered in Henan Guard, Henan, belonged to a military household and was a student of the National University. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Boji. He was first in birth order, aged forty-two, and born on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wang, his grandfather Tong, his father Yong, and his mother née Li. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Zhou, and his wife was née Shen. He ranked eleventh in the Henan Provincial Examination and 265th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tang Mu, from Qiongshan County, Qiongzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the National University. He specialized in the Book of Rites; his courtesy name was Jingwen. He was first in birth order, aged forty-one, and born on the second day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather Qiansheng and grandfather Zheng were each posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Revenue. His father Zhou was Left Vice Minister of Revenue, and his mother, née Zhong, was granted the title of Lady of Virtue. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Zhi and Jia. He married a woman née Li and subsequently a woman née Gao. He ranked fourth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and sixtieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Tingchen, from Hongtong County, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, belonged to a military household and was a student of the county school. He specialized in the Classic of Changes; his courtesy name was Bolin. He was second in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the fourteenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xian. His grandfather Gong was an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions and was granted the title of Vice Commander of a Wardens’ Office. His father Rong was an Assistant Prefect. His father's principal wife, née Ji, was granted the title of Lady; his birth mother was née Lin. His father was deceased, and he attended his living mother. His elder brother Tingxiang was a tribute scholar; his younger brothers were Tingbi and Tingpin. His wife was née Duan. He ranked first in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 196th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan Ji, from Zhending County, Zhending Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the prefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Rites; his courtesy name was Tingji. He was third in birth order, aged twenty-seven, and born on the eighteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather Shu was an office clerk; his grandfather Yun was posthumously granted the title of Investigating Censor. His father Cheng was a Vice Prefect and formerly an Investigating Censor. His mother, née Li, was granted the title of Lady. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were 𣐍 [pronunciation uncertain], a student of the National University, and Gui, a titular official of the seventh rank. His wife was née Zhang. He ranked twenty-fourth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 314th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Chen Xian, registered in a civilian household in Jiaxing County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Daofu; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-three, born on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Jian, his grandfather Zhao, and his father Qing; his mother was née Li. His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His younger brothers were Cai, Hong, and Zhou. He married a woman née Liu and subsequently a woman née Jin. He placed tenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 124th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Changji, registered in a military household in Taihe County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zifa; he ranked fourth among his brothers and was aged thirty, born on the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Zhengda, his grandfather Bixun, and his father Zhude; his mother was née Luo. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Deming, an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner; Dewen, a tribute scholar; Changmo; and Changjun. His younger brother Changfu was a District Magistrate. He married a woman née Luo and subsequently a woman née Zhu. He placed first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 295th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xie Huai, registered in a civilian household in Renqiu County, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was originally from Gaoyang County. He was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yuhui; he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-eight, born on the twelfth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Ju, his grandfather Zhen, and his father Fang; his mother was née Wang. His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His elder brother was Qin, and his younger brothers were Jiang and Wei. He married a woman née Bian and subsequently another woman née Bian. He placed sixteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 161st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hou Ruliang, registered in an official household of the Taiyuan Left Guard in Shanxi, was originally from Hua County in the directly administered metropolitan region. He was an added student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Shuzhen; he ranked third among his brothers and was aged twenty-four, born on the ninth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather Shouxian and grandfather Sheng each held the prestige title General of Military Strategy and served as Vice Battalion Commander. His father Lun was Chief Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud. His father’s former wife, née Yu, was posthumously granted the title Lady of Peace; his mother, née Wang, was granted the same title. His mother was deceased, and he attended his surviving father. His elder brothers were Ruzhong, a Vice Battalion Commander; Ruqian; Rune; Ruduan; and Ruhui. His younger brothers were Rushen, Ruchen, and Rujing. He married a woman née Kan. He placed nineteenth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and sixteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Weng Dali, registered in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Rucan and ranked first in family order. He was twenty-two, born on the twenty-eighth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Min, his grandfather Quan, his father Zuo, and his mother Lady Yang. His parents and members of the grandparental generation were living. His elder brother was Ci; his younger brothers were Dayin, Dazhang, and Dayi. He married Lady Jiang. He placed sixty-fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and seventy-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Qiu, registered in Guixi County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Rites, he had the courtesy name Kejing and ranked 119th in family order. He was thirty-four, born on the twenty-second day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jingshen, his grandfather Tingjun, and his father Xuan. His father's former wife was Lady Xu, his mother Lady Zhu, and his stepmother Lady Qiu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Zhuo, a Vice Prefect; Feng, a District Magistrate; Jin, an Instructor; Si, a former Investigating Censor; Qian; and He. His younger brother was Chu. He married Lady Ye. He placed ninety-fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 249th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Maozhi, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household. An additional student of the county school specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Junben and ranked first in family order. He was twenty, born on the nineteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ji, Director of a Tax Office; his grandfather was Duo, an honorary official; his father was Huan. His mother was Lady Fang and his stepmother Lady Chen. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yingbiao, a Surveillance Vice Commissioner; Yuntong, an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner; Yingcai, a tribute scholar; Yinggui; Yingshu; and Yingdong. His younger brothers were Yinggou, Yingji, and Yingnan. He was betrothed to Lady Song. He placed third in the Fujian Provincial Examination and fifty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Min, registered in Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Qinfu and ranked fifth in family order. He was thirty-seven, born on the nineteenth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Kongzhao, his grandfather Mengzhi, and his father Chenshuang. His mother was Lady Liao and his stepmother Lady Deng. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Jing; his younger brothers were Jiao and Xiao. He married Lady Gong. He placed second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 115th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Yang Jin, registered in a military household in Dangtu County, Taiping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Chongnan; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-five years old, born on the twenty-third day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lisan; his grandfather Tong was posthumously granted the titles Grand Master for Forthright Service and Vice Director in the Nanjing Ministry of Revenue; his father Jian was a Vice Director in the Nanjing Ministry of Revenue. His mother, née Zhang, was granted the title Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Luan, and his wife was née Xu. He placed fortieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 121st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Bi was registered in an officer household of the Nanjing Yulin Right Guard and was a native of Xuyi County in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Guoxian; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-nine years old, born on the ninth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather Wen, grandfather Zhen, and father Sheng were each a Guard Commander; his mother was née Guo. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother Lei was a Company Commander, and his younger brothers were Ying and Run. His wife was née Xu; he subsequently married a woman née Jiang. He placed eighty-fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and twenty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Qi, registered in a civilian household in Wu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a native of Wujiang County. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Ziyou; he ranked fourth among his brothers and was forty-one years old, born on the twenty-first day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Duan; his grandfather Ben held a seventh-rank prestige title; his father Jing was a Medical Instructor. His father's former wife was née Fang, and his mother was née Wu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ao and Yue, both Subprefectural Clerks, and Shan; his younger brothers were Yan and Dai, the latter a student of the Directorate of Education. His wife was née Guo. He placed fortieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 300th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hong Shiwen, registered in a civilian household in Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Guohua; he ranked fifth among his brothers and was twenty-nine years old, born on the eleventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather Ying was Grand Master for Fostering Virtue and Right Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate; his grandfather Chang was a student admitted by imperial favor; his father, whose given name is transcribed as 𤐣 [?], was a District Magistrate. His legal mother was née Zheng, and his birth mother was née Huang. His father was deceased and his mother living. His younger brother was Shiqian, and his wife was née Deng. He placed fiftieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and tenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wenren Dexing 聞人悳行 was registered in a civilian household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a prefectural school student specializing in the Record of Rites. His courtesy name was Yuanke; he ranked first in birth order and was twenty-seven years old, born on the eighth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Chou; his grandfather, Yan, was a county Registrar; his father was Zhuang; his mother was née Xu, and his stepmother née Zheng. His grandparents and parents were living. His younger brothers were Derong, Deye, Dejiao, Delong, Dehua, Dezheng, Defu, and Deying. He married a woman née Yu. He placed tenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and thirty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Xian 俞憲 was registered in a civilian household in Wuxi County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Rucheng; he ranked first in birth order and was thirty-one years old, born on the eighth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Gongyuan; his grandfather, Tingjun; his father, Hui; and his mother, née Yang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Yue, and his younger brothers were Cai, Yin, Guan, Jian, Bin, Shi, and Xuan. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed sixty-third in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 195th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Hao 張鎬 was registered in a civilian household in Dingxing County, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Jingyang County, Shaanxi. He was an Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Qizhou; he ranked third in birth order and was thirty-eight years old, born on the twentieth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Jian; his grandfather, Cai; his father, Jingfang, held an honorary office for longevity; and his mother was née Li. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jin and Quan, the latter bearing the designation “General with Cap and Girdle” [?]; his younger brother was Jian 鑑. He married a woman née Zhao and subsequently a woman née Xu. He placed fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 147th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Kun 周鯤 was registered in a military household in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Shaoyu; he ranked second in birth order and was thirty-two years old, born on the eighteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather, Nian, was an Assistant Instructor; his grandfather, Qiu, was an Assistant Instructor posthumously granted the title of Investigating Censor; his father, Xuan, was Left Provincial Administration Commissioner in a Provincial Administration Commission; and his mother, née Chen, had been invested with the title of Lady (ruren). His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Ao. He married a woman née Ke. He placed seventy-third in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 211th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Xianqing, courtesy name Lianfu, was registered in Kunshan County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. An additional student of the county school, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He ranked first in family order and was thirty-three years old, born on the twelfth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Mao, his grandfather Cong, and his father Yu; his mother was née Du. His mother alone was still living. He married a woman née Gu. He placed tenth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 255th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Tingchun, courtesy name Maoren, was registered in Yugan County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household. An added student of the county school, he specialized in the Book of Odes. He ranked first in family order and was twenty-six years old, born on the first day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhan, his grandfather Jing, and his father Xian; his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were still living. His younger brothers were Tingxiang, Tingdui, Tingshi, Tingyu, and Tingshi. He was betrothed to a woman née Liu. He placed twenty-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and thirty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan Zhong, courtesy name Zhifu, was registered in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in an artisan household. An additional student of the county school, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He ranked first in family order and was twenty-eight years old, born on the twenty-eighth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Hao, his grandfather Chen, and his father Ang; his mother was née Zou. Both parents were still living. His younger brother was He. He married a woman née Chen. He placed sixty-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 231st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Bi, courtesy name Wenfu, was registered in Puzhou, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Odes. He ranked eleventh in family order and was forty years old, born on the thirteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yin; his grandfather Zhen was an Honorary Official; his father Yuan was an Imperial Son-in-Law; and his mother was the Lady of Yongchuan Commandery. Both parents were still living. His elder brothers were Lu, Zan, Qi, Xuan, and Huan. His younger brothers were Mao, Bao (an Imperial Son-in-Law), Yu, Hu (an Imperial Son-in-Law), Lian (an Honorary Official), and Jie (an Imperial Son-in-Law). He married a woman née Wang. He placed tenth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 153rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

順天府鄉試第四十三名 會試第一百六名
劉志 貫山西平陽府翼城縣民籍 國子生
治易經字寧卿行三年三十六正月初九日生
曾祖復嚴 祖贇〔恩例冠帶〕 父珊〔訓導〕 母曹氏
具慶下 兄愈 弟拯 聰 娶李氏
山西鄉試第七名 會試第三百十三名
punctuated:
陳鎏，貫直隸蘇州府吳縣，匠籍，縣學附學生。治易經，字子兼，行二，年三十三，三月二十三日生。曾祖寧〔王府教授〕，祖懷，父冕，前母沈氏，母莫氏。具慶下，娶曹氏，繼娶韓氏。應天府鄉試第二名，會試第四十二名。

譚維，貫四川潼川州遂溪縣，民籍，國子生。治易經，字元立，行九，年四十七，五月二十五日生。曾祖必成，祖宣〔知縣〕，父宗簡〔封監察御史〕，母陳氏〔封孺人〕。慈侍下，兄珪、儼、伋、冠〔府同知〕、采〔鹽運司副使〕、纘〔按察司副使〕、純〔義官〕，弟繼〔監生〕，娶張氏。四川鄉試第三十七名，會試第二百七十一名。

王楠，貫直隸興州後屯衛，官籍，浙江會稽縣人，三河縣學生。治詩經，字惟喬，行四，年四十六，九月二十日生。曾祖忠〔指揮僉事，贈錦衣衛都指揮同知〕，祖鑑〔指揮僉事，贈錦衣衛都指揮同知〕，父玉〔錦衣衛都指揮同知，充漕運參將〕，母邢氏〔封夫人〕。永感下，兄桐，弟楊〔兵部員外郎〕、棟、稠、栩、槐，娶袁氏。順天府鄉試第四十三名，會試第二百六名。

劉志，貫山西平陽府翼城縣，民籍，國子生。治易經，字寧卿，行三，年三十六，正月初九日生。曾祖復嚴，祖玘〔恩例冠帶〕，父珊〔訓導〕，母曹氏。具慶下，兄愈，弟悊、聰，娶李氏。山西鄉試第七名，會試第三百十三名。
translation_en:
Chen Liu 陳鎏 was registered in Wu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in an artisan household, and was an additional student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Zijian. Second in birth order, he was aged thirty-three and was born on the twenty-third day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Ning (Professor in a princely establishment), his grandfather Huai, and his father Mian; his father's former wife was née Shen, and his mother was née Mo. Both parents were living. He married a woman née Cao and subsequently a woman née Han. He ranked second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and forty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tan Wei 譚維 was registered in Suixi County [?], Tongchuan Subprefecture, Sichuan, in a civilian household, and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Yuanli. Ninth in birth order, he was aged forty-seven and was born on the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Bicheng, his grandfather Xuan (County Magistrate), and his father Zongjian (granted the title of Investigating Censor); his mother, née Chen, was granted the title of Lady (ruren). His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Gui, Yan, Ji, Guan (Vice Prefect), Cai (Vice Commissioner of the Salt Distribution Commission), Zuan (Vice Commissioner of the Provincial Surveillance Commission), and Chun (Honorary Official); his younger brother was Ji (an Imperial University student). He married a woman née Zhang. He ranked thirty-seventh in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and two hundred seventy-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Nan 王楠 was registered in an official household in the Xingzhou Rear Agricultural Garrison of the directly administered metropolitan region. He was a native of Kuaiji County, Zhejiang, and a student of the Sanhe County school. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Weiqiao. Fourth in birth order, he was aged forty-six and was born on the twentieth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather Zhong and grandfather Jian were both Assistant Commanders, each posthumously granted the title of Regional Vice Military Commissioner of the Embroidered Uniform Guard. His father Yu was Regional Vice Military Commissioner of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, serving as Assistant Regional Commander for grain transport; his mother, née Xing, was granted the title of Lady (furen). Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Tong; his younger brothers were Yang (Vice Director in the Ministry of War), Dong, Chou, Xu, and Huai. He married a woman née Yuan. He ranked forty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and two hundred sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Zhi 劉志 was registered in Yicheng County, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, in a civilian household, and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Ningqing. Third in birth order, he was aged thirty-six and was born on the ninth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Fuyan, his grandfather Qi (accorded the privilege of wearing official cap and belt under regulations for imperial grace), and his father Shan (Assistant Instructor); his mother was née Cao. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yu; his younger brothers were Zhe and Cong. He married a woman née Li. He ranked seventh in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and three hundred thirteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

徐緯〔貫浙江紹興府山陰縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字文成，行四十三，平三十九，二月十四日生〕。曾祖瑾，祖鋼，父惟，母沈氏。具慶下，兄糾、級、綺，弟綬、縝、縯、綰、縿，娶周氏。浙江鄉試第二十三名，會試第二百九十六名。

鄭廷鵠〔貫廣東海南衛軍籍，浙江慈谿縣人，國子生，治易經，字元侍，行一，年三十二，八月二十四日生〕。曾祖籥，祖順宗，父文，母俞氏。具慶下，娶海氏。廣東鄉試第十九名，會試第三名。

章煥〔貫直隸蘇州府長洲縣民籍，吳縣人，國子生，治易經，字懋實，行二，年三十四，七月十一日生〕。曾祖思恭，祖澄，父棟，母唐氏，繼母魯氏。具慶下，兄炤，弟燦、爌、燁、焯，娶沈氏。應天府鄉試第一百二十一名，會試第三百十七名。

蔣懷德〔貫浙江紹興府山陰縣民籍，府學生，治詩經，字維寧，行十四，年三十九，九月二十日生〕。曾祖玉，祖孝，父實，母潘氏。嚴侍下，兄懷正、懷義、懷遠，弟懷禮、懷貞，娶毛氏，繼娶王氏、趙氏。浙江鄉試第六十八名，會試第七名。
translation_en:
Xu Wei 徐緯 was registered in a civilian household in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Wencheng, and he ranked forty-third in family order. He was aged thirty-nine [?; the transcription has 平 in place of the expected 年] and was born on the fourteenth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jin, his grandfather Gang, his father Wei 惟, and his mother née Shen. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jiu, Ji, and Qi; his younger brothers were Shou, Zhen, Yan, Wan, and Shan. He married a woman née Zhou. He placed twenty-third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 296th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Tinghu 鄭廷鵠 was registered in a military household of Hainan Guard, Guangdong, and was a native of Cixi County, Zhejiang. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Yuanshi; he ranked first in family order, was aged thirty-two, and was born on the twenty-fourth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yue, his grandfather Shunzong, his father Wen, and his mother née Yu. Both parents were living. He married a woman née Hai. He placed nineteenth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Huan 章煥 was registered in a civilian household in Changzhou County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Wu County. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Maoshi; he ranked second in family order, was aged thirty-four, and was born on the eleventh day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Sigong, his grandfather Cheng, his father Dong, his mother née Tang, and his stepmother née Lu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Zhao; his younger brothers were Can, Kuang, Ye, and Zhuo. He married a woman née Shen. He placed 121st in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 317th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jiang Huaide 蔣懷德 was registered in a civilian household in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a prefectural school student. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Weining, and he ranked fourteenth in family order. He was aged thirty-nine and was born on the twentieth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yu, his grandfather Xiao, his father Shi, and his mother née Pan. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Huaizheng, Huaiyi, and Huaiyuan; his younger brothers were Huaili and Huaizhen. He married a woman née Mao and subsequently married women née Wang and née Zhao. He placed sixty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Qing Wenrui, courtesy name Ruxian, was registered in an artisan household in Gong’an County, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first in birth order, was forty years old, and was born on the seventh day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Lun; his grandfather was Xi, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his father was Cheng; and his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Wenyuan. He married a woman née Zhu and subsequently a woman née Tian. He placed forty-second in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 204th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Weiping, courtesy name Shude, was registered in a military household in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian. An supplementary student of the county Confucian school specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first in birth order, was twenty-five years old, and was born on the third day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Zhao, an Instructor posthumously awarded the title of Secretary in the Nanjing Ministry of War; his grandfather was Yingxing; his father was Zhizong; and his mother was née Zhou. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Weihan. He married a woman née Lin. He placed ninetieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 319th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Peng Xixian, courtesy name Jifu, was registered in a military household in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked second in birth order, was thirty-seven years old, and was born on the third day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Tizi; his grandfather was Zhao; his father was Liangpu; and his mother was née Chen. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Xisheng, and his younger brothers were Xiwu, Xiying, Xican, Xiyan, Xibin, Xiqu, and Xilian. He married a woman née Xu. He placed fifty-sixth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 114th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Xu, courtesy name Bangli, was registered in a civilian household in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked sixteenth in birth order, was forty-four years old, and was born on the twelfth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Mengyan; his grandfather was Heng, an Assistant Instructor; his father was Wenbin; and his mother was née Song. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yunqu, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), Yuncheng, Yunjie, and Mu. He married a woman née Yu. He placed sixty-eighth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 260th in the Metropolitan Examination.
