茅坤〔貫浙江湖州府歸安縣民籍，縣學生，治書經，字順甫，行二，年二十七，七月二十一日生〕。曾祖剛，祖珪，父遷，母李氏。重慶下，兄乾，弟艮、益、應龍、大有、應虎，娶姚氏。浙江鄉試第十一名，會試第十三名。
translation_en:
Ru Qixian, registered in a civilian household in Wujiang County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Maosi, he ranked third in his family, and he was thirty years old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Sicong, Commander of a Wardens' Office; his grandfather was Zhongqi, posthumously appointed Director in the Ministry of Personnel; and his father was Tai, a Prefect. His father's former wife, née Yu 郁, was posthumously granted the title Lady of Suitability; his mother, née Yu 于, was granted the same title. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Weixian, an Assistant Prefect of a subprefecture, and Gong and Zhi [?]; he married a woman née Zhang. He placed fifty-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and twelfth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Weiyue, registered in a military household in Xiaofeng County, Anji Subprefecture, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a county school student specializing in the Book of Rites; his courtesy name was Junbo, he ranked fifth in his family, and he was twenty-five years old, born on the fourth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qi, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his grandfather was Song, granted the titles Grand Master for Governance and Director in the Ministry of Personnel; and his father was Lin, a District Magistrate and formerly an Investigating Censor. His father's former wife, née Wang, was posthumously granted the title Lady of Obedience; his birth mother, née Fang, was granted the same title. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Weichuan, Weixia, Weijing, and Weicheng; he married a woman née Zang. He placed fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 197th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Yukai, registered in a civilian household in Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Maoqing, he ranked ninth in his family, and he was thirty-four years old, born on the thirteenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jingxing, his grandfather Bichang, and his father Guangzai; his mother was née Fu and his stepmother née Li. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yutuo and Yushi, and his younger brothers Yurui and Yulin; he married a woman née Xiao. He placed eighty-sixth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 139th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Mao Kun, registered in a civilian household in Gui'an County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a county school student specializing in the Classic of Documents; his courtesy name was Shunfu, he ranked second in his family, and he was twenty-seven years old, born on the twenty-first day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gang, his grandfather Gui, and his father Qian; his mother was née Li. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brother was Qian, and his younger brothers were Gen, Yi, Yinglong, Dayou, and Yinghu; he married a woman née Yao. He placed eleventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and thirteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:

曾祖德昭祖成美父友剛母順氏

曾祖秀　祖虎〔贈知州〕　父恭〔知府〕　嫡母焦氏〔封恭人〕　生母張氏
永感下　兄經〔　〕　綸〔監生〕　繼〔監生〕　緒〔監生〕　純　弟緯〔　〕　娶彭氏

punctuated:
汪宗伊〔貫湖廣武昌府崇陽縣軍籍，縣學生，治《詩經》，字子衡，行三，年二十九，正月十五日生〕。曾祖璉〔壽官〕，祖藻〔監生，封兵部主事，累贈通議大夫、都察院右僉都御史〕，父文盛〔都察院右僉都御史〕，母彭氏〔封恭人〕。具慶下〔兄宗元、宗藝、宗凱、宗禮、宗臯，弟宗召、宗魯、宗夔、宗周、宗光、宗本、宗賓、宗表、宗越、宗華，娶蔡氏〕。湖廣鄉試第一名，會試第二十三名。

馮璋〔貫浙江寧波府慈谿縣軍籍，國子生，治《春秋》，字如之，行六十七，年三十七，七月十四日生〕。曾祖民，祖魯，父雋，前母張氏，母魏氏。慈侍下，兄禮、良、貴、岳〔知府〕，弟節，娶陳氏。浙江鄉試第三十八名，會試第九名。

林紳〔貫陝西鳳翔府寶雞縣民籍，國子生，治《書經》，字佩之，行六，年四十七，九月十三日生〕。曾祖秀，祖虎〔贈知州〕，父恭〔知府〕，嫡母焦氏〔封宜人〕，生母張氏。永感下，兄經〔聽選官〕、綸〔監生〕、繼〔監生〕、緒〔監生〕、純，弟綽〔上林苑監錄事〕，娶彭氏。陝西鄉試第三十九名，會試第二百七十名。

順境〔貫湖廣武昌府江夏縣軍籍，府學生，治《詩經》，字履常，行三，年三十八，四月十五日生〕。曾祖德昭，祖成美，父友剛，母順氏。慈侍下，兄鋐、錫，娶郝氏。湖廣鄉試第四十四名，會試第五十六名。
translation_en:
Wang Zongyi 汪宗伊 was registered in a military household in Chongyang County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang. A county school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he had the courtesy name Ziheng and was third in family order, aged twenty-nine, born on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lian, an honorary official for longevity; his grandfather was Zao, an Imperial University student who received the honorary appointment of Secretary in the Ministry of War and successive posthumous honors as Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His father was Wensheng, Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate, and his mother, née Peng, was granted the title Respectful Lady. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Zongyuan, Zongyi 宗藝, Zongkai, Zongli, and Zonggao; his younger brothers were Zongzhao, Zonglu, Zongkui, Zongzhou, Zongguang, Zongben, Zongbin, Zongbiao, Zongyue, and Zonghua. He married a woman née Cai. He ranked first in the Huguang Provincial Examination and twenty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Feng Zhang 馮璋 was registered in a military household in Cixi County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he had the courtesy name Ruzhi and was sixty-seventh in family order, aged thirty-seven, born on the fourteenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Min, his grandfather Lu, and his father Jun; his father's former wife was née Zhang, and his mother was née Wei. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Li, Liang, Gui, and Yue, a prefect; his younger brother was Jie. He married a woman née Chen. He ranked thirty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Shen 林紳 was registered in a civilian household in Baoji County, Fengxiang Prefecture, Shaanxi. An Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Documents, he had the courtesy name Peizhi and was sixth in family order, aged forty-seven, born on the thirteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xiu; his grandfather was Hu, posthumously appointed a subprefect; and his father was Gong, a prefect. His father's principal wife, née Jiao, was granted the title Suitable Lady; his birth mother was née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Jing, an official awaiting selection for appointment; Lun, Ji, and Xu, all Imperial University students; and Chun. His younger brother was Chuo, a registrar in the Directorate of Imperial Parks. He married a woman née Peng. He ranked thirty-ninth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 270th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shun Jing 順境 [?] was registered in a military household in Jiangxia County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang. A prefectural school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he had the courtesy name Lüchang and was third in family order, aged thirty-eight, born on the fifteenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Dezhao, his grandfather Chengmei, his father Yougang, and his mother née Shun. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Hong and Xi. He married a woman née Hao. He ranked forty-fourth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and fifty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄

punctuated:
李槃〔貫湖廣岳州府澧州官籍，四川内江縣人，國子生，治易經，字新甫，行三，年三十六，十一月初六日生〕。曾祖蕃〔兵科左給事中，累贈資政大夫、禮部尚書兼都察院左副都御史〕，祖充嗣〔戶部尚書，贈太子太保，謚康和〕，父振嗣，前母馬氏，母程氏。永感下，兄楹、棠〔太僕寺寺丞〕、舟〔百戶〕，弟點、松〔光祿寺署丞〕。娶張氏，繼娶陳氏。湖廣鄉試第二名，會試第一百十九名。

李嵩〔貫河南歸德衛軍籍，陝西華陰縣人，歸德州學增廣生，治易經，字子中，行二，年二十二，正月初六日生〕。曾祖貴，祖通，父芳，母宋氏，繼母周氏。具慶下，兄崑。娶陳氏。河南鄉試第十七名，會試第八十六名。

劉存德〔貫福建泉州府同安縣民籍，縣學生，治易經，字志仁，行一，年三十，十一月初六日生〕。曾祖弘淵，祖朝權，父恭，母葉氏，繼母林氏。具慶下，弟存業。娶葉氏。福建鄉試第四十六名，會試第四十五名。

阮高〔貫直隸保定府大寧都司官籍，中衛人，國子生，治詩經，字思抑，行二，年二十九，二月初一日生〕。曾祖璿〔都指揮使〕，祖洪，父泰，母李氏。慈侍下，兄登。娶李氏，繼娶尹氏。順天府鄉試第十一名，會試第二百二十九名。
translation_en:
Li Pan 李槃, courtesy name Xinfu, was registered in an official household in Lizhou, Yuezhou Prefecture, Huguang, and was originally from Neijiang County, Sichuan. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was third in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the sixth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather, Fan, was Left Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for War and received successive posthumous titles of Grand Master for Aid in Governance, Minister of Rites, and concurrent Left Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His grandfather, Chongsi, was Minister of Revenue, posthumously honored as Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, with the posthumous name Kanghe. His father was Zhensi; his father's former wife was née Ma, and his mother was née Cheng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ying, Tang (Assistant Director of the Court of Imperial Studs), and Zhou (Company Commander); his younger brothers were Dian and Song (an Office Assistant in the Court of Imperial Entertainments). He married a woman née Zhang and subsequently a woman née Chen. He placed second in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 119th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Song 李嵩, courtesy name Zizhong, was registered in a military household of Guide Guard, Henan, and was originally from Huayin County, Shaanxi. An added-quota student at the Guide Subprefectural School specializing in the Book of Changes, he was second in birth order, aged twenty-two, and born on the sixth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Gui, his grandfather Tong, and his father Fang; his mother was née Song and his stepmother née Zhou. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Kun. He married a woman née Chen. He placed seventeenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and eighty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Cunde 劉存德, courtesy name Zhiren, was registered in a civilian household in Tong'an County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian. A county school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the sixth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Hongyuan, his grandfather Chaoquan, and his father Gong; his mother was née Ye and his stepmother née Lin. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Cunye. He married a woman née Ye. He placed forty-sixth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and forty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ruan Gao 阮高, courtesy name Siyi, was registered in an official household under the Daning Regional Military Commission in Baoding Prefecture, Zhili, and was from the Central Guard. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the first day of the second month. His great-grandfather, Xuan, was Regional Military Commissioner; his grandfather was Hong, his father Tai, and his mother née Li. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Deng. He married a woman née Li and subsequently a woman née Yin. He placed eleventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 229th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
游震得〔貫直隸徽州府婺源縣民籍國子生治易經字汝潛行六十三三十四月十月初五日生〕
曾祖敬寬〔壽官〕祖侃父泰亨前母程氏母汪氏
慈侍下兄孟得弟再得三得牲得同得明得後得娶詹氏

李遇春〔貫直隸蘇州府常熟縣民籍，吳縣人，國子生，治詩經，字時芳，行三，年三十八，八月二十四日生〕。曾祖邕，祖梗，父乾，母杭氏。具慶下，兄應春〔省祭官〕、秀春，娶蔣氏。順天府鄉試第八十七名，會試第一百七十名。
translation_en:
You Zhende, registered in a civilian household in Wuyuan County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Ruqian, and he ranked sixty-third in family birth order; his age was apparently thirty-four [?; the transcription reads 三十四月]. He was born on the fifth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Jingkuan, an honorary longevity official; his grandfather was Kan, and his father was Taiheng. His father's former wife was née Cheng, and his mother was née Wang. His mother was living, and his father was deceased. His elder brother was Mengde; his younger brothers were Zaide, Sande, Shengde, Tongde, Mingde, and Houde. He married a woman née Zhan. He placed eighty-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and thirty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Ruzhen, registered in a civilian household in Nanchong County, Shunqing Prefecture, Sichuan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Gongning; he ranked third in family birth order and was thirty-six years old, born on the seventh day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Ming, a prefectural Registrar; his grandfather was Hua, an Administrator; and his father was Chun, a prefectural Assistant Prefect. His mother was née Ren. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Ben, Ruji, Mian, Han, and Can; his younger brothers were Gai and Rugan. He married a woman née Yang and subsequently a woman née Chen. He placed forty-eighth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and ninety-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sheng Tang, registered in a civilian household in Jiashan County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yuantao; he ranked first in family birth order and was thirty years old, born on the fifteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Wan, his grandfather was Zhuang, and his father was Kui. His mother was née Shen. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Yu, and he married a woman née Dai. He placed sixtieth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and ninety-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Yuchun, registered in a civilian household in Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a native of Wu County and a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Shifang; he ranked third in family birth order and was thirty-eight years old, born on the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Yong, his grandfather was Geng, and his father was Qian. His mother was née Hang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yingchun, a Sacrificial Attendant, and Xiuchun. He married a woman née Jiang. He placed eighty-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and one hundred seventieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

許東望〔貫山東平山衛旗籍，直隸宿松縣人，國子生，治易經，字應魯，行五，年三十，閏九月初一日生〕。曾祖宏〔贈知縣〕，祖麾〔太僕寺寺丞〕，父尭〔引禮舍人〕，母田氏。永感下，兄東周〔聽選官〕、東高〔監生〕、東喬〔千戶〕、東迎〔監生〕、東華〔總旗〕，弟東聚、東作〔文思院副使〕、東漸、東光〔義官〕，娶沈氏。山東鄉試第四十三名，會試第二百五十三名。
translation_en:
Zheng Zhi 鄭直 was registered in a military household in Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong. A student of the subprefectural school, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zijing; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-eight, born on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Guan, Judicial Supervisor in a Provincial Administration Commission, posthumously granted the title of Secretary in the Nanjing Ministry of Revenue; his grandfather was Lun; and his father was Weiyuan, an Assistant Prefect. His mother was née Li, and his stepmother née Liang. His grandfather and parents were living. His younger brothers were Li, an Imperial University student, Shi, Jian, Tong, and Deng. He married a woman née Xu. He placed thirtieth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 205th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Kang Jinliang 亢進良 was registered in a civilian household in Ansu County, Baoding Prefecture, in the Metropolitan Region. He was Instructor at the county school of Anyi, Shanxi, and specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Rushuai; he ranked third among his brothers and was aged forty-four, born on the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Gong; his grandfather was Feng; and his father was Dagang, a County Registrar. His mother was née Yan. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jinxian and Jinshan, and his younger brothers were Jinchen, Jinyan, Jindao, and Jinyou. He married a woman née Li and subsequently married women née Guo, Li, and Wang. He placed ninety-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 312th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Feng Weine 馮惟訥 was registered in a military household of Guangning Left Guard, Liaodong, and was a native of Linqu County, Shandong. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Ruyan; he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged twenty-six, born on the nineteenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Chun; his grandfather was Zhen, posthumously granted the title of Vice Director acting as Director in the Nanjing Ministry of Revenue; and his father was Yu, Vice Commissioner of a Provincial Surveillance Commission. His mother, née Fu, had been granted the title Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Weijian, a tribute scholar; Weizhong, a metropolitan graduate in the same examination cohort; and Weimin, a tribute scholar. His younger brother was Weizhi. He married a woman née Xiong. He placed fifty-sixth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 123rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Dongwang 許東望 was registered in a banner household of Pingshan Guard, Shandong, and was a native of Susong County in the Metropolitan Region. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Yinglu; he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged thirty, born on the first day of the intercalary ninth month. His great-grandfather was Hong, posthumously granted the title of County Magistrate; his grandfather was Hui, Assistant Director of the Court of the Imperial Stud; and his father was Yao, a Ceremonial Usher. His mother was née Tian. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Dongzhou, an official awaiting selection for appointment; Donggao, an Imperial University student; Dongqiao, a Battalion Commander; Dongying, an Imperial University student; and Donghua, a Company Commander. His younger brothers were Dongju; Dongzuo, Vice Commissioner of the Institute of Artistic Productions; Dongjian; and Dongguang, an honorary official recognized for public benefactions. He married a woman née Shen. He placed forty-third in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 253rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

諸敬之〔貫浙江紹興府餘姚縣民籍，縣學附學生，治易經，字守禮，行三，年三十二，正月二十七日生〕。曾祖琳，祖永言，父巽，母徐氏。重慶下，兄桂，弟學之，娶王氏。浙江鄉試第三十四名，會試第二百九十九名。

譚大初〔貫廣東南雄府始興縣民籍，府學生，治詩經，字宗元，行二，年三十五，九月三十日生〕。曾祖遜〔縣丞〕，祖昇，父驥〔訓導〕，嫡母劉氏，生母劉氏。慈侍下，兄大中〔訓科〕，娶陳氏。廣東鄉試第七十五名，會試第二百四十六名。
translation_en:
Hu Zongxian, registered in a civilian household in Jixi County, Huizhou Prefecture, Zhili, was an附生 supplementary student of the county school specializing in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Ruqin, he ranked first in family order, and he was twenty-seven sui, born on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ruochuan, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his grandfather was Kun, an honorary official recognized for philanthropy; his father was Shangren; and his mother was née Fang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Zongyu and his younger brother was Zongting; he married a woman née Zhang. He placed one hundredth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xiao Shi, registered in a civilian household in Jishui County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Zhongjing, he ranked fifth in family order, and he was thirty-one sui, born on the sixteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shizhen; his grandfather was Tingtong, posthumously appointed a Secretary in the Ministry of Justice; his father was Wan, a Surveillance Vice Commissioner; and his mother was née Yang, who held the title Lady of Peace (anren). Both parents were living. His elder brother was Gan and his younger brother was Zhe, a tribute scholar (gongshi); he married a woman née Hu. He placed eighty-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 277th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Jingzhi, registered in a civilian household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a supplementary student of the county school specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Shouli, he ranked third in family order, and he was thirty-two sui, born on the twenty-seventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lin; his grandfather was Yongyan; his father was Xun; and his mother was née Xu. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brother was Gui and his younger brother was Xuezhi; he married a woman née Wang. He placed thirty-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 299th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tan Dachu, registered in a civilian household in Shixing County, Nanxiong Prefecture, Guangdong, was a prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Zongyuan, he ranked second in family order, and he was thirty-five sui, born on the thirtieth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xun, a County Vice Magistrate; his grandfather was Sheng; and his father was Ji, an Assistant Instructor. His legal mother and his birth mother were both née Liu. His father was deceased and his mother was living. His elder brother was Dazhong, a Medical Instructor; he married a woman née Chen. He placed seventy-fifth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 246th in the Metropolitan Examination.

萬文彩〔貫雲南臨安衛官籍，江西南昌縣人，國子生，治詩經，字國華，行一，年三十二，三月十一日生〕。曾祖俊，祖昻，父祚〔八品散官〕，母賈氏。慈侍下，兄言策〔貢士〕、文奎，弟文光，娶何氏。雲貴鄉試第三十一名，會試第二百八十二名。

邵梗〔貫浙江杭州府仁和縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字良用，行三，年三十六，二月三十日生〕。曾祖惟政〔贈文林郎、大理寺評事〕，祖琮〔按察司副使，進階從三品階〕，父昺，母陳氏。嚴侍下，弟楷、楙、榥、桂、桐、檟、榴、梓，娶趙氏。浙江鄉試第五十一名，會試第二百九十二名。

李僅可〔貫直隸廣平府清河縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字子與，行一，年三十五，正月初三日生〕。曾祖祥，祖璽，父隆，母閻氏。具慶下，弟學可、許可，娶張氏。順天府鄉試第三十一名，會試第一百二十七名。
translation_en:
Xu Heling, registered in a military household in Haining County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was an additional student at the prefectural school and specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Renfu; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-one, born on the twenty-sixth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Qing, his grandfather Lan, and his father Wenqing, a government student granted the cap and girdle of official status; his mother was née Wang. His grandparents and parents were living. His younger brothers were Hexiang, Heming, Hesheng, and Henian. He married a woman née Shen and subsequently a woman née Sun. He placed fifty-ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 247th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Wencai, registered in an official household in Lin’an Guard, Yunnan, was originally from Nanchang County, Jiangxi. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Guohua; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-two, born on the eleventh day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Jun, his grandfather Ang, and his father Zuo, a titular official of the eighth rank; his mother was née Jia. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Yance, a tribute scholar (gongshi), and Wenkui; his younger brother was Wenguang. He married a woman née He. He placed thirty-first in the Yunnan–Guizhou Provincial Examination and 282nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shao Geng, registered in a civilian household in Renhe County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Liangyong; he ranked third among his brothers and was thirty-six, born on the thirtieth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Weizheng, posthumously granted the titles of Gentleman of Literary Service and Case Reviewer in the Court of Judicial Review. His grandfather Cong was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner, advanced to a prestige title of the lower third rank. His father was Bing and his mother née Chen. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Kai, Mao, Huang, Gui, Tong, Jia, Liu, and Zi. He married a woman née Zhao. He placed fifty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 292nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Jinke, registered in a civilian household in Qinghe County, Guangping Prefecture, in the directly administered territory, was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Ziyu; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-five, born on the third day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Xiang, his grandfather Xi, and his father Long; his mother was née Yan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Xueke and Xuke. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed thirty-first in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 127th in the Metropolitan Examination.

羅崇奎〔貫江西南昌府南昌縣，民籍，國子生，治易經，字子文，行八，年三十一，五月十三日生〕。曾祖九錫〔義官〕，祖貢任，父大輔，母賈氏。慈侍下，兄崇貞、崇進，弟崇信、崇睿、崇簡、崇明、崇震，娶徐氏。江西鄉試第二十一名，會試第二十七名。

孟養性〔貫山東濟南府齊河縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字存甫，行一，年三十，十一月十九日生〕。曾祖昉，祖璉，父宗儒〔監生〕，母楊氏。嚴侍下，娶趙氏。山東鄉試第四十四名，會試第一百九十八名。

阮朝策〔貫湖廣黃州府麻城縣，民籍，國子生，治春秋，字子定，行七，年三十八，八月十八日生〕。曾祖剛〔縣丞〕，祖大用〔壽官〕，父圭〔贈給事中〕，前母賀氏，母蔡氏〔贈孺人〕。永感下，兄朝陽〔貢士〕、朝東〔按察司提學副使〕、朝南、朝端、朝隨〔貢士〕、朝士、朝儀、朝倚、朝佳，娶梅氏。湖廣鄉試第八名，會試第一百十名。
translation_en:
Luo Chongkui, courtesy name Ziwen, was registered in Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was eighth in family order, aged thirty-one, and born on the thirteenth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Jiuxi, an honorary official recognized for public benefactions; his grandfather was Gongren; his father was Dafu; and his mother was née Jia. His mother alone was living. His elder brothers were Chongzhen and Chongjin, and his younger brothers were Chongxin, Chongrui, Chongjian, Chongming, and Chongzhen. He married a woman née Xu. He placed twenty-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and twenty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Ke, courtesy name Zhongsheng, was registered in an official household of Zhuolu Left Guard in the directly administered metropolitan region and was a native of Zunhua County, Jizhou, Shuntian Prefecture. An supplementary student of the subprefectural school specializing in the Book of Documents, he was sixth in family order, aged twenty-eight, and born on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather Yu and grandfather Guang both held the prestige title General of Manifest Courage and served as Guard Commanders. His father, Yuan, was a Vice Director in the Ministry of Revenue; his mother, née Guo, was posthumously granted the title Lady of Suitability. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Pei, a General of Manifest Courage and Guard Commander; Rui, an honorary official recognized for public benefactions; and Zhen, a holder of a seventh-rank prestige title. His younger brothers were Kun, Huang, Yao, and Gong. He married a woman née Wang. He placed 105th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 183rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Meng Yangxing, courtesy name Cunfu, was registered in Qihe County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, in a civilian household. A county-school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in family order, aged thirty, and born on the nineteenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Fang; his grandfather was Lian; his father was Zongru, a student of the Directorate of Education; and his mother was née Yang. His father alone was living. He married a woman née Zhao. He placed forty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 198th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ruan Chaoce, courtesy name Ziding, was registered in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was seventh in family order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the eighteenth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather Gang was a County Vice Magistrate; his grandfather Dayong held an honorary title granted for longevity; and his father Gui was posthumously appointed Supervising Secretary. His father's former wife was née He, and his mother, née Cai, was posthumously granted the title Lady. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Chaoyang, a tribute scholar; Chaodong, an Education Intendant serving as Vice Commissioner of the Provincial Surveillance Commission; Chaonan; Chaoduan; Chaosui, a tribute scholar; Chaoshi; Chaoyi (朝儀); Chaoyi (朝倚); and Chaojia. He married a woman née Mei. He placed eighth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 110th in the Metropolitan Examination.

歐思賢〔貫順天府薊州，民籍，福建連江縣人，國子生，治書經，字希甫，行五，年三十五，十月初七日生〕。曾祖寶〔贈兵部郎中〕，祖俊，父弘悳〔府通判，進階承德郎〕，母孟氏〔封安人〕。具慶下，兄思廉〔義官〕、思誠〔大理寺右寺副〕、思孝，弟思齊〔義官〕、思法、思元、思遷，娶賈氏。順天府鄉試第六十名，會試第二百六十二名。

楊皆〔貫福建興化府莆田縣，民籍，府學生，治詩經，字同卿，行十九，年三十二，閏正月十三日生〕。曾祖察〔贈奉直大夫、吏部員外郎〕，祖瓚〔布政使司左參政〕，父褒，母翁氏。慈侍下，兄魯、晳、曹，娶林氏。福建鄉試第六十五名，會試第三百五名。
translation_en:
Zhou Shan, registered in Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Ziren. He ranked first among his brothers and was forty-eight sui, born on the twelfth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhongjie, his grandfather Yu, his father Rong, and his mother née Wu. His mother was living, and his father was deceased. He married a woman née Xu. He placed 128th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 260th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Yu, registered in Wan’an County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Weishi. He ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-seven sui, born on the seventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shouyue, his grandfather Ziyun (an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions), his father Shiyou, and his mother née Liao. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Ting, Xiao, Zhan, and Ji. He married a woman née Liu. He placed twenty-fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and twenty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ou Sixian, registered in Jizhou, Shuntian Prefecture, belonged to a civilian household and was originally from Lianjiang County, Fujian. He was a student of the Imperial University and specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Xifu. He ranked fifth among his brothers and was thirty-five sui, born on the seventh day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bao (posthumously appointed Director in the Ministry of War), his grandfather Jun, and his father Hongde (a prefectural Assistant Prefect, advanced to the prestige title Gentleman for Receiving Virtue). His mother, née Meng, was invested with the title Lady of Repose. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Silian (an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions), Sicheng (Right Assistant Judge in the Court of Judicial Review), and Sixiao; his younger brothers were Siqi (an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions), Sifa, Siyuan, and Siqian. He married a woman née Jia. He placed sixtieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 262nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Jie, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was a prefectural government student. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Tongqing. He ranked nineteenth among his brothers and was thirty-two sui, born on the thirteenth day of the intercalary first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cha (posthumously granted the title Grand Master for Upright Service and appointed Vice Director in the Ministry of Personnel), his grandfather Zan (Left Administration Vice Commissioner in a Provincial Administration Commission), his father Bao, and his mother née Weng. His mother was living, and his father was deceased. His elder brothers were Lu, Xi, and Cao. He married a woman née Lin. He placed sixty-fifth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 305th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Jing Yingchun, registered in a military household in Wuzhi County, Huaiqing Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the National University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Ziyuan; he ranked second in birth order and was twenty-six years old, born on the twenty-second day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Qin, a deliberative official [?]; his grandfather was Luan, an honorary official for longevity; his father was Hua, and his mother was née Zhao. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yingjie, and his younger brothers were Yingxia, Yingqiu, and Yingdong. He married a woman née Wang. He placed fifty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and sixty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Chong, registered in a civilian household in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang, was a student of the National University specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Yuanxun; he ranked second in birth order and was thirty years old, born on the fifth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Shanfang, an Instructor in Taoist Arts; his grandfather was 𦘠 [name reading uncertain]; his father was Wenyu, a government student granted the cap and girdle of official rank; and his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Cai 采, a Ceremonial Usher, and his younger brothers were Zai, Cai 寀, Zan, and Le. He married a woman née Zou. He placed thirty-eighth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and two hundred second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Yaori, registered in a civilian household in Luyi County, Guide Subprefecture, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the National University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Mingshi; he ranked third in birth order and was thirty-seven years old, born on the twenty-first day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Zhi, a Guard Registry Manager; his grandfather was Ji; and his father was Cong, a Keeper of the Seal. His mother was née Pu, and his stepmother was née Luo. His father alone was living. His elder brothers were Yaochun and Yaonian, and his younger brothers were Yaoshi, Yaochen, and Yaojie. He married a woman née Wan. He placed ninth in the Henan Provincial Examination and one hundred seventy-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wei Mengxian, registered in a civilian household in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the National University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Liangfu; he ranked tenth in birth order and was twenty-nine years old, born on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Da, his grandfather was Ying, and his father was Chun. His father's former wife was née Wang, and his mother was née Zhu. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Mengbu. He married a woman née Zhu. He placed seventy-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and seventy-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Gu Jiao, registered in an official household of Xingzhou Front Garrison Guard in Zhili and originally from Xi County, Henan, was a student of the National University specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Weisheng; he was first in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the twenty-third day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Liang, an Assistant Commander; his grandfather was Yong; his father was Xuan; and his mother was née Dong. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Luan, and his wife was née Yang. He ranked twenty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and three hundred third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wen Xin, registered in an official household of the Luoyang Central Escort Guard in Henan and originally from Yidu County, Shandong, was a student of the National University specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Boming; he was first in birth order, aged forty-eight, and born on the twelfth day of the third month. His great-grandfather Quan, grandfather Hou, and father Sheng were all Vice Commanders. His mother was née Wang, granted the title of Lady (shuren), and his stepmother was née Zhang. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his surviving mother. His younger brothers were Xiu, an Associate Administrator, and Xi; his wife was née Wang. He ranked second in the Henan Provincial Examination and three hundred sixteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Ping, registered in a civilian household in Dongguang County, Jingzhou, Hejian Prefecture, Zhili, was a county government student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zizhen; he was first in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the nineteenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Jian; his grandfather was An; his father was Qing; and his mother was née Xi. Both parents were deceased. His first wife was née Wang, and his subsequent wife was née Zhuang. He ranked one hundred fourteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Hu, registered in a civilian household in Yangshuo County, Guilin Prefecture, Guangxi, was a student of the National University specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Bingzhi; he was ninth in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the first day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Longguang; his grandfather was Sheng, a Prefectural Registrar posthumously granted the title of Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice; his father was Bi, a National University student; and his mother was née Rong. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Luan and Peng, both County Magistrates; Lu; E, a National University student; Yuan; Hong; Zhi; and Ji. His wife was née Wang. He ranked twentieth in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and one hundred seventeenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Yin Lun, registered in a civilian household in Qihe County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, was a native of Dezhou and a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Ruyu; he ranked fourth in birth order, was aged thirty-nine, and was born on the eighteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jin, his grandfather Qin, and his father Tianzhang, a Police Chief; his mother was née Wang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Tang, Chao, and Jing, and his wife was née Li. He placed twenty-first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 255th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Dayou was registered in a civilian household in Chaoyang County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Duanshi; he ranked first in birth order, was aged twenty-four, and was born on the twentieth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Weisi, his grandfather Jinjing, and his father Huiqian; the record lists two mothers, née Zhao and née Fan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Dazhuang and Daxu, and his wife was née Xiao. He placed sixtieth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 235th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Chongyi was registered in a military household in Zichuan County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Ziyou; he ranked fourth in birth order, was aged thirty, and was born on the sixteenth day of the intercalary ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jun, his grandfather Zhen, and his father Kui; his mother was née Lu and his stepmother née Cao. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Chongde, Chongru, a sacrificial official (shengjiguan), and Chongren; his younger brothers were Chongwen, Chongxue, and Chonghua. His first wife was née Xu, and he subsequently married a woman née Liu. He placed sixteenth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 129th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Bai was registered in a civilian household in Fuliang County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, and was a prefectural school student specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Tingjie; he ranked twenty-ninth in birth order, was aged twenty-six, and was born on the thirteenth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wenqi, his grandfather Jun, and his father Si; his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jia, Zha, Song, and Lin; his younger brothers were Wu, Li, and Ping. His wife was née Zheng. He placed sixteenth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 126th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Daping, registered in Anqiu County, Qingzhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was a county school student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Xiangxing; he ranked fourth in the family and was twenty-eight, born on the seventeenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhen, his grandfather Bocheng, and his father Yu; his mother was née Li. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Dahua, Daren, and Dajun; his younger brothers were Daye, Dayong, Daxi, Dahao, and Daming. He married a woman née Huang. He placed sixteenth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 206th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Yingkui, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was an auxiliary student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Fuyuan; he ranked fifth in the family and was twenty-nine, born on the second day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yu, an Imperial University student; his grandfather Zhong was a prefectural vice prefect; and his father Huai was a government student entitled to wear the official cap and girdle. His mother was née Yong, and his birth mother was née Yang. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brothers were Zaibang, Zaike (an official awaiting selection for appointment), Zaixian, and Zaitian. He was betrothed to a woman née Zheng. He placed twenty-ninth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 284th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Zheng, registered in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a military household and was an auxiliary student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Zimin; he ranked 204th in the family and was twenty-four, born on the twenty-fifth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shuzhi, his grandfather Yuhuan, and his father Shixi; his mother was née You. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Bian, Zhuo, Zhuan, Zhuo, Yang, and Jie. He was betrothed to a woman née Zou. He placed twenty-third in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and seventy-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Xin, registered in Longjiang Right Guard in the directly administered region, belonged to a military household and was a native of Dinghai County, Zhejiang. He was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Weiyi; he ranked second in the family and was thirty-eight, born on the fourteenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jingxiang, his grandfather Lei, and his father Hao; his mother was née Yang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brother was Yan. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed thirty-first in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 267th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xu Wenheng, registered in an official household of Dingliao Rear Guard in Liaodong and originating from Yugan County, Jiangxi, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Daoxing; he ranked second in his family and was thirty-four years old, born on the thirteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bodi, a Company Commander; his grandfather was Ang, posthumously appointed Battalion Commander; his father was Yuan, and his mother was née Wan. His mother alone was still living. His elder brothers were Wenxian and Wenfang, and his younger brothers were Wenzhen, Wenzhong, Wenhe, and Wenzheng. He married a woman née Wang. He placed 113th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 304th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Niu Shendu, registered in a civilian household in Ye County, Nanyang Prefecture, Henan, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Xuanfan; he ranked first in his family and was forty-four years old, born on the twenty-sixth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lin; his grandfather was Duo, posthumously appointed Director in the Ministry of Personnel; his father was Feng, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices in Nanjing; and his mother was née Ren, granted the title Lady of Suitability. Both parents were still living. His younger brother Shenyu was a tribute scholar. He married a woman née Li and subsequently another woman née Li. He placed 39th in the Henan Provincial Examination and 28th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Song Weiyuan, registered in a salt-producing household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a National University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Yizhen; he ranked fourth in his family and was forty-two years old, born on the seventh day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tingfang, posthumously appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate; his grandfather was Lian, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his father was Xuan, a Chief of Police; and his mother was née Wang. His father alone was still living. His younger brothers were Weixing, Weikui, Weixin, and Weiji. He married a woman née Chen and subsequently women née Hu and née Xu. He placed ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 213th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en: …As soon as the ruler acts according to righteousness, they call him harsh and severe, saying: “His Majesty relies on punishments to govern; this is not the government of the Three Dynasties.” Yet they never once turn their scrutiny back upon themselves. The people of the Three Dynasties were all human beings; without waiting for righteousness to be imposed upon them, they exercised self-restraint, fearing only that they might become unrestrained and extravagant. title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣茅瓚
臣對臣聞帝王之御臨天下也內必有敬天
之心而外必有憲天之政夫天者理之原也
人君代天理物故其所行必求端於天天之
道雖廣博而難終窮神妙而不可測而其端
不過有二曰陰與陽而已矣陽居大夏以長
育爲事有剛道焉王者繼天而爲之子則用
仁而凡爲慈愛爲謙屈無非仁之統體矣陰
居秋冬以肅殺爲事有柔道焉王者繼天而
爲之子則用義而凡爲果斷爲裁制無非義
===
之散殊矣故天道運而無所積帝德運而無
所私以此存之於中是謂敬天純王之心也
以此發之於事是謂憲天純王之政也合心
與政皆純乎天夫是之謂格天之治而堯舜
禹湯文武由此其選也奚獨三代之治爲然
乎欽惟
皇帝陛下稟剛健中正之資備文武聖神之德自
即位以来信賞必罰威行如雷霆發姦摘伏明
照如日月對時茂育容保如
天地蓋粹乎斯道之中而建維皇之極者也臣也

punctuated:
臣茅瓚。

臣對：臣聞帝王之御臨天下也，內必有敬天之心，而外必有憲天之政。夫天者，理之原也。人君代天理物，故其所行必求端於天。天之道雖廣博而難終窮，神妙而不可測，而其端不過有二，曰陰與陽而已矣。陽居大夏，以長育爲事，有剛道焉。王者繼天而爲之子，則用仁，而凡爲慈愛、爲謙屈，無非仁之統體矣。陰居秋冬，以肅殺爲事，有柔道焉。王者繼天而爲之子，則用義，而凡爲果斷、爲裁制，無非義之散殊矣。故天道運而無所積，帝德運而無所私。以此存之於中，是謂敬天，純王之心也；以此發之於事，是謂憲天，純王之政也。合心與政，皆純乎天，夫是之謂格天之治，而堯舜禹湯文武由此其選也。奚獨三代之治爲然乎？

欽惟皇帝陛下，稟剛健中正之資，備文武聖神之德。自即位以来，信賞必罰，威行如雷霆；發姦摘伏，明照如日月；對時茂育，容保如天地。蓋粹乎斯道之中，而建維皇之極者也。臣也
translation_en:
Your servant, Mao Zan.

Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings rule over all under Heaven, inwardly they must possess a heart that reveres Heaven, and outwardly they must conduct government that models itself on Heaven. Heaven is the source of principle. The ruler orders things on Heaven’s behalf; thus, in all that he does, he must seek his starting point in Heaven. Although Heaven’s Way is so vast that it cannot be fully fathomed, and so wondrous that it cannot be measured, its fundamental aspects number only two: yin and yang. Yang occupies high summer [?], taking growth and nurture as its work; therein lies the way of firmness. The king succeeds Heaven and becomes its son, and accordingly employs benevolence. All his acts of loving kindness and humble deference belong to the comprehensive unity of benevolence. Yin occupies autumn and winter, taking stern destruction as its work; therein lies the way of yielding. The king succeeds Heaven and becomes its son, and accordingly employs righteousness. All his acts of resolute decision and discriminating regulation are differentiated expressions of righteousness. Thus Heaven’s Way moves without accumulation, and imperial virtue moves without partiality. To preserve this inwardly is called revering Heaven: it is the heart of pure kingship. To express this in affairs is called modeling oneself on Heaven: it is the government of pure kingship. When heart and government together accord purely with Heaven, this is called government that reaches Heaven. Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu were outstanding exemplars of this. How could it have been true only of the government of the Three Dynasties?

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed with firmness, vigor, centrality, and uprightness, and possesses the virtues of civil refinement, martial prowess, sageliness, and spiritual insight. Since ascending the throne, you have faithfully rewarded and unfailingly punished, your might moving like thunder; you have exposed wickedness and uncovered hidden wrongdoing, your illumination shining like the sun and moon; you have fostered abundant growth in accordance with the seasons, embracing and protecting like Heaven and Earth. You have indeed attained purity within this Way and established the sovereign’s supreme standard. As for your servant…

punctuated:
竊伏草茅，遥被治化久矣。乃者叨有司之薦，得以與於大廷之對，而清問及焉。永惟聖經之言，而有取於仁義並行之道；既而有慨於庶官之龐，而欲以兼夫治教之法；且兾臣等以除弊革私之道，為仁育義斷之方，而戒之以勿諱勿欺也。顧臣之愚陋，何足以仰裨休德之萬一乎？雖然，有所言而不實，是之謂欺，則上負陛下矣；有所言而不盡，是之謂諱，則下負所學矣。上負天子，下負所學，疇昔之所自許者謂何？朝廷之作養者謂何？而可如此也？臣敢披瀝衷悃，就陛下之所問及者而條陳之。陛下試垂聽焉。
臣惟天下之道有經有權。經也者，一定而不可易者也；權也者，或相兼以適其宜，或相濟以補其所不及者也。人君撫輿圖之廣，臨兆民之衆，天下之所恃以立命者也。
translation_en:
…living humbly in obscurity, I have long received, even from afar, the transforming influence of your rule. Recently, through the undeserved recommendation of the responsible officials, I gained the opportunity to present an answer at the great court, and your august questions reached me. Reflecting deeply on the words of the sages’ classics, Your Majesty has embraced the way of practicing benevolence and righteousness together. Concerned, moreover, at the proliferation of officials, you wish to combine the methods of government and moral instruction. You also hope that we, your servants, will propose ways to eliminate abuses and private interests as means of nurturing through benevolence and deciding through righteousness; and you admonish us neither to conceal anything nor to deceive. Yet how could someone as ignorant and uncultivated as I contribute even the smallest part to your splendid virtue? Nevertheless, to speak untruthfully is deception and would betray Your Majesty above; to speak without saying everything is concealment and would betray what I have learned below. If I betrayed the Son of Heaven above and my learning below, what would become of the aspirations I have long held for myself? What would become of the court’s efforts to nurture and educate me? How could I act thus? I venture to lay bare my sincere thoughts and address, point by point, the matters Your Majesty has asked about. May Your Majesty graciously hear me.
Your servant considers that the Way governing all under Heaven has both constant principles and discretionary applications. Constant principles are fixed and cannot be altered. Discretionary applications sometimes combine with one another to suit the circumstances, and sometimes supplement one another to make up for their respective deficiencies. The ruler governs an immense territory and presides over a multitude of subjects; he is the one upon whom all under Heaven depend to sustain their lives.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
苟一於義則威之太震民畏之而不敢親一
於仁則惠之太褻民狎之而不知敬是仁之
與義猶天之有陰陽而不容以或偏也臣故
曰道之一定而不可易者也然德教以象天
之生育仁矣而義者未嘗不防之於中刑戮
以象天之震撼義矣而仁者未始不貫乎其
內是仁義之交相為用猶陰陽之互為其根
臣故曰道之相兼以適其宜也然天下之勢
有強弱而人君之政有德與刑乘弱之後者
利用威而乘強之後者利用惠此其斟酌操

punctuated: 苟一於義，則威之太震，民畏之而不敢親；一於仁，則惠之太褻，民狎之而不知敬。是仁之與義，猶天之有陰陽，而不容以或偏也。臣故曰，道之一定而不可易者也。然德教以象天之生育，仁矣，而義者未嘗不防之於中；刑戮以象天之震撼，義矣，而仁者未始不貫乎其內。是仁義之交相為用，猶陰陽之互為其根。臣故曰，道之相兼以適其宜也。然天下之勢有強弱，而人君之政有德與刑。乘弱之後者，利用威；而乘強之後者，利用惠。此其斟酌操縱之間，猶之天道之雨以潤而日以晅，雷以動而風以散，既成萬物而人莫窺其神。臣故曰，道之相濟以補其所不及者也。是故仁義之為道也，一定而不可易者，以立天下之經；或相兼以適其宜，相濟以補其所不及者，以達天下之變。稽之於聖經，驗之於往古，何莫不然？彼其去義以為論，專任德而不用刑者，何其失之偏乎！臣伏讀聖制之篇，而有以辨人言之為妄矣。人之言曰：「人君纔一用義，即謂之嚴刻任刑，非三代之治。」
translation_en:
If a ruler attends exclusively to righteousness, his authority becomes too terrifying: the people fear him and dare not draw near. If he attends exclusively to benevolence, his favors become too indiscriminate: the people grow overly familiar with him and cease to show respect. Benevolence and righteousness are thus like Heaven’s yin and yang: neither may be favored to the exclusion of the other. Hence your servant speaks of what is fixed in the Way and cannot be altered. Yet moral instruction, which emulates Heaven’s generation and nurture of life, is benevolent, while righteousness invariably sets limits within it. Punishments and executions, which emulate Heaven’s shaking and thunder, are righteous, while benevolence invariably runs through them. Benevolence and righteousness thus operate together, just as yin and yang each serve as the root of the other. Hence your servant speaks of aspects of the Way working together to suit what is appropriate.

The condition of the realm, however, may be strong or weak, and a ruler’s government employs both virtue and punishment. One who succeeds a period of weakness should employ stern authority; one who succeeds a period of strength should employ kindness. The weighing of circumstances and the exercise of restraint or relaxation resemble Heaven’s workings: rain moistens, sunshine warms, thunder stirs, and wind disperses. They bring the myriad things to completion, yet no one can fathom their mysterious efficacy. Hence your servant speaks of aspects of the Way assisting one another to make good what each lacks. Thus, in the Way of benevolence and righteousness, what is fixed and cannot be altered establishes the enduring principles of the realm; their working together to suit circumstances and assisting one another to supply deficiencies enables one to respond to changes in the realm. Examine this in the sages’ Classics and test it against antiquity: is it not so in every case? How grievously one-sided are those who exclude righteousness from their arguments, relying exclusively on virtue and dispensing with punishment!

Your servant has reverently read Your Majesty’s composition and thereby gained the means to discern the falsity of what people say. They say: “As soon as a ruler employs righteousness, this is called harshness and reliance on punishment, rather than the government of the Three Dynasties.”

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣愚以為用義之與嚴刻任刑不同也既曰
用義則不可謂之嚴刻任刑曰嚴刻任刑則
不得謂之用義人君之於天下何容心哉視
其理之所宜而已矣苟於義所當用則雖殺
人而不可謂之嚴雖致人於死而不得謂之
刻蓋以義之為道當如是也至謂用義非三
代之治此尤非所謂知理者臣不暇遠引泛
取即以三代之事明之禹之承舜也先罰後
賞以示威湯之革夏也申伐誓衆以張武而
文武之繼殷也驅除元惡殲滅暴國以救民
===
故夏有禹刑商有湯刑周有甫刑三代之得
天下雖曰以仁而未嘗專倚於仁有義以濟
其仁之所不及也後世事不師古遂以為三
代之治純用德而不用刑何失之遠歟是故
不朝者賜之几杖受賂者媿之金錢言寬仁
者莫如漢之文帝矣然姑息成風乾綱罔斷
故不再傳而有指大如股脛大如腰之怠刑
以不殺為威財以不蓄為富言仁厚者亦莫
如宋之仁宗矣然聲容盛而武備衰議論多
而成功少故不再傳而有流言道路變令推

Your foolish servant considers the application of righteousness to be different from harshness, cruelty, and reliance on punishment. If it is called the application of righteousness, it cannot be called harshness, cruelty, and reliance on punishment; if it is called harshness, cruelty, and reliance on punishment, it cannot be called the application of righteousness. In dealing with all under Heaven, how could a ruler allow private intentions to intrude? He need only attend to what principle makes appropriate. Where righteousness ought to be applied, even killing someone cannot be called harsh, and even putting someone to death cannot be called cruel, for the Way of righteousness requires that it be so. As for saying that applying righteousness was not the government of the Three Dynasties, this especially betrays a failure to understand principle. Your servant has no leisure to draw on distant examples or range widely for evidence; I shall clarify this simply through the affairs of the Three Dynasties. When Yu succeeded Shun, he placed punishments before rewards to display his authority. When Tang overthrew Xia, he pressed his punitive campaign and addressed an oath to his host to display martial might. When Wen and Wu succeeded Yin, they drove out the chief evildoers and destroyed violent states to save the people. Thus Xia had the Punishments of Yu, Shang the Punishments of Tang, and Zhou the Punishments of Fu. Although the Three Dynasties are said to have won all under Heaven through benevolence, they never relied exclusively upon benevolence: righteousness supplemented what their benevolence could not accomplish. Later generations failed to model their affairs on antiquity and consequently supposed that the government of the Three Dynasties employed virtue alone and never punishment. How far they strayed!

Thus, to those who did not attend court he granted an armrest and staff; those who accepted bribes he shamed with gifts of money. In generosity and benevolence, none could compare with Emperor Wen of Han. Yet indulgence became habitual, and the sovereign's authority failed to act decisively. Hence, before the throne had passed twice to a successor, laxity in punishment had produced a condition in which “fingers were as large as thighs, and shins as large as waists” [?]. He took refraining from killing as his awe-inspiring authority, and, as for wealth, took refraining from hoarding as riches [?]. In benevolence and generosity, likewise, none could compare with Emperor Renzong of Song. Yet ceremonial display flourished while military preparedness declined; discussions were many, but achievements few. 太祖高皇帝承元人積弊之後故其所以

恩之譏。夫二君則漢宋之良也，一於仁而不義，而其流弊猶不免有如此者。若是而謂三代之專於任德，後世之專於任刑，可乎？不可乎？由是觀之，三代之所以治隆俗美者，以其仁義之並用，內有敬天之心，而外有憲天之政也。後世之所以不古若者，以其仁義之或偏，而不能審時以度勢，其於天也，或褻焉而不知敬，或悖焉而不知法也。
我太祖高皇帝承元人積弊之後，故其所以創制立法者，大率以嚴為本。及天下巳定，又戒聖子神孫不得復用國初之典。是其仁義之並行，剛柔之相濟，其所以察乎天人之際，審乎消息之宜，而為萬世慮者深矣。
但國家承平日久，重熈累洽，民志日趨於玩愒，事體日廢於因循。蓋自正德以来，兹弊極矣。肆陛下入繼大統，始振起而一新之。故自臨馭十有七年以来，革者故，鼎者新，蟄者奮，困者蘇，天下欣欣，咸覩太平於有象矣。而陛下猶有歉於官人者負國虐民，若追羡於三代
translation_en:
…the criticism concerning the extension of imperial favors. These two rulers were among the best of the Han and Song dynasties. Yet, devoted exclusively to benevolence without righteousness, they still could not escape harmful consequences such as these. In that case, can one say that the Three Dynasties relied exclusively on virtue and later ages exclusively on punishment? Can one, or can one not? Viewed in this light, the Three Dynasties attained excellent government and admirable customs because they employed benevolence and righteousness together: inwardly they possessed hearts that revered Heaven, and outwardly they governed in imitation of Heaven. Later ages fell short of antiquity because they sometimes favored one over the other and could not assess the times and weigh circumstances. In their dealings with Heaven, they either treated it irreverently, without knowing to revere it, or acted contrary to it, without knowing to take it as their model.
Our Emperor Taizu Gao inherited the accumulated abuses of Yuan rule. Thus, in establishing institutions and laws, he generally made severity their foundation. Once the realm had been pacified, however, he admonished his sage sons and divine grandsons that they must not again employ the statutes of the dynasty’s founding years. In this, benevolence and righteousness operated together, and firmness and gentleness complemented one another. Profound indeed was his concern for countless generations to come, as he examined the relationship between Heaven and humanity and discerned what was appropriate amid decline and growth.
Yet the state has long enjoyed peace, with successive generations of prosperity and harmonious government. The people’s dispositions have increasingly inclined toward idleness and neglect, while public affairs have increasingly deteriorated through habitual inaction. Since the Zhengde era, these abuses had reached their utmost extent. Then Your Majesty succeeded to the imperial line and began to rouse the realm and renew it completely. Thus, in the seventeen years since you assumed rule, the old has been reformed, the new established, the dormant stirred to action, and the distressed revived. All under Heaven rejoice and see tangible signs of great peace. Yet Your Majesty remains dissatisfied that officials betray the state and oppress the people, as though yearning to emulate those of the Three Dynasties…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
之英而未之逮者臣愚以為雖堯舜在上不
能無小人此在君人者馭之得其道耳馭之
之道臣前所謂仁義之並用者是也盖嘗聞
之法禁之不行自上犯之也而小民之所以
敢為非義者庶官之貪頑者啟之也今天下
之大其在於
朝廷輦轂豈無有秉義竭忠之臣然而違上所
好朋家作仇者未盡無也其在於百工庶府
豈無有亮采惠疇之臣然而脅權相滅誣上
行私者未盡無也其在於都邑藩省豈無有
===
旬宣和惠之臣然而違道干譽尸禄養望者
未盡無也甚者削民之膏脂以肥其家竊君
之榮寵以張其勢掠眾之美以示其恩恣己
之私以敗其度者未盡無也
陛下尊禮大臣愈久益親體悉羣臣有隆弗替其
於股肱之良而謨明弼諧者固嘗
撫之以恩而勸之以禮矣而於此不悛之徒明
罰勅法懲一以警其百是猶春陽之後而震
之以雷雨之威天下方將感
陛下之仁而畏

之英而未之逮者。臣愚以為，雖堯舜在上，不能無小人，此在君人者馭之得其道耳。馭之之道，臣前所謂仁義之並用者是也。盖嘗聞之，法禁之不行，自上犯之也；而小民之所以敢為非義者，庶官之貪頑者啟之也。今天下之大，其在於朝廷輦轂，豈無有秉義竭忠之臣？然而違上所好、朋家作仇者，未盡無也。其在於百工庶府，豈無有亮采惠疇之臣？然而脅權相滅、誣上行私者，未盡無也。其在於都邑藩省，豈無有旬宣和惠之臣？然而違道干譽、尸禄養望者，未盡無也。甚者，削民之膏脂以肥其家，竊君之榮寵以張其勢，掠眾之美以示其恩，恣己之私以敗其度者，未盡無也。

translation_en:
…the outstanding men of the Three Dynasties, whom you have yet to equal. In my humble view, even when Yao and Shun ruled, they could not prevent petty men from existing. It rests with the ruler to find the proper way to govern them. That way is precisely what I mentioned earlier: employing benevolence and righteousness together. I have heard that laws and prohibitions fail to take effect because those above violate them, and that ordinary people dare to act unrighteously because greedy and obstinate officials lead them to do so. Across the vast realm, are there no ministers at court, in the imperial capital, who uphold righteousness and devote themselves wholly to loyalty? Yet neither are there entirely absent those who oppose what their sovereign favors, form factions, and act as enemies. Among the many offices and government departments, are there no officials who faithfully discharge their duties and work harmoniously with their colleagues? Yet neither are there entirely absent those who wield power to intimidate and destroy one another, deceive their sovereign, and pursue private interests. In the cities and provinces, are there no officials who spread imperial beneficence and administer affairs with harmony and kindness? Yet neither are there entirely absent those who depart from the Way to seek praise, draw salaries without performing their duties, and cultivate their reputations. Worse still, there remain those who drain the people's substance to enrich their own households, appropriate their sovereign's honors and favor to expand their own power, steal credit for others' good deeds to display their own generosity, and indulge their private interests to undermine established standards.
Your Majesty honors and treats the great ministers with propriety, drawing ever closer to them as time passes; your considerate understanding of your officials grows deeper and never diminishes. Those worthy ministers who serve as your limbs, whose counsels are enlightened and whose assistance brings harmony, you have indeed cherished with favor and encouraged through ritual propriety. But for these unrepentant men, make punishments clear and enforce the laws: punish one to warn a hundred. This would be like following spring's warmth with the awe-inspiring force of thunder and rain. All under Heaven will then be moved by Your Majesty's benevolence and stand in fear of…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
陛下之法奚爲而不可行乎雖然處今之時勢而
義之所當用者非獨一馭臣爲然也夷狄跳
梁而橫於西北則薄伐之師不可以不整也
庶民僭越而擬於王章則奢汰之禁不可以
不嚴也軍旅疲弊而闕於勇敢則簡閱之令
不可以不怒也凡若此者要皆以精明之治
而敦夫渾厚之體以立君道之紀綱以躋
中興之盛業道莫有先於此者矣抑臣又聞之
仁育而義正者王者之政也所以主是政者
心也故必有純王之心斯有純王之政而憲
===
天之政謂非有敬天之心不可也臣嘗莊誦
陛下敬一之箴而有以知
陛下之心直可以質諸
天地而無疑也有德弗敦是違天之所喜矣敢不
敬歟有惡弗懲是渝天之所怒矣敢不敬歟
以此常存於心兢兢業業罔敢失墜夫然後
以達於政也仁足以育天下而天下莫不歸
於仁義足以正天下而天下莫不彊於義憲
天之政由是而會其全格天之功至是以要
其極矣雖然敬亦未易言也隱微之間真妄

陛下之法，奚爲而不可行乎？雖然，處今之時勢，而義之所當用者，非獨一馭臣爲然也。夷狄跳梁而橫於西北，則薄伐之師不可以不整也；庶民僭越而擬於王章，則奢汰之禁不可以不嚴也；軍旅疲弊而闕於勇敢，則簡閱之令不可以不怒也。凡若此者，要皆以精明之治而敦夫渾厚之體，以立君道之紀綱，以躋中興之盛業，道莫有先於此者矣。
抑臣又聞之：仁育而義正者，王者之政也；所以主是政者，心也。故必有純王之心，斯有純王之政，而憲天之政，謂非有敬天之心不可也。臣嘗莊誦陛下敬一之箴，而有以知陛下之心，直可以質諸天地而無疑也。有德弗敦，是違天之所喜矣，敢不敬歟？有惡弗懲，是渝天之所怒矣，敢不敬歟？以此常存於心，兢兢業業，罔敢失墜，夫然後以達於政也。仁足以育天下，而天下莫不歸於仁；義足以正天下，而天下莫不彊於義。憲天之政，由是而會其全；格天之功，至是以要其極矣。雖然，敬亦未易言也。隱微之間，真妄
translation_en:
… Your Majesty’s laws—what could not be put into effect? Nevertheless, in the circumstances of the present age, the application of righteousness is certainly not confined to controlling ministers. When the foreign peoples run rampant and wreak havoc in the northwest, the forces sent to chastise them must be put in order. When commoners overstep their station and emulate royal distinctions, prohibitions against extravagance must be strictly enforced. When the troops are exhausted and depleted and lack courage, orders for selection and inspection must be made forceful [?]. All such matters require discerning government to strengthen the substantial foundation of generous rule, establish the guiding principles of the sovereign’s way, and attain the great achievement of dynastic resurgence. No course takes precedence over this.
Your servant has also heard this: nurturing through benevolence and correcting through righteousness constitute the government of a true king; what directs this government is the heart. Thus only with the heart of a true king, free of admixture, can there be the government of a true king, free of admixture. Government modeled on Heaven cannot exist without a heart that reveres Heaven. Your servant has solemnly recited Your Majesty’s Admonition on Reverent Unity (Jingyi zhen), and thereby knows that Your Majesty’s heart can indeed be submitted to Heaven and Earth for judgment without doubt. To fail to foster virtue is to oppose what Heaven delights in: dare one be irreverent? To fail to punish evil is to disregard what angers Heaven: dare one be irreverent? Keep this constantly in the heart, vigilant and conscientious, never daring to let it lapse; only then extend it into government. Benevolence will suffice to nurture all under Heaven, and none under Heaven will fail to turn toward benevolence. Righteousness will suffice to rectify all under Heaven, and none under Heaven will fail to exert themselves in righteousness. Government modeled on Heaven will thereby attain its completeness, and the achievement of moving Heaven will thus reach its utmost fulfillment. Nevertheless, reverence is not easily discussed. Amid what is hidden and subtle, the genuine and the false…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
錯雜毫釐之差千里之繆苟辨察之功不悉
於幾微持守之力不繼於厥服則人得以勝
天欲得以奪理又惡知其爲仁而在所當體
惡知其爲義而在所當用也哉故曰勿參以
三勿貳以二行顧其言終如其始靜虛無欲
日新不已然則
陛下之言固可謂能自得師者矣除弊革私之道
仁育義斷之方豈外此而他求乎哉臣始以
仁義並行之道爲
陛下告終以主敬協一之功爲
===
陛下勉初非有驚世可喜之論然直意
陛下以言求士而臣之所以獻言於
陛下者惟以明諸其心上不敢負
明問下不敢負所學而已惟
陛下矜其愚不錄其罪而
留神採納焉臣不勝惓惓隕越之至臣謹對

translation_en:
…are intermingled; a deviation of a hair’s breadth leads to an error of a thousand miles. If the work of discernment does not fully attend to the subtlest beginnings, and the strength to hold fast does not persist in its practice, then the human can overcome Heaven, and desire can displace principle. How, then, could one recognize benevolence as what one ought to embody, or righteousness as what one ought to put into practice? Thus it is said: “Do not introduce a third and make three; do not divide into a second and make two.” Let conduct accord with words, and the end be as the beginning; remain still, empty, and free of desire, renewing oneself daily without cease. Your Majesty’s words may indeed therefore be said to show that you can find a teacher within yourself. How could the way to eliminate abuses and eradicate selfish interests, or the means of nurturing through benevolence and deciding through righteousness, be sought anywhere else?

Your servant began by explaining to Your Majesty the way of practicing benevolence and righteousness together, and concludes by urging Your Majesty to make reverent attentiveness the guiding principle and to strive for unity. From the outset, I have offered no startling arguments calculated to delight the world. I have simply thought that Your Majesty seeks worthy men through their words, and that, in presenting my words to Your Majesty, I seek only to make clear what is in my heart: above, I dare not fail your enlightened inquiry; below, I dare not betray what I have learned. May Your Majesty pity my ignorance, decline to record my offenses, and give these words your attention and accept them. Your servant is overcome with earnest devotion and the utmost trepidation. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
者仁義無偏舉之弊也漢唐宋所以治不古
若者或一於仁或一於義均之各有所失也
欽惟
皇帝陛下剛健純粹之資高明光大之學仁以育
萬民而天下皆覆冒於陽春嫗煦之內義以
正萬民而天下皆震悚於風行電刷之餘道
洽政治大法小廉一十七年于茲矣乃謂承
平既久玩愒或生慨然欲興起而振刷之
萬幾之暇進臣等于
廷而
===
賜之清問臣有以知
陛下之心即天地之於物父母之於子也臣雖至
愚陋敢不撫拾所聞以對乎夫世之稱極治
者曰唐虞曰三代然稽諸往牒考之前聞則
其治道班班可見故稱堯曰其仁如天稱舜
曰其德好生固也然而四凶之誅三苗之伐
其於義未嘗偏廢也稱禹曰文命四敷稱湯
曰德及禽獸稱文武曰仁厚立國固也然五
刑之用五罰之訓八刑之糾其於義亦未嘗
偏廢也雖曰不賞而民勸不怒而民威未施

者，仁義無偏舉之弊也。漢唐宋所以治不古若者，或一於仁，或一於義，均之各有所失也。
欽惟皇帝陛下，剛健純粹之資，高明光大之學，仁以育萬民，而天下皆覆冒於陽春嫗煦之內；義以正萬民，而天下皆震悚於風行電刷之餘。道洽政治，大法小廉，一十七年于茲矣。乃謂承平既久，玩愒或生，慨然欲興起而振刷之。萬幾之暇，進臣等于廷，而賜之清問。臣有以知陛下之心，即天地之於物、父母之於子也。臣雖至愚陋，敢不撫拾所聞以對乎？
夫世之稱極治者，曰唐虞，曰三代。然稽諸往牒，考之前聞，則其治道班班可見。故稱堯曰：「其仁如天。」稱舜曰：「其德好生。」固也。然而四凶之誅、三苗之伐，其於義未嘗偏廢也。稱禹曰：「文命四敷。」稱湯曰：「德及禽獸。」稱文武曰：「仁厚立國。」固也。然五刑之用、五罰之訓、八刑之糾，其於義亦未嘗偏廢也。雖曰不賞而民勸，不怒而民威，未施
translation_en:
…because benevolence and righteousness were free of the fault of emphasizing one at the expense of the other. The reason government under the Han, Tang, and Song did not equal that of antiquity was that they concentrated either on benevolence or on righteousness; each approach had its shortcomings.
We reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses a firm, vigorous, pure disposition and lofty, enlightened, and expansive learning. Through benevolence you nurture the myriad people, and all under Heaven are sheltered within the genial warmth of spring sunshine; through righteousness you set the myriad people straight, and all under Heaven tremble in awe after your wind-swift, lightning-like acts of reform. The Way has spread everywhere and government is well ordered; great officials observe the law and lesser officials maintain integrity. It has now been seventeen years. Yet you consider that, after so long a period of peace, heedlessness and indolence may arise, and you earnestly desire to rouse and reinvigorate the realm. Amid the countless affairs of state, you have summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed these discerning questions upon us. From this I know that Your Majesty's heart is like that of Heaven and Earth toward all things, or of parents toward their children. Though I am exceedingly ignorant and uncultivated, how could I fail to gather what I have heard and offer a reply?
When people speak of the highest excellence in government, they name Tang and Yu, and the Three Dynasties. If we examine the records of the past and investigate what has been transmitted, their way of governing is clearly discernible. Thus Yao is praised with the words, “His benevolence was like Heaven,” and Shun with “His virtue cherished life.” This is certainly true. Yet the punishment of the Four Evildoers and the campaign against the Sanmiao show that righteousness was never neglected. Yu is praised with “His civilizing influence spread to the four quarters”; Tang with “His virtue extended even to birds and beasts”; and Kings Wen and Wu with “They founded their state upon benevolence and generosity.” This too is certainly true. Yet the application of the Five Punishments, instruction in the five penalties, and correction through the eight punishments show that righteousness likewise was never neglected. Although it is said that without rewards the people were encouraged, and without displays of anger the people stood in awe, before putting into effect…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣羅程
臣對臣聞人君法天以爲治有仁以育天下
必有義以裁天下夫天之於物也有春生必
有秋殺有長養必有斂藏非有心於物也公
而已矣不如是不足以爲天之道也人君宰
制天下嚮明而治所以成一統之治繫四海
之心者亦惟法天之公而已矣是故慶賞爵
秩懋官懋祿所以奔走天下之豪傑仁以爲
治猶之天之於物春以生之也威嚴以督責
教戒而懲創所以振起一時之怠惰義以爲
===
治猶之天之於物秋以止之也故一於仁則
流於姑息其失也則縱一於義則流於苛刻
其失也則嚴仁義並用恩威兼舉久安長治
不外是也然仁義之爲施雖殊而君人之爲
心則一是故父母之於子也撫摩而鞠育之
愛也勞苦而鞭策之亦愛也知天之於萬物
之心則知父母於子之心矣知父母於子之
心則知人君於臣之心矣故曰父母愛之喜
而勿忘父母惡之勞而無怨又曰惟天聰明
惟聖時憲唐虞三代所以成雍熈悠久之治

punctuated:
臣羅程。

臣對：臣聞人君法天以爲治，有仁以育天下，必有義以裁天下。夫天之於物也，有春生，必有秋殺；有長養，必有斂藏。非有心於物也，公而已矣。不如是，不足以爲天之道也。人君宰制天下，嚮明而治，所以成一統之治、繫四海之心者，亦惟法天之公而已矣。是故慶賞爵秩，懋官懋祿，所以奔走天下之豪傑，仁以爲治，猶之天之於物，春以生之也；威嚴以督責，教戒而懲創，所以振起一時之怠惰，義以爲治，猶之天之於物，秋以止之也。故一於仁，則流於姑息，其失也則縱；一於義，則流於苛刻，其失也則嚴。仁義並用，恩威兼舉，久安長治，不外是也。然仁義之爲施雖殊，而君人之爲心則一。是故父母之於子也，撫摩而鞠育之，愛也；勞苦而鞭策之，亦愛也。知天之於萬物之心，則知父母於子之心矣；知父母於子之心，則知人君於臣之心矣。故曰：「父母愛之，喜而勿忘；父母惡之，勞而無怨。」又曰：「惟天聰明，惟聖時憲。」唐虞三代所以成雍熈悠久之治
translation_en:
Your servant, Luo Cheng.

Your servant replies: I have heard that the ruler models his governance on Heaven. If he possesses benevolence with which to nurture all under Heaven, he must also possess righteousness with which to regulate all under Heaven. In Heaven’s dealings with things, where there is generation in spring, there must be destruction in autumn; where there is growth and nurture, there must be gathering and storing away. Heaven has no deliberate designs upon things: it is simply impartial. Without this, it would not suffice to constitute the Way of Heaven. The ruler governs all under Heaven, facing the light as he attends to government. What enables him to achieve unified rule and bind together the hearts of all within the Four Seas is simply his emulation of Heaven’s impartiality. Thus, rewards and ranks, offices and stipends bestowed upon the worthy, serve to rally the outstanding men of the realm to his service. Governing through benevolence is like Heaven bringing things to life in spring. Exercising stern authority to supervise and hold men accountable, instructing and admonishing them, and punishing them as a deterrent serve to rouse the indolent of the age. Governing through righteousness is like Heaven bringing things to a halt in autumn. Hence, exclusive reliance on benevolence descends into indulgence, its failing being laxity; exclusive reliance on righteousness descends into harshness, its failing being excessive severity. Lasting peace and enduring good government require nothing beyond employing benevolence and righteousness together and exercising both kindness and authority. Although benevolence and righteousness differ in their application, the ruler’s underlying intention is one and the same. Thus, when parents caress and nurture their children, this is love; when they make them toil and discipline them with the rod, this too is love. Understanding Heaven’s intention toward the myriad things, one understands parents’ intention toward their children; understanding parents’ intention toward their children, one understands the ruler’s intention toward his ministers. Thus it is said: “When your parents love you, rejoice and do not forget them; when your parents dislike you, toil without resentment.” It is also said: “Heaven alone is clear-sighted and keen of hearing; the sage alone models himself upon it.” The means by which the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties achieved harmonious, flourishing, and enduring government…

title: 嘉靖十七年進士登科錄
text:
信而民信未施敬而民敬而威克愛克剛克
柔克威福予奪抑揚進退一張一弛以撫世
酬物者固未嘗得此而失彼舉一而廢一也
故天有陰而無陽則所以覆萬物者或幾乎
息矣地有柔而無剛則所以載萬物者或幾
乎息矣君人者仁而不足於義何以贊天地
之化育以並立而爲三哉傳曰刑罰不可弛
於國征伐不可弛於天下鞭扑不可弛於家
彼以去義爲言是豈知治體之所尚乎又有
王者尚德緩刑之說聖人遭時定制之說是
===
曲儒之偏見而不知聖人爲治大中至正之
道也夫人之情大抵樂放肆而惡撿束喜便
安而厭準繩不知人君所以馭臣下者仁與
義而已矣仁非姑息之謂也所以結其心也
義非慘刻之謂也所以閑其邪也三后成功
惟殷于民士制百姓以教祗德穆穆明明惟
德之勤率乂于民以棐其彝古之聖帝明王
豈不欲與天下相安於無事哉知天下之君
子固常多而小人亦不少知天下之慕仁者
固常多而不畏義者亦不少故仁義並用威

Whether prevailing through awe or love, firmness or gentleness, those who govern the world and respond to affairs through punishments and rewards, giving and taking away, lowering and raising, advancing and withdrawing, tightening and relaxing, have never gained one at the expense of the other or employed one while discarding the other. Thus, if Heaven possessed yin without yang, its capacity to cover the myriad things would almost cease; if Earth possessed softness without firmness, its capacity to bear the myriad things would almost cease. If a ruler possesses benevolence but lacks righteousness, how can he assist the transforming and nurturing powers of Heaven and Earth and stand alongside them as a third? The tradition says: “Punishments must not be relaxed within the state, punitive expeditions must not be relaxed throughout the realm, and flogging must not be relaxed within the household.” Those who advocate dispensing with righteousness—how can they understand what is essential to the proper conduct of government? There are also arguments that a true king esteems virtue and mitigates punishments, and that sages establish institutions according to the circumstances of their age. These are the partial views of narrow-minded scholars who do not understand the sages’ way of governing through perfect balance and utmost rectitude.
Human feelings generally incline toward license and dislike restraint, delight in ease and comfort and detest rules and standards. People do not understand that the means by which a ruler governs his subjects are simply benevolence and righteousness. Benevolence does not mean indulgence: it is the means of binding their hearts to him. Righteousness does not mean cruelty: it is the means of restraining their wrongdoing. “The three sovereigns accomplished their work by attending diligently to the people. They knew that although gentlemen were always numerous in the realm, petty men were also far from few; they knew that although those who admired benevolence were always numerous, those who did not fear righteousness were also far from few. text:
惠並舉仁以主之義以輔之惠以維之威以
懾之無偏而不全之敝固不一於仁而忘乎
義也有兼而並用之美固不專乎威而弛乎
惠也唐虞尚矣夏之四百商之六百周之八
百且過其歷何莫而不本於此哉是雖三代
之人心忠信誠愨而三代之英君誼辟所以
維持天下之具防範人心之道者則一言以
蔽之曰仁與義而已矣臣嘗觀之天下之日
趨於變也猶江河之日趨於下也然挽而回
之其機端有在也我
===

休德百工既已惟時庶績既已惟凝軼唐虞三

祖宗矣而恬嬉之念猶不忘焉

國之禮度其何賴焉
宵旰勤勞視民如子而司民牧者恬不加意此
